Amazing experience. Stardew Valley is a game where you can cozy up and take your time, build friendships, and contribute (heavily) to the community around you in a variety of ways. You could also speedrun to your heart's content, and challenge yourself in the pits of darkness slaying foes, gathering every item and resource, completing every milestone and achievement that there is to offer (if you dare to go for the last two achievements in this game...wishing you the best of luck). There are numerous opportunities with every new farm you start, so things don't feel too repetitive. It's not hard to find different ways to spice up your playstyle or goals and experiences for a new farm.

There are also options with playing the game vanilla, or adding mods to your experience. But nonetheless, if you enjoy cozier games that let you take your time, cultivate a farm and enrich the community around you; and can also challenge you in some unexpected ways, depending on your approach, you'll likely enjoy this game. 

Whenever things get tough and some distraction is needed from the real world to level your head, Stardew is usually the first place many people go to, including myself. Stardew Valley can give people a space of comfort in today's world. And the authentic creativity required to make this game is a joy to see, and respectable.

I miiiiiiight have gotten slightly addicted to this game, but in my defense, it's tons of fun. The graphics are incredible, the music rocks, and the open world lets you go at your own pace. You can farm crops as well as raise animals (I recently got the Deluxe Barn and a sheep let's go); depending on how you play and what you want to accomplish, there isn't a "wrong" way to go about playing the game.

There are several advancements that keep you from getting bored. Without getting into spoilers, you can mine in the caves, develop friendships and romance, forage for wild plants, and even fish. (I am terrible at the fishing minigame, but maybe you won't be!) There's also the option to forage around in trashcans if you wish to do a bit of trolling.

There's a loose overarching story, but day-to-day life consists of working on your farm, mining, etc. It definitely lives up to its cozy reputation, but there are some deeper elements thrown in there such as an evil corporation and more somber elements in some characters' arcs. You're not being railroaded into liking a certain character or doing a certain thing on a certain day (other than celebrating festivals, but you technically don't HAVE to go to those). So yeah, I'd say this game is pretty lit.

Too addictive. Vanilla has enough interesting content to keep you hooked on for hours, and if you're bored of the main game, then the mods you can add can overhaul the game massively. Every aspect of the game is just perfect, be it the skill set (Farming, Fishing, Fighting, etc) to the relationship system with the Villager's, there is truly no end to a Stardew save.

Somewhere between 350 and 480 hours depending on how Steam decides to count it. Either number is more than anything else in my library, and I have a lot of games in there that I love. I want to be clear about what that number is not. It is not because Stardew is the deepest game I own, or the hardest, or the one with the best story. It is because it is the one I can always come back to. Bad week, nothing else clicking, brain fried from work, I load the farm and I know exactly what I am doing for the next two hours and I know I am going to feel better at the end of it. There are maybe three games in my life that can do that reliably and this is the one that has done it the longest.

The thing people get wrong when they call it a cozy game is that it is actually a planning game wearing a cozy game as a coat. Every season is a deadline. Crops have a window and if you plant the wrong thing on the wrong day you eat the loss. The mines have a rhythm, the deeper floors want you to come prepared, and the first time you figure out which floors the iron actually lives on you feel like you unlocked something. The community center is a checklist that quietly organizes your entire first year without ever telling you it is doing that. And every single day, every day, you are making small tradeoffs about energy and daylight that add up. Do I water or do I fish. Do I go to the mines or do I talk to someone. Do I spend the money on seeds or do I save it for the building. None of those decisions are big. All of them matter. That is the exact part of my brain that Factorio and Timberborn and Banished scratch, it is just running at a slower heartbeat here, and that slower heartbeat is why I can play it when I cannot play anything else.

The farm is never finished. That is the hook and it never dulls. There is always one more building you want, one more sprinkler layout that would save you a trip, one more thing you need to fix before winter, one more villager you have not actually talked to. The game gives you a space and a clock and a hundred ways to spend both, and it does not grade you. You can minmax it into a greenhouse money printer or you can wander around fishing for a season because you felt like it and the game is equally happy. I have done both. I have had farms I laid out like a spreadsheet and farms I let grow weird and ugly and loved more. It meets you wherever you are that week.

Then there is the question of who made it. One guy. One guy built this, scored it, drew it, wrote every villager, and has kept it alive for a decade without charging for it twice. The 1.6 update dropped years after launch and added a whole new layer to a game people already thought was done. Green rain, new events, new fish, new reasons to go back. He just handed it to everyone. I am not sentimental about developers but I think that matters, and I think you can feel it in the game. Nothing in Stardew is there because a meeting decided it should be. It is all there because one person thought it would be nice. That is a different texture than a game made by a hundred people and you notice it.

I will say one honest thing against it. The first spring is slow, on purpose, and if you come in expecting the game to tell you what it is about you will bounce. It does not explain itself. It just hands you a watering can and some parsnip seeds and lets you figure out that the real game starts once you have a little money and a little confidence and a reason to care about the people in town. Push through to summer. It opens up.

If you have never played it, play it. If you have played it, you already know everything I just said and you probably have your own version of the bad week story. That is kind of the point. Shout out to ConcernedApe.

This game is The Best Game In Existence. Hands down. Literally the only game that I have absolutely zero complaints about the game play itself, and absolutely love the story. 

The very few complaints I had earlier in the game's existence, have all been fixed in subsequent patches (thank you for making snake tail skeletons easier to find, omg that was giving me the irrates!!)

I only have one serious complaint, and it relates to ableism in the story. I have a big issue with the cut scene between Penny and George, and to a lesser extent between Harvey and George:

The player arrives to see George struggling to reach something, and then Penny walks in and just does it for him, without asking whether he wants help. For those of us in the disabled community, we know just how frustrating an experience this can be. You should ask us before getting involved! Maybe we would like some help, but it removes our power over our own lives when people don't even ask what we want. 

George's reaction to get angry about this is completely natural and understandable. However, if the player sides with George in the resulting dialogue, we lose friendship points with Penny and gain nothing with George. 

Penny being the sort of ernest and caring person she is, I feel would actually want to be educated about how things are for disabled people, and how important it is to respect our agency and autonomy. I wouldn't necessarily expect to gain friendships points with her for giving her the critical feedback, but I really don't think we should be penalised for taking the ethicial dialogue option. 

Similarly, when Harvey is giving George his doctor's recommendations, I chose the option to tell Harvey that the choice of how he lives his life is ultimately up to George - and lost friendship points with Harvey for it. 

I just skip both these scenes every time now. 

I deeply love and appreciate Eric Baroney and this masterpiece of a game he has created. But I would truly love it if he could learn a bit about issues facing disabled people, and help advocate for us in his dialogue options and resulting bonuses. At the very least, supporting George should earn us friendship points with him, surely??

Also minor spoilers

Stardew Valley was released at a time when there was a long drought of Harvest Moon games (just as Story of Seasons split from HM), and was released before the "comfy" genre was birthed.  In fact SDV could be considered the "father" of the indie comfy game genre.  Unfortunately this means everything that made the game appealing on release has been iterated and improved upon by games made in the 10 years since its release.

For the moment-to-moment gameplay, these types of games structure their mechanics so there's a kind of "interdependency" of progress.  There might be 3-5-ish activities to progress in, and things unlocked in one activity allow the player to progress in another.  In SDV there's essentially 2, time and money.  Progress on getting new animals or collecting a specific bundle of items for the community center (the game's "main story" objective) either come down to grinding enough money or waiting for the correct season to begin.

What this means is that you almost never think to yourself "once I finish making X item it will unlock Y and allow me to Z" and instead think "If I rewater my crops and make mayonnaise for another week I can buy a barn so I can add making cheese to my morning routine".  By the end of Spring year 1 when the player has the basics of crops/fishing/mining/chickens/gift-giving figured out the gameplay loop is basically 100% complete and doesn't evolve or change in any noticeable way for the rest of the game.  You will be poking all your farm animals and replanting crops every morning in year 1 and will still be doing it in year 10.  The only change you can make is having crops auto-watered with sprinklers and having the animals auto-fed and their resources auto-collected with a few upgrades, reducing the monotony somewhat.

The crop variety especially suffers under this system.  The game has a pretty big variety of crops and lots of different dishes the player can make but they're mostly useless.  Outside of harvesting a single batch of a plant for the community center, recipe, or 1-off quest the only thing that matters is the how much the crop makes. This means there's only really 3 crops worth bothering with (1 for each season minus winter) and then only 1 crop once you get the greenhouse and can grow it year-round.

The biggest issue I had with the game though, were the caves.  In order to get metals like copper or iron which the player needs for a ton of recipes and upgrades they have to go into a cave north of the town.  It's a 100~ish level dungeon with an unlockable elevator every 5 floors and the player is encouraged to complete it.  The combat is bad.  This game has some similarities to Terraria but I've never played it so instead I'll have to compare it to Minecraft.  The combat is worse than Minecraft.  It's more awkward and less fluid than Minecraft which isn't exactly known for having good combat to begin with.  There's lot's of annoying things like the player changing attack direction feeling stiff, enemies and hitboxes being obscured by walls due to the art style, it's not a fun time.   And yet, in order to get access to material like gold, the player is expected to spend way more time grinding dungeon floors than they'll spend actually running their farm.  If I had to split my game time up by percents 30% of the time was probably spent farming/foraging/fishing, 10% spent on gift giving and organizing community bundles, and 60% of my time was spent just on the caves.  The worst part is even after you finish it you're not free, there's several more 100 floor dungeons to discover with harder enemies and more annoying mechanics.

Also the gamepad controls are bad.  Navigating the crafting menu and aiming your slingshot are a nightmare.  The left and bottom face buttons (X and A on xbox) are both inconsistently used as interact/use/confirm buttons which makes things awkward when you're trying to put the milk in the cheesemaker and not drink it or pulling hay out of the haybale.  Neatly separating them to "use equipped item" and "interact with world" inputs would've gone a long way to make things less frustrating.  There's really no excuse for the UI navigation though.

That being said I didn't 100% hate my time with this game, it definitely has a certain charm only a game made by 1 dude purely out of passion can afford.  There's lots of secrets and easter eggs to discover, there's plenty of post-game activities, the game seems comfortable allowing the player to engage with the story/social aspect or completely ignoring it as they see fit.  The game has massive mod support for pretty much anything (I only used the "show NPCs on the map" mod since finding people is a nightmare without it).  But in Anno Domini 2026+, with all of the available options on the market, Stardew Valley looks very plain and repetitive by comparison.  In a lot of ways a victim of its own success, I don't even think modern Story of Seasons games would sell as well if SDV didn't show up to remind everyone why we like these kinds of experiences to begin with.

★★★★★ — I came for the farming. I stayed for the emotional damage.

Bought this game thinking I'd live a peaceful little cottagecore life, grow some vegetables, pet some animals, and maybe fall in love.

Now I'm micromanaging a winery, interrogating trees for their resin, hoarding rocks like a Victorian chimney sweep, and planning my entire financial future around the production of alcohol.

The villagers have more emotional baggage than a Dostoevsky protagonist, the economy is somehow dependent on turning fruit into wine, and I have developed an unhealthy attachment to a man who spends his time in a basement and looks like he listens to Radiohead.

I have spent five in-game days decorating my farm. FIVE. DAYS. And I'm still not done.

The mines? Terrifying. The fishing? Surprisingly addictive. The Community Center? A full-time administrative position. The crafting system? My personal nemesis.

And yet, every time I tell myself I'll play for just twenty minutes, it's suddenly 3 AM and I'm researching whether cranberries are more profitable as jelly or dried fruit.

This isn't a farming simulator. It's a lifestyle.

10/10. Would neglect my responsibilities for a fictional rural economy again.

This game has a lot of content and it took me a long time to beat.  When I say "beat," I mean "perfect."  Because the only way to really beat the game is to 100% it, which is very time-consuming.

There's not really much of a story except for at the beginning.  Otherwise, you basically just build up your life, family, friends and town.  There are really only two mutually exclusive choices to make, but they mostly lead to similar outcomes, and the rewards are different.

When starting the game, you can choose what kind of farm you want between a regular farm, beach farm, a forage farm, a farm with monsters, etc.  The goal is still the same; sow, harvest, get paid.

I lost track of how many quests there were, mostly because a lot of them repeat.  If I were to summarize it into different parts, I'd limit it to the following:  Farming, mining, relationships and community.

Farming is what you would think; grow crops, build coops and stables, care for animals, produce artisan goods, craft stuff, cook dishes, etc.

Mining is more of the adventurous and combative part of the game where you explore the floors of mines, fight enemies, find rare resources and artifacts, forge, find and upgrade weapons, etc.

Relationships involve the local and non-local citizens.  Talking to them, gifting them things they like or completing quests for them increase your relationship.  In contrast, saying mean things, hitting trashcans in front of them, or gifting them things they don't like will decrease your relationship.  There are events that happen at various times and places once you've reached a certain relationship threshold with a particular person and it reveals a little more depth to their lives and develops their character further.  There are bachelors and bachelorettes that can be romanced and eventually married, after which they move in with you, enabling you to have/adopt up to 2 children.  Some of this cannot be done until you've upgraded your house sufficiently.  There are a number of characters that are either already married or cannot otherwise be romanced.  There are mods that can change this, FYI.  I didn't use any of them, for the record.

The community-related part of the game involves developments that improve things around town, like fixing buses, boats or bridges that lead to new places, fixing the greenhouse on your property for indoor farming, removing rocks so that ore and minerals flow through the town's water, etc.  This is the part where there are two mutually exclusive ways to go about it.  The developer has made it very apparent that one of these ways is their preferred way, and is a lot more in-depth and time-consuming in nature.  The other way is more efficient, but is made to feel more empty in the end.  Some of the new places revealed by these developments are beyond the local town, and there are different caves, mines, farms, people and quests to work with.  Like I said, this game has a lot of content.

I can see why so many people like this game.  I'd say the unfortunate part for me was that I got overwhelmed at one point and had to put it down.  I came back a few years later to complete it.  It's difficult to do this, however, because I had to remember how everything worked and how I left things originally. 

Anyway, I think most adventure gamers, or people who like games such as Terraria or Minecraft would enjoy this game a lot.

Feels silly to leave a review on a game so well known as this, but gotta let CA know I appreciate his attitude towards fans. 

Lots of replayability because you can decide if you want to prioritize money, friendships, or resources at the start of your run as well as farm layouts, marriage options, pets/farm animals, etc. 

It's no secret that a lot of us hate the fishing mechanic so it would be nice if there was an option to adjust it outside of rod and equipment purchases. However there is a way to get to level 5 fishing without fishing much or using mods.

Community Center Completion tip: [spoiler]I complete bundles the best I can/want to for easy rewards/farm help and then purchase the joja membership and pay to complete the remaining ones (it's the fish tank lets be honest). Membership fee is still the same but you only have to pay to complete bundles you haven't already completed so the overall cost is much less than if purchased from the beginning. It will no longer be a community center but a joja mart warehouse or whatever, so be sure to consider that. [/spoiler]

Mastering Fishing: [spoiler]Use the crab pots and just fish wherever it's easiest for you to do so. Better rods and bait/bobbers are available eventually to help further. The REAL way to quickly do this is read books. The fishing books help obviously BUT there are a handful of books that will send xp points to other skills if the main skill it's meant to benefit is maxed. I mastered fishing this way within 4years without prioritizing it. Bookseller and traveling cart merchant are where to go. [/spoiler]

Pretty much anything else can be modded and CA has always openly supported the mod community. I recommend playing without mods as long as possible to best understand the game as many popular mods add a lot of new content and it can be overwhelming for new players.

Stardew Valley is not just a game; it is a pure emotion. My journey to finally playing this masterpiece has been nothing short of a roller-coaster ride, and it truly tested my patience as a gamer.
I waited from July 9th all the way until October 1st at 10:30 PM just to catch a single glimpse of this game. During this long, agonizing wait, watching YouTube videos of the game every single night became my daily ritual, which only fueled my excitement even further.
However, the biggest setback hit me on September 4th when my Steam account was hacked. I was devastated. Honestly, I had the choice to easily download a cracked or pirated version of the game to bypass the trouble, but I chose not to. I wanted to respect the immense hard work of the solo developer (ConcernedApe) and support the game the right way.
Now that I am finally playing it, I can proudly say that every single day of waiting was absolutely worth it. The soothing music, the cozy atmosphere, the farming, and the beautiful pixel art completely transport you into a different, peaceful world.

I brushed this game off as overhyped for almost a decade. I even took a bit of pride in not liking it, as it’s such a beloved game. I knew I was going against the grain by saying it “wasn’t for me.” And I’ve always enjoyed standing out from the crowd.

Clearly, I regret that now.

It’s been in my library since my college roommate made me buy it in 2019, but for the first 6 years I could claim about 60 minutes of playtime, and all of that was creating my character and wandering around the farm for the first day wondering what to do. We realized after I bought it that we couldn’t collab using a Switch and a PC, unfortunately. So I never touched it again.

Until I got bored last year and my friend wanted to play multiplayer. 

I’ve now put in over 500 hours on my Steam Deck and another 500 hours on my Switch, where I first fell in love with it.

I have made a different character to explore and flesh out every farm type, memorized the Community Center bundles and every loved gift, and dated all the candidates as of 1.6. I still need to marry some of them though… I’ve also gotten every achievement if you pretend that those stupid arcade games don’t exist.

I’ve not only spent over a thousand hours playing this game, but I’m sure I’ve spent something close to that watching other people play it, too. I love Salmence and NinoKito. Mod exploration is also hilarious, though I’m not interested in doing it myself. The fact that a VANILLA game can be so interesting that you can easily sink 1,000 hours into it is a testament to the skills of one man: Eric Barone… and the quality of the friends you play with, of course.

I haven’t fallen this deeply in love with a game since I discovered Terraria as an 11 year old. I feel like a kid again when I play Stardew. I will chase that feeling until it disappears. But with games like Fields of Mistria coming out ten years later, being so clearly inspired by a burning passion to make Stardew but better, I can say with confidence that I don’t believe that day will ever come.

This is a great little fun and quirky life-sim game.  It includes farming, fishing, mining, socializing with NPCs, and even combat.  You can play this game at your own pace, hard or casually, if you like.  The game offers a multiplayer co-op option without a PVP mode.  

Stardew Valley offers a day/night mechanic separate from real-world time and the ability to create multiple play throughs without deleting previous runs.  The one downside that I have with this game is that saving only occurs at the conclusion of the in-game day.  So closing the game during a play through can cause you to lose your progress for that day... for better or for worse.

As of today, its creator, ConcernedApe, is still coming out with updates and has not announced a conclusion to the game.

Been a huge fan of the farming/life game genre since the OG, Harvest Moon on the SNES, the first game that started the farming genre afaik.  It may seem weird to some people, a game about doing chores... Played many other Harvest Moon, Rune Factory, and the subsequent Story of Seasons/HM split games along with some other titles to death and tried many others before and since SDV.  Despite all my forays, SDV remains the best farming game ever made imo, even now 10 years later.  

It helps that the fanbase is so huge and it was such a ridiculous success.  Hard to imagine only one man built this masterpiece.  Because of its popularity there seem to be thousands of mods, some being expansion mods which drastically change the game and story, others utility and QoL, others visuals, theres even a pron mod (XXX) that I would never get due to morality and silliness....so that you can create your own new experience.

I had spent about 200 hours in it 7 years ago, 7 years later I came back to experience the updates I had missed out on in the Vanilla over that time period.  I did get a few mods but mostly utility, QoL and visual mods.  Still as addictive as the first time I played it. 

I guess its not for everyone, but this is one of the greatest games ever made even if you dont like this niche.  Have not been playing anything else for a few weeks now again...from reading update/patch notes there was a ton added since my last playthrough and an endgame that is much more fleshed out as it seems.

Compared to other big name farm titles, like Fields of Mistria, this game just has such a richness and depth, and a charm with the beautiful pixel art, that other games which are touted as being equals pale in comparison.  I was disappointed with Fields of Mistria, and some others; SDV just seems so massively superior in so many ways.

Highly recommend, even if you are into hyper realistic violent shooters or something, I trust many people are eclectic gamers and should at least try it.  One of my all time faves and its a blast to come back to it.

A game that no longer needs introduction or praise to demonstrate the value it holds; it's reputation precedes it. Still, I just want to take the time to thank ConcernedApe for creating this genuine masterpiece of a game and providing free, meaningful updates to it after all these years. It's found you success and it couldn't be more deserved.

This game is fun to both min-max and relax in, a game that can actually get me and my partner sitting down to play together, good to get groups of friends joined in on a game, fantastic at making memories, and has a brilliant modding scene to support it. I have many hours here and many more on the switch copy, and I suspect that even after all this time, I'll still be finding new ways to approach the game.

The game is also accessible, both in terms of being able to run it, and that you don't need to be a 'gamer' to get into it. I have played with people that have a difficulty with controls able to find themselves enjoying it and getting better at it.

If I had to make some suggestions for what I would want to see out of the game, as someone who has played thoroughly, I'd start with cleaning up the interface/menus. There's a bit of charm to the wonkiness of changing controls and the crafting menu, but I find that more often than not, I struggle to find the option I need, or select the crafting recipe I'm aiming for. I believe this change would be a positive change for most. I also think a custom game option would be fun- I know there's some changes you can make when creating a farm, but expanding on this would be nice for players looking for a shift in the game's pacing.

If you're still looking for a reason to purchase and try the game; just go for it. The amount of time you get out of the game versus the price tag is a really good ratio. The core gameplay loop is addicting, and I've found that some players really prefer different elements of gameplay, and at least one will really grab you.

💜 TOM RECOMMENDS

Before anything else, a little context for the playtime shown above. At the time of writing I have just under three hours recorded on this PC version of Stardew Valley, but this isn't my first time on the farm. I originally played on Xbox around the time the game was released and put well over 200 hours into it there.

For some reason that I genuinely can't remember, I never actually finished that original journey.

So, many years later, I'm starting again.

And within minutes of arriving back in Stardew Valley, I remembered exactly why I spent so much time here in the first place.

🌱 What I love most about Stardew Valley is that it lets me play Stardew Valley.

That probably sounds like a ridiculous statement, but it's important to me. I don't feel as though the game is constantly trying to dictate what I should be doing. I can wake up planning to clear part of the farm, become distracted by something in town, decide to do some fishing, wander off exploring and eventually crawl into bed having achieved absolutely none of the things I'd originally intended.

And I've still had a good day.

There are crops to grow, fish to catch, mines to explore, things to craft, people to meet, relationships to build and an initially rather sorry-looking farm waiting to become whatever I decide to make of it.

But I don't need to rush any of it.

🏡 That's perhaps even more important to me returning to Stardew Valley now than it was when I first played it. I have absolutely no interest in creating the most efficient farm possible, following somebody else's perfect route or squeezing maximum profit out of every waking minute.

I'm going to potter.

I'll grow things because I fancy growing them. I'll rearrange something because I don't like where I originally put it. I'll probably spend entire days doing something completely unnecessary simply because it caught my attention.

And Stardew Valley is perfectly happy to let me.

🍂 I'm also returning after years of updates, so there's a lovely mixture of familiarity and discovery. I recognise the world I spent hundreds of hours enjoying, while knowing there's now plenty waiting for me that I've never experienced before.

That's a rather wonderful position to be in.

Stardew Valley doesn't need another review explaining why it became one of the best-known farming life sims ever made. Millions of players have already discovered their own reasons for loving it.

Mine is quite simple.

💜 Stardew Valley gives me a world where I can slow down, make something my own and spend an evening doing whatever happens to make me happy.

My only real complaint is that there aren't enough hours in the day to play games like this for as long as I'd like.

This time I'm also determined to find out where the journey eventually leads.

I'm in absolutely no hurry to get there, though.

After all, the farm will still be there tomorrow. 🌱

[b]My score: 10/10[/b]
⭐ [b]TL;DR:[/b] The gold standard of cozy and farming games. Unmatched in variety, depth and sheer amount of content, with enough freedom to make the game whatever you want it to be.

🟦 [b]NOTE:[/b] Although I only had around 30 hours on Steam at the time of writing, I've played hundreds of hours on other platforms over the years.

[h2]Overview[/h2]
The best game in its genre, hands down. There's really very little to say: [i]Stardew Valley[/i] is the modern benchmark for cozy and farming games, and I don't think there's anything else on the market that matches its variety, mechanical depth and sheer amount of content.

And, much like [i]No Man's Sky[/i] (read my review [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/averagemage/recommended/275850/]🔗here[/url]), this is a game that has received constant free updates for ten years, with more still to come. That's an absurd amount of value for a game that already had plenty to offer at launch.

[h2]One Thing I Liked / One Thing I Didn't[/h2]
✔️ [b]Liked:[/b] The sheer flexibility. You can take your time, plan a speedrun to wealth, become a farmer, a rancher, a fisherman, an explorer, or even treat the whole thing like a dating sim. The game rarely tells you how you're supposed to play it.
✖️ [b]Didn't:[/b] The late game can get a little too grindy for my taste.

[h2]Key Points[/h2]
[list]
[*][h3]DIFFICULTY:[/h3] Highly customizable. There is combat and there are time-based challenges, but there are virtually no penalties for ignoring them or coming back when you're better equipped. You can set your own pace and choose how much challenge you want.
[*][h3]PRESENTATION:[/h3] Don't let the almost amateurish-looking sprites and environments fool you: that naïve charm is an integral part of the game's visual identity and remains remarkably consistent. The soundtrack is beautifully composed, with several tracks already considered classics, while the sound effects have been copied by countless other games in the genre.
[*][h3]STORY:[/h3] A classic farming game/cozy game with an ongoing narrative and a touch of magic. The real strength of its story and relationships is that every player gets to experience them differently.
[*][h3]GAMEPLAY:[/h3] You can genuinely do almost anything. If you like fighting, you can fight. If you like fishing, you can fish. If you like exploring, there's plenty to explore. If you like challenges, you have plenty to tackle. If you just want to take it easy, nobody is stopping you.
[*][h3]TECHNICAL POLISH:[/h3] Aside from a few glitches that can occasionally be useful, the game is surprisingly clean and elegant under the hood. Controls and collisions are consistently reliable, and the systems work together with an impressive level of polish, especially considering [b]the game was developed primarily by one person[/b].
[*][h3]MONEYxCONTENT VALUE:[/h3] Absolutely worth it. At €14, it's practically a steal, and there's no real reason to wait for a sale. There's simply too much game here for the price.
[/list]

🟪 [b]NOTE:[/b] If you're into mods, it's worth knowing that ConcernedApe has always been very active in keeping updates compatible with the modding scene. There are countless mods available to refresh or expand the experience, and many of them remain compatible even after major updates. That's a big plus for a developer who clearly understands the needs of PC players.

Personally, I've put off stardew valley for a long time, mainly due to the fact that new games keep appearing and I never got the downtime to try it, but upon now playing it, I must say I wish I got into it earlier.

While writing this, I'm currently into what most would consider the end game of stardew, with everything unlocked and just getting money for a few endgame items. I intend to do a second run as it is required to get all achievements for this game and I do quite enjoy it and want to continue playing.

Now to the actual review, while most people would consider stardew valley a farming simulator, I wouldn't really say so, the reason being that my entire first 2 years of stardew valley(in game years) had minimal farming. Instead I would say its more of an RPG. It has all the essential elements of an RPG, such as levelling skills, different "routes" you could take, NPC quest, unlockables, a story(ish), etc. Without going into too much spoilers, there are essentially 5 "main routes" you can take your character, combat, mining, farming, foraging and fishing. Each of these are a solid choice to start off and there are even certain farm types(a choice u make at the start) that complement certain classes. That being said, you will eventually be able to level up all of them, it just depends on which you focus on first.

In my honest opinion, Stardew felt quite overwhelming at the start, being given too much freedom is often a double-edged sword, and I think stardew is one of the games that suffer from this. This was my second attempt at picking stardew up, and since then I've had a policy of forcing myself through the game awhile before deciding to drop it, and I'm really glad I did, because once the gameplay loop started to make more sense to me, it all clicked. There's nothing that you NEED to do, theres nothing that is on a strict time limit(except for the reoccuring daily and weekly quest), so there really is no rush, and I feel thats the best part about this game, you can take your time and do whatever you want with it, you can choose to optimize fully or just make things look pretty, the choice is yours.

Wow…I don’t know where to begin. I’m VERY late to the party, one might say. 
I recently finished school and lost my job at the same time. I was at a really low point in my life. Usually video games bring me comfort, but nothing in my library was doing that for me. I became really depressed. Stardew valley had been on my wishlist for YEARS, and it was the only game that was different enough for me to even want to try it. The reviews were good and it looked like a simple cozy game I’d maybe play for a few hours, get lost in, and then quickly get bored of. I was wrong! It immediately drew me in with its simple mechanics and complex characters. (I say simple mechanics because I have played many survival games in the past, including Rust, Sons of the forest, and seven days to die. I am not saying this game is too basic by any means)  I was genuinely surprised by how in depth everything was. I found myself wanting to learn more about the characters and the world around them. I could relate to many of them. Harvey and Shane to be more specific. The farm became more of a farm to me. It became something I was actively building, coexisting with the real life I was trying to rebuild. I know there are dozens of reviews like mine, and I’m being completely honest when I say this game changed my life. It changed my perspective. It gave me hope. It made me want to write  and draw again. (Fanfics and fanart) Something that I had been missing and no longer had energy for, from being so burnt out from everything that was happening to me. Playing stardew valley between job applications and interviews helped me stay positive and have something to look forward to when things didn’t go as planned. I eventually did end up getting a job, and things did start working out. It took time. And while I am still working towards ‘Perfection’ in the game, I am also learning that my own life doesn’t have to be perfect, it just has to be lived.
Thank you ConcernedApe for helping an anxious depressed fellow find his motivation to create again. Follow your passion. Things will get better. There is always someone out there who cares. The world is a better place with you in it.

“Stardew Valley” is a great game that feels very different depending on whether you play solo or with a friend or two. Alone, it has a lot of things to do and master, like fishing and farming, while you work to get to know the villagers and find someone to marry. But there’s a point when it starts to feel drawn out once you’ve mastered most skills and maxed affection with your chosen love interest. Meanwhile, with friends, it can keep you engaged for hundreds of hours easily. (8/10)

As a result, I’d recommend the game more if you intend to play with friends, but that doesn’t mean it’s not worth it for solo play as well. Just don’t expect quite the same longevity unless you really enjoy repeating the same tasks for years on end. If you do, then hunting for all achievements and reaching self-set goals should provide hundreds of hours of fun regardless.

The pace of the in-game clock is very rushed. That’s a feature, and many will enjoy it, but I never liked how quickly the days pass. Often, it feels like by the time you reach the beach for a day of fishing, it’s already time to turn back. Much of the game’s difficulty comes from the few hours you really have at your disposal to get things done, at least until your farm is automated with sprinklers and other upgrades.

The rewards for the different skills also aren’t particularly balanced. You can spend all day fishing, and even fish that are difficult to catch won’t compare to the massive income you get from crops once your farm is running smoothly. You’re clearly meant to invest in all aspects of the game and not focus too much on any one thing. But this is where the online aspect shines. Your friend can handle the farming or whatever suits them, while you focus on the parts you find most enjoyable. (8/10)

I truly believe above all else that Stardew Valley is a cosy farming game of its own calibre; with so many other avenues and aspects to explore, it almost leaves you with the same singular thought with each passing day: "One more"—one more day, one more task, action or upcoming event. It can be both relaxing and engaging, where you can play as if you're racing against the clock or at a leisurely pace, and either way is neither wrong nor right.
The game begins with your character seeking to break from the chains of your boring 9-5 office job, seeking refuge in the countryside town called Pelican Town where your grandfather spent his final days before entrusting the unkempt farm to you. It pairs a simple but interesting style of progression where doing more than just farming will unlock more ways to produce different products, from cooked foods and artisan goods to animal products, in a constant escalation of progress that feels fulfilling and rewarding. Though the game supports multiplayer, which I highly recommend with a friend or loved one, you can definitely go your own path if you wish. I thoroughly enjoyed everything about this game, if my hours weren't proof enough, and I suspect that in the future I may continue to play this from time to time. I just wanted to note that with each game I play, I find a deeper appreciation for indie developers and still find it inspiring how even a single person can make such a vivid and inviting world.

I honestly didn't expect to get this attached to a farming game, but Stardew Valley completely got me.

It starts off pretty simple — you inherit a run-down farm, plant some crops, and figure things out as you go. But there's so much more underneath that. Farming, fishing, mining, exploring, relationships, collecting, decorating... there's always something to work toward, but the game never makes you feel like you *have* to do any of it.

That's probably what I love most about it. You can play efficiently and plan everything out, or completely ignore your plans and spend the entire day fishing or wandering around town. Somehow, both feel equally rewarding.

The progression is also ridiculously satisfying. Watching your farm slowly turn into something that actually feels like *yours*, getting better tools, unlocking new areas, discovering new things, and slowly getting to know everyone in town makes the whole experience feel personal.

It's not perfect. The early game can be a little slow, and some things are definitely easier to understand after looking them up. And if you're even slightly a completionist, prepare to lose an unreasonable amount of time to this game.

But that's Stardew Valley's magic. It's cozy without being boring, relaxing without being empty, and deep enough that you can keep discovering things long after you think you've seen everything.

Been playing this game on my phone for years, but only recently got it on Steam. For some reason, there were some obvious QoL things that were present in the mobile version that weren't present here. I had to actively mod some in static chest inventory slots because any time you would put down something in a chest in this version of vanilla Stardew, you cannot pick what slots are used and your only option to sort it is through a button that auto-sorts for you. I don't know why you would take away the obvious advantage of having static slots by spending MORE work coding in an auto sort button and an auto place button, and then making it so it isn't even an option to make them static. I will never understand that, but thankfully I was able to mod this game really easily despite running Linux and I respect ConcernedApe for allowing that. Oh and for some reason the mobile version has faster tool use animations and if you want to match that speed on PC you have to animation cancel. 
  Aside from my nitpicks about the lack of QoL on this version, the game itself is incredibly solid. It's a sandbox-style map with completionist-style achievements, a low stress gameplay loop, very affable and believable NPCs, and very haptically satisfying minigames that make up the main "Skill Paths" you can pursue in this game. There is no real pressure to do much in this game, but there is so much depth in what you can accomplish that it can be played as both a slice-of-life game and as a highly gameable RPG. Just based purely on this formula being copied by so many other devs, I would say this is a Balatro-esque game that is not technically undefinable in modern gaming but nevertheless ends up creating its own genre. That will never stop being impressive. 
  Personally, based on my own playstyle, I am one of those people who loves replayability. My favorite games have usually always been high-skill puzzle games or roguelikes because I can spend hours learning to understand them better in a way that doesn't reflect the same AAA standard for storytelling that turns any beautiful project into a marketable experience. I have been playing this game for years because there are so many ways I can challenge myself. I've "beaten" this game (completed the community center) in multiple challenging ways, like no crafting, no shipping, only able to level one skill path at a time, only able to sell things that have been processed, always needing to treat any quests as mandatory, and so on. Because while on the one hand, you have this fantasy of living a cozy, farm life. So, Stardew Valley.

I think it's very good, it has a lot of personality that helps it stand on its own two feet compared to other games of it's genre. It goes for a cozy, relaxing feel, but has adds in it's own flavor that'll keep players relatively engaged from time to time. There's farming; which is essentially most of the money you'll be making, and helps it stand alongside other farming sims. There's fishing, which has been made into this fun little minigame where you have to keep a fish trapped in this little green bar that can be moved up by holding the A button (I played on a controller), and there's even mining; which is the best part of the game. (More on that in a bit.)

But there's a few things about Stardew Valley that don't click with me. For one thing; I've never been one for "Life Simulation" games; I couldn't even stick with Animal Crossing. It's just a genre of games that really don't click with me; and I think it ultimately comes down to the occasional monotony of doing the same things each day. Granted I think Stardew Valley makes the most of it's inherent weaknesses; but it's still a style that I'm not a fan of.

There's also generally a lot of randomness throughout the game; it's random what fish you get; and some fish may be required to finish a task. It's random what the fortune you get each day; which can drastically shake up how well you do in the mines; and it's random what you get from geodes; and all of that randomness gets to a point where you can really feel it after a while.

But to avoid dwelling on the negatives for too long, I want to talk about the best part of the game; The Cave Sections.

I think The Caves are an excellent skill check on how well you can manage breaking all of the stones, fending off enemies, all the while trying to survive and searching for ladders to climb down further to the bottom. I know I was just complaining about the randomness earlier, but for some reason it really doesn't bother me with the caves; and perhaps that's because of how fast paced it is. The exhilarating feeling of you and your friends scrambling around looking for the ladder is something that I find quite enjoyable. Sometimes; you can also find a hole that'll allow you to fall down multiple levels. This adds a Risk and Reward factor to each and every level of the cave; as whenever you find a ladder; you always have the thought; "But what if there's a hole on this floor?" Which will lead to you lingering longer on the floor; sometimes it'll lead to you finding a hole, and sometimes it won't, meaning you'll have just wasted your time; and the clock's always ticking here in old Pelican Town, so you better not waste your time too much. Or else you'll have no choice to leave the caves to avoid paying the 1000g penalty, or succumbing to tiredness; or a swarm of enemies. The Cave Sections are an incredibly fun and surprisingly smart challenge that makes Stardew Valley FAR more exciting than if it hadn't included these sections; and is the single thing saving this game from being a 7/10.

On that note; I'm going to rate Stardew Valley an 8/10.

Very fun, simple and easy-to-understand game. Enjoyable and appropriate for all ages. This game definitely does have a slow start which can be boring especially if it's not your first save, but the game picks up around summer of the first year. The storyline is also interesting & it doesn't get too repititive like one might think because there are always more & more things to do whether it be mining, fishing, decorating, farming, working on relationships, etc. Another thing, this game is very easy to mod so if you do find yourself getting bored or wishing a feature existed, it's very easy, compared to other games, to install mods. All around, I think this game is very fun alone but definitely more fun with friends. It's a very simple chill game so you can have a nice conversation with others while playing as it's not intense at all. It might not be for everyone but I would definitely recommend this game to anyone who likes chill, cozy games. It's also very reasonably priced, so that's another plus.

The Ship of Theseus is a thought experiment about whether an object is the same object after having all of its original components replaced with others over time. It is also an incredibly fitting paradox for my feelings towards Stardew Valley.

I always thought I dislike farming games. As it turns out, farming games were never the issue, Stardew Valley was. I am usually the type of gamer that wants a game to keep as much of its original aesthetic as possible and usually refrain from using any gameplay overhauls so I can honour the original creator(s).

This was entirely impossible for me when it comes to Stardew. Frankly, I think the artstyle is atrocious and the gameplay is much more stressful than relaxing, especially when you play the multiplayer version of it. Cutscenes neither stop time nor do you have the possibility to slow down the passage of time in a day, meaning that you have to plan ahead whether you want to socialise or grind to make grandpa happy. This often meant that my co-op player had to do all the farming and grinding while I played my own little social sim.

My pixelated neighbours also didn't really draw me in - at best, I can say I liked Sebastian (how original) and disliked Lewis. At worst, I have to question how much of this stems from fan-interpretations of the characters and the mods I had installed. The fact that I mostly have no strong feelings about any of the other characters isn't a good thing. Cue me installing Stardew Valley Expanded and at least getting a little bit more out of the game, with some additional characters that ended up being more interesting than the ones I was initially given.

The worst part is that some emotional scenes didn't hit the way they were intended to - a certain character on the beach, talking about his backstory with some... less than stellar pixels to set the scene - as the cutscene actually looked so ridiculous that I couldn't take it seriously, and naturally my character was forced to drink in other scenes, even though I dislike alcohol. Same old. At some point in the game, you also just simply lose the drive to keep going, which is not a great sign either. And I tried to give this game multiple chances, as I know some of my loved ones enjoy it.

Frankly, after having experienced RRRR once (which plans to break away from Stardew modding and instead intends to become its own game), I don't think I can ever go back to a version of Stardew without it. A meaningful romance option, with changes to the characters and his character arc beyond the initial wedding, with children that matter? Stardew Valley could only DREAM of this. I am also simply tired of people calling everything a Stardew Valley clone when Harvest Moon came first (and I never even played it, so it's not the nostalgia speaking here) and other games, like Fields of Mistria and Coral Island, simply do the formula better AND are prettier, no mods required. It also seems hilarious to me that the creator now scrambles to finally update children after years of not giving a care and other farming sims deciding that they wanted to do better. Will we get non-binary options as well and meaningful updates to the characters, or will this just be a half-hearted attempt to keep being "the best"?

I ended up having a lot of fun with my co-player in the end - but the question is at what point am I truly still enjoying Stardew Valley instead of all the modders' additions? I don't believe that if I consider 100+ mods "a Must" in order to play a game, I truly enjoy the game itself.

Alas, I thus cannot recommend the game in its base form. But hey, perhaps some mods will get the job done for you, too.

Unquestionably Recommended – A Beautiful and Relaxing Adventure Full of Possibilities

Stardew Valley is an incredible farming and life simulation game that offers an experience that is both relaxing and surprisingly deep. From the moment you arrive in the valley, there is always something to do, whether that means farming, fishing, exploring, mining, or simply enjoying the peaceful atmosphere. The game makes even the smallest activities feel rewarding and gives players the freedom to create their own experience.

One of the game's biggest strengths is its progression system. Starting with a small farm and gradually turning it into something much bigger creates a satisfying sense of accomplishment. There are always new crops to grow, upgrades to unlock, areas to explore, and goals to work toward, making it easy to spend hours playing without realizing how much time has passed.

The characters and world are another major reason Stardew Valley feels so special. Every villager has their own personality, story, and daily routine, making the valley feel like a real community rather than just a backdrop for farming. Building relationships, discovering new events, and learning more about the people around you adds a meaningful layer to the experience.

The pixel-art style and soundtrack perfectly match the game's peaceful atmosphere. Stardew Valley can be relaxing when you want a slower experience, but it can also become surprisingly exciting when you're exploring dangerous areas, working toward difficult goals, or trying to improve your farm. That variety makes the game enjoyable whether you're playing for a few minutes or settling in for a long session.

For anyone looking for a game with incredible replay value, relaxing gameplay, meaningful progression, and a world worth getting lost in, Stardew Valley is unquestionably recommended. It manages to be comforting, rewarding, and endlessly entertaining at the same time, making it one of those games that can become a memorable part of your gaming experience.

Don't let my Steam playtime fool you, I probably have over 1,000 hours in this game from playing offline. 

No matter what type of gamer you are, this game is ubiquitously fun. Despite the simple premise of inheriting a farm and integrating into a wholesome community, the game has constantly surprising depth and variety. I'd highly recommend it to anyone regardless of what you usually play because of how well-crafted the gameplay loop is. 

There's a bit of a grind at the beginning when all your skills are low and you barely have any energy for activities, but just like in The Elder Scrolls, you gain experience by doing the skill, so the more you do anything the easier it will get, and before you know it your overgrown farm has turned into something totally new and unique depending on what you choose to focus on. 

Usually when I play a game, my romance option is pretty clear. There are people I dig and people I don't. But in Stardew Valley all of the romance options are genuinely great characters and it's difficult to choose between them. All of the villagers have plenty of character depth development and compared to other games, the world feels more alive. Every person in Pelican Town has their own schedule and tasks they do throughout the day, and it's very very easy to get distracted by simply how much there is to do in Stardew Valley.

⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ 500+ Hours Later… I Think I Have a Problem

I originally bought Stardew Valley back in 2016 on the PlayStation, thinking, “Oh, this looks like a nice little relaxing farming game.”

I played it, enjoyed it, and then eventually moved on to other games.

Fast forward to now, and I've somehow fallen completely back in love with it — this time playing it with my eight-year-old daughter.

She uses an old PC, I fire up mine, and together we run our little farm in multiplayer. And honestly, it's probably one of the best gaming experiences I've ever had.

Of course, playing Stardew Valley with an eight-year-old is slightly different to playing it on your own. I might be carefully planning the farm, thinking about crops, money and what we need to achieve that day... Meanwhile, she's wandered off to fish for three hours, bought something completely unnecessary, given someone a random gift, and is now standing in the middle of the farm asking me why we have so many chickens.

And somehow, that's exactly what makes it brilliant.

500+ hours later, we have a highly organised agricultural empire, strong opinions about which villagers deserve gifts, and absolutely no idea where those 500 hours went.

Stardew Valley is basically digital crack disguised as a wholesome farming simulator.

You start off with a few parsnips, a rusty watering can and a dream. Before you know it, you're planning crop rotations, arguing with Pierre, desperately trying to remember someone's birthday, and running home at 1:50am because apparently your character has the sleep schedule of a Victorian factory worker. And somehow, we love every second of it.

The genius of Stardew is that there is always something to do. Farming? Yep. Fishing? Sure. Mining? Absolutely. Fighting monsters? Why not. Dating the locals? Apparently that's now my responsibility too. Need to spend an entire afternoon putting mayonnaise into machines?

Yes. This is our lives now. We've played for over 500 hours and we still find ourselves saying: “Just play one day.”... Three hours later:... “WHY IS IT WINTER?”

The characters are fantastic, the music is ridiculously relaxing, the pixel art has aged beautifully, growing up with an Amiga and a SNES this is throwback central, and there's an incredible amount of depth hiding underneath what initially looks like a simple farming game.

And playing it with my daughter has given the game a completely different feeling. It's not just about completing the Community Centre or making as much money as possible anymore. It's about sitting beside her while we decide what to plant, laughing when something goes wrong, exploring the mines together and watching her get genuinely excited about things that I've probably taken for granted after hundreds of hours.

It's one of those rare games where you can actually sit down and play together without everything becoming a competitive bloodbath. Although she does seem to have a suspicious amount of control over the chickens.

And the best part? Stardew Valley never feels like it's rushing you. There are no stupid deadlines screaming at you, no endless notifications demanding your attention, and no massive glowing arrow telling you what to do every five seconds.

You just exist.

You farm.
You fish.
You mine.
You make questionable romantic decisions.
You accidentally give someone the wrong present.
You pass out at 2am because you were “just going to check one more thing.”... Then you wake up and do it all again.

I've put more than 500 hours into this game, came back to it years after buying it, and somehow an eight-year-old has managed to make me fall in love with it all over again.

At this point, I don't play Stardew Valley.

I live there.

And apparently, so does my daughter.

ConcernedApe understood the greatest parts of Harvest Moon. His love for the early entries to the franchise really is exemplified in all of the choices within this game. When I first started playing, I had a lot of fun just tracing down the genealogy of a lot of the choices made within Stardew Valley to other places within the Harvest Moon/Story of Seasons/Rune Factory/River King franchises. Big stumps and rocks needing upgraded tools, stamina being increased with berries. My favourite game within the franchise is DS Cute and I see its fingerprints all over this game. Bachelors and bachelorettes are reminiscent of those seen in entries like Friends of Mineral Town/HM64 or A Wonderful Life. The mining is similar to games like DS, in which you look for the exit while avoiding/killing monsters. The way you are able to place buildings and barns in any location of your farm is Harvest Moon DS. He had built a dream from the ground up, combining things that he had loved from his past experiences and breathed life into all facets of the game. By creating a game with all of the best parts of past entries within this genre and porting it for a system that had not yet seen a cosy farming strategy simulation game (we didn't get a PC Story of Seasons until 2020!) at only 15 dollars, he created an accessible experience that goes beyond what Harvest Moon did for its fans.

I am (and was at the time of release) deeply into the Harvest Moon/Story of Seasons franchise. I had followed the development of Stardew Valley for three years (since 2012), excitedly looking for the PC experience for Harvest Moon if you can believe that there was not a lot of options at the time. The closest thing at the time was Harvest Moon DS Cute in its execution and delivery such as building placement, and even DS Cute had its limitations! It's now 10 years since the game has come out; I am now 25 and the way that this game has shaped my life even when I was not actively playing it astounds me. Though my sessions and periods of fixation were on and off, I still seeked a lot of the experiences I had from this game in other games I played. This level of love and detail can not be easily found especially in a gaming climate that prioritises output over outcome. 

Stardew Valley breathed life into a genre which had almost exclusively been dominated by one franchise; the face that launched a thousand ships. Cosy indie gaming would not be the same without ConcernedApe.

Okay readers, settle down, make a cup of tea and get a snack, because this is going to be a long review ; Stardew Valley is the ultimate farming game where you can do countless things : mine, fight slimes, farm ( I think you readers know that already but just in case ), breed animals ... the list is never-ending. I bought this game at the age of six expecting to enjoy a nice, calm farming RPG, until I discovered that you could slay countless amount of enemies brutally wielding swords, daggers or clubs, it's up to you. But don't get me wrong, Stardew Valley isn't all about mercilessly slashing enemies in the mines, there is a peaceful side to it too ; every morning you wake up at 6:00 am ( to be honest , I wouldn't want to be a farmer ) then you water your crops, then feed your animals,  go out to do some fishing and then go to bed and then you do that again, and again and again until it becomes a loop that goes on for hours on end. For me, Stardew isn't just a game, it's a black hole that gradually consumes hours, that progress into days, that turn into weeks of your life. I know, I know I'm getting carried away but once you buy this game, you won't be able to halt and take your eyes of the screen, trust me. So all in all, this is a game that I'll never forget.

Let’s be honest: anyone brave enough to make a “slow game” like this in this day and age has my respect.

It starts with that same old setup: a burnt-out office drone flees the cubicle and inherits a patch of weeds from Grandpa. I didn’t expect that messy plot of land—all rocks, dead stumps, and tall grass—to become my most important safe house over the last few years.

First, the game itself. It looks simple, but it’s so greedy.

It steals your days, then your weeks.

Spring has you crouched by the river chasing midnight carp; summer sends you sprinting after strawberry seeds; autumn makes your heart race when you finally plant an Ancient Seed; and in winter, snowed in, you just hang out in the mines hitting rocks. It packs in everything a farming sim needs—fishing, mining, animals, dating, decorating—but the best part? It never rushes you.

No one yells at you if you ignore the Community Center bundles. You can live off Parsnips alone and still survive. You can spend every night drinking at the Saloon with Pam. The Joja route exists for those of us who are tired and just want to buy our way through life. No shame here.

People call the pixel art nostalgia, but I’d rather call it gentle.

The sound of rain on leaves, that orange-gold light on a summer evening, the little ghosts darting past in Cindersap Forest at night… put on headphones, and the real world hits mute. And there are moments—buying your first sprinkler, chugging coffee to sprint home, getting Shane’s clumsy “thanks”—where you realize: oh, I actually built a life here.

And I have to talk about the social stuff.

It’s not just gift-farming for marriage points. Shane’s whole arc still sticks with me—a depressed guy working graveyard shifts at JojaMart, slowly learning to care about his chickens because you kept showing up. It doesn’t feel like grinding NPCs; it feels like watching a friend claw their way out of a hole. You can tell ConcernedApe genuinely loves these people, not just his product.

It’s not perfect, sure.

The fishing minigame early on is pure thumb abuse. Mobile controls in the Skull Cavern should count as a war crime. And once you unlock perfection tracking, the cozy farm can turn into an Excel spreadsheet with sprinklers. That “just one more day” curse is very real—you say you’re going to bed, then remember it’s Egg Festival tomorrow and suddenly it’s 3 AM again.

But none of that is why I wrote this.

I really just want to say thank you to Eric Barone.

One person. Years of solo dev work—coding, pixel art, composing, writing—with no microtransactions, no battle passes, no FOMO. A game you buy once, and it just… keeps giving. In an era where everything wants to monetize our attention, he made something that asks for nothing except that you come back when you’re tired.

Life is loud. Rent, deadlines, things we can’t control—it adds up. But in Stardew, if you hoe the dirt, the seed sprouts. If you feed the chicken, it lays an egg. If you’re kind to someone, they don’t ghost you; they just take their time warming up.

It’s not a masterpiece because of its graphics or scope. It’s a warm, stupidly kind pixel blanket.

Go home for a bit. Spring is starting in Pelican Town again.

If you're like me and heard about Stardew Valley for years without playing, I cannot recommend buying it enough. The fact that it was (originally) made entirely by ONE person is still mind blowing, with regular updates and several well fleshed out mechanics already incorporated. My first farm reached perfection after 222 hours and the one I'm on now (after 143 hours) is just a couple million gold away from perfection!

Given that this game has been glazed everywhere over the last decade, I would like to offer a counterpoint. Most of my playtime (around 40 hours or so) have been on the PS5.

The graphics in Stardew aren't just "retro", they're honestly so... ugly. One only needs to look at Littlewood for pixel graphics that are pretty to look at and comfortable to play with.

The gameplay is no longer anything special. While it's true that Stardew offers a ton of content and replayability for its price point, other games are much more beautiful and can offer comparable if not deeper levels of graphics, gameplay and story. Coral Island being one, My Time at Sandrock being another.

The genre of cozy, farming games owes a lot to Stardew (just as Stardew owed plenty to Harvest Moon). However, it's been more than a decade. It's high time for players to move onto aesthetically pleasing games with modern QOL and comparable gameplay loops.

Stardew Valley is farming without the stress—unless you forget to plan your crops, then it’s farming with heartbreak. It’s cozy, charming, and somehow more satisfying than real life. With friends, it’s a countryside sitcom. Alone, it’s therapy with turnips.

Positives:
+ Co-op farming chaos with friends makes every season hilarious.
+ Relaxing gameplay loop—plant, water, harvest, repeat.
+ Community Center bundles give you long-term goals (and occasional heartbreak).
+ It’s real life but better: no bills, no traffic, just pixel chickens.

Negatives:
- Forget to plan your crops? Enjoy waiting a whole year for that bundle.
- Fainting at 2 AM on your own farm is peak Stardew cruelty.
- The grind can feel slow if you don’t pace yourself.
- Fishing. Enough said.

TL;DR – Stardew Valley is cozy chaos. Plan your crops, respect 2 AM, and enjoy farming without the stress.

When the daily life of day to day dull and drab office work feels soul-crushing, sometimes you just want to leave it behind and enjoy the simple life in the vast fields of the great outdoors, and this game is the embodiment of that. Sure its hard work, but its the sense of freedom that makes the whole thing rewarding. You take over your grandfather's farm and be part of a small town community while trying to improve it while you're at it. You go fishing, explore mine, make friends, rebuild the community center (or sell out like a jerk) and overall enjoy life at your own pace. Its the kind of game that makes you feel "just one more day" regardless of whatever you're doing as there's always something to be done out in the valley. Music and art are great and still hold up well to this day. This game was a one man passion project that has been continuously updated and honestly deserves the praise for how expansive this game ended up getting. You seriously can't go wrong with the rustic beauty that this game has presented itself as. Its been 10 years since the game was released and its still an amazing game that holds it head up high in relevance. In short, this is a game worth picking up for what is and everything it has provided since.

A TRUE LOVE LETTER TO HARVEST MOON

Stardew Valley is one of the greatest indie games ever made. Built as a massive passion project by a single developer, it captures everything that made the classic Harvest Moon games special while expanding the formula in almost every possible way.

The game is huge, charming, and incredibly relaxing. Whether you're farming, fishing, mining, decorating your farm, building relationships with the townsfolk, or simply exploring at your own pace, there's always something meaningful to do. It's the kind of game that's easy to lose hundreds of hours in without even noticing.

What impresses me the most is the postlaunch support. For years, ConcernedApe has continued to release enormous free updates packed with new content, features, and improvements. Many large publishers would have easily sold these additions as paid DLC, but here they've all been included at no extra cost.

Stardew Valley is a perfect example of what can happen when a developer creates a game out of passion rather than chasing trends.

Pros:

+ Incredible amount of content
+ Relaxing and highly addictive gameplay
+ Excellent pixel art and soundtrack
+ Huge variety of activities and progression systems
+ Massive free content updates over the years
+ One of the best spiritual successors to Harvest Moon

Cons:

- Some activities require a bit of grinding
- The opening hours are slower than the rest of the game

Time flies when I'm playing this game. I actually enjoy Stardew Valley a lot. As a man, I wasn't exactly expecting to have this much fun playing it. I play with my brother, and it's been a great experience overall. We just spend time together—mining, farming... for example, I do the farming while he takes care of the animals, or sometimes we switch. During winter, we usually do both.

I also tried to play this game without watching tutorials or guides because I wanted to experience it the way it was intended. The first comparison that came to mind was Minecraft. Back when I first played it, there weren't many videos or guides. Even for crafting recipes, you had to Google most of them. Looking back, I think that made the game feel much more real. In real life, you wouldn't just know how to make everything either. Figuring things out and exploring was a huge part of what made Minecraft so special. There was always a sense of mystery until you slowly learned how everything worked.

I'd say Stardew Valley gives me that same feeling. Even as I'm writing this, I'm sure there's still so much more for me to discover. I'm around 50 hours in, and it doesn't even feel like I'm close to finishing the game. There's still a lot left to explore, and I'm just having fun. I hope that feeling lasts.

If you have someone to play with, I definitely recommend trying co-op. I can't really compare it to single-player since I haven't played Stardew that way, but co-op has been an amazing experience.

I used to be a huge tryhard, so playing games were indeed fun through all the tremendous, rapid grinding. I did everything as fast as I could to make do, and what only satisfied me was immediate results. This strained me to the point where I had practically headaches playing games all the time. You could argue its also just from having a gaming addiction. I suppose that is true. One day, I heard the name of Stardew Valley, and was pleasantly intrigued. So I immediately bought it during a huge sale and started playing. I cherish the days when I woke up from bed and immediately booted up my PC just to spend the most of my time fishing at Willy's deck and stash them in a large chest to sell them at the end of each month. Listen, I would literally fish past my curfew, sometimes almost until 1 AM. I fished everyday until like, what, mid-year 2? I can't exactly remember, so I might be completely off, but I can't deny that it was extremely boring. It was slow and dull, yet quiet and peaceful... and I know I have never felt so relaxed in such a long time. This game taught me to take things slow and just not overthink. That you'll get there someday. All I had to do is just not rush things and take my time. Because moments pass much quicker than you think, and you will miss them someday. So for people who just have a lot of stress in their life, I highly recommend this.

I wish the mines had more randomness to them. I personally love a good dungeon crawling experience and I really wish the cave crawling had more to it. It's sad knowing that there actually were plans for that originally and that they unfortunately couldn't make it into the game. And while you can play through the game solely through only mining in the caves, you shouldn't, because the game is a lot more fun when you're trying to do everything, all at once. I recommend playing the game with someone, even if you're not playing the same farm. This game is something to be celebrated and enjoyed. Write spreadsheets, memorize the wiki, download all the community mods, speedrun the game; try everything and you won't regret it.

Just have fun, that's all that matters.

At first this game did not hook me at all but as someone who likes to 100% games, I was determined to play it through fully. 

It's a well made game I'll give it to the dev. You can really tell that there's one brain behind it all. I love the details and the hidden secrets, the notes that you have to carefully read and solve mysteries, all the characters and their unique personalities, schedule, character development. While it seems like a chill game, you really need to pay a lot of attention and plan ahead. 

It's a grindy game and it takes quite some days to get the first achievement which in my opinion is pretty nice to not instantly get that dopamine kick. Rather it will reward you after you've worked hard enough. Most things are so expensive in this game, but I guess that's part of the grind. It's not easy and you have to figure out the best way to play this game, what to focus on, what sell price is the best, plan ahead based on day and season, and so on. Slowly you get rewarded in different ways. 

Early game is intensive, slow, and confusing. Mid game you start to get a hang of everything, and start the real money making and crafting grind, motivation to play can be on and off here. End game is kinda odd and confusing. That's when you finally get max level of everything and that's when you get the real "support" that I would have appreciate if I had them earlier. To me it makes no sense, especially the [spoiler]obelisks[/spoiler]. What is the point of having access to the "support" crafts/items after completing everything in the late game stage?

Overall, a fun game. It fits many play-styles like those who want to just farm and craft, those who like to fish, those who like to slay monsters. I wish you could save anytime during the day like the smartphone version, don't understand why that's not a thing on PC. But good game!
