Simple concepts, executed to utter perfection. 10 years after release and it's still going viral... and for good reason. This game was the passion project of a genius. It's a rare sincere and genuine product, with true heart and soul, in a world full of corporate cash grabs. Stardew Valley is sill getting major updates, and the next one is expected soon. Typically being on sale for $7.49 and/or $4.99 for the mobile version means the ONLY game with more value for your $ is Terraria. Yes, seriously it is THAT good.

Easy to learn, and rewarding to master. Full of easter eggs and hidden game mechanics. You'll still learn things after 1000+ hours (PC, Consoles, Mobile). Don't let the 2-D pixels fool you, this is an absolute masterpiece of a game! Chill or grind. Be a collector of everything or play for the stories. The final "dungeons" have no skill ceiling. You make the game however difficult or easy you want it to be based on your playstyle.

Stardew Valley has a crazy (in a good way...) online community and cult following. It's full of wholesome pixelated charm but still ripe for shenanigans. (There's "official" speedrun categories called "Underwear Soup" and "Drink Mayonnaise" and try putting some slime incubators in town if you want a laugh). 

The game's soundtrack is so good that there's literally a touring concert series for it called "Stardew Valley: Festival of Seasons".

There are ENDLESS options for modding. Game is too slow? Speed mods. Game is too grindy? Automation mods. Story is over? Look up Stardew Valley Expanded and add another 100+ hours of gameplay and stories...

Are you the type that craves efficiency and optimization? The money and reward progress snowballs really well and early planning pays off BIG in the end. (Pro Tip: Get a quick jump on Tappers for Oak Resin and start stuffing Ancient Fruit into seed makers ASAP.) There's an achievement for "Perfection" but if you're a hoarder who collects every item I wish you good luck... I still haven't gotten a Living Hat yet...

Do you just want to chill and not care about grinding? There's no incentive to rush at all. Don't worry about the clock. Spend time decorating your house & farm. (Be careful decorating outside of your farm though, look up some tutorials before doing it.) If you REALLY wanna skip some grind there's glitches you can use. For example: putting [279] in your farmer's name will get you a lot items for easy money and easy friendship. Just be warned that Grandpa might be a little disappointed in you... but it won't break the game.

The minor gripes:

The Fishing minigame is brutal for beginners, but there's some tricks to grinding out those first few Fishing levels and then it gets much easier (Hint: Crab Pots and Fish Ponds give Fishing EXP). You can accidentally cancel quests in the Quest Journal and there's no way to undo it, forcing you to restart the game day. There's a very small amount of missable things, mostly minor cutscenes. The game can sometimes be pretty frustrating when you die or run out of time far from home (skill issue, tbh). There is no cross-platform multiplayer (except between mobile and PC). Be warned that Stardew Valley can be dangerously addictive. Time will melt way almost as bad as playing MMORPGs, but at least there's no "pay-to-win" or microtransactions. I struggle to find anything to really complain about here even after 1000+ hours across 15+ save files.

Not only is Stardew Valley a firm [h2]10 out of 10[/h2] across the board, it's a solid contender for one of the top 10 best video games of all time.

[h2] In short, [/h2]  

[h3] you will enjoy Stardew Valley if you like: [/h3] 
-simple controls 
-straight to the point presentation 
-collecting and hoarding 
-easy to get into, but also high skill/knowledge ceilings in games 
-lots of content, especially post game, in which more are added over time 
-replayability in life sim 
-really cordial and pro-consumer developer 
-a lot of surprises and secrets to discover 
-a surprising lot of customization  

[h3] you may not like Stardew valley if you don’t like: [/h3]
-too simple combat 
-chore-esque gameplay 
-time sensitive mechanics, which limit what you can access 
-shallow relationship mechanics 
-just simple gameplay, as there is nothing too insane or groundbreaking regarding its genre 
-tedious inventory management  

[h1] Full review: [/h1]   
*as of this review, I have started playing right before the 1.4 update(movie theater)*  

[h3] What is Stardew Valley? [/h3]  
You have all probably heard of this game already back to back by now considering the games very positive reputation. This game is a farming sim, it still has other life sim elements such as mining or woodcutting, relationship mechanics, and time management. Plus you can still play the whole game without farming at all. First and foremost though, it is a farming sim based on presentation alone.  

[h3] General gameplay [/h3]  
There are 5 major ways to play the game; farming, fishing, mining, foraging is stuff like chopping wood or gathering, and combat. All of which is based on the skills you can improve over time for you to unlock more items or mechanics, and play the game more efficiently. There is also a lot of items in the game that have some kind of use, and there is a simple crafting system for more items you can utilize, along with other townspeople who can make things for you. There is a large variety of crops, ores, forages, fish, etc. to the point it can be hard to keep track of things, but there is an in game log that tracks items. There is also some free customization such as where to place farm buildings or furniture in your house. It should also be noted you can place things everywhere else even in town, though they will be destroyed if an npc walks into their path. Speaking of, there is a relationship meter for NPCs where you can improve relations with them by talking or gifting them things each with different likes and wants. You can also decrease relationships through gifts they don’t like, or over time. There are also cutscenes with NPCs which can have dialogue choices that could affect your relationship. As for the NPCs, they do have interesting stories and implications about them as you progress their relationship, the NPCs themselves may surprise you due to how unassuming they may seem.  

[h3] Gameplay loop [/h3]  
You are limited by ‘energy’, shown by a green bar that gets reduced over time as you do things such as fish or chop wood, (using a weapon or a scythe does not spend stamina) and it gets replenished by sleeping in your bed, which progresses you to the next day. There is also a strict time limit in where you must go to bed before a specific time, otherwise it could set you back giving you less energy the next day, and losing items or even more energy if do no make it to bed by the STRICT time limit. Energy can also be replenished in other ways such as eating food. Having no energy sets you back in speed and running out forces the next day to start. There is also a health bar, which is for combat, and will show if you take damage. Losing all health causes you to lose items, and teleport you into the clinic. There are also a few short or long term quests you can do and also get rewarded for doing them via more things that could help you, such as the museum, and the community center. What could be considered the ‘endpoint’ of the game is once the community center/Joja development has been completed, or [spoiler] by the beginning of year 3 spring one, your grandpa will appear and give you a score based on how you did the past 2 years. [/spoiler]. That being said, you can still keep playing the game for as long as you like  

[h3] what I like about Stardew Valley [/h3]  
The game takes a lot of things from previous farming sim games, and further enhances them, especially at the time around 2015 where the monopoly of farming sims that is Harvest Moon, has been declining. If it was already evident by the amount of farming sims that are now prevalent at the time of writing this review, Stardew Valley had a hand in inspiring farming sims, and I respect it for that. The controls and mechanics of Stardew Valley is also extremely straightforward where if you wanted to do something in game, you can easily do so especially if you haven’t played in a long time. This is also the case for multiplayer, where other players can drop in/drop out pretty much whenever in game. You also get a pretty engaging gameplay loop where it does seem like a cozier game, but has a learning curve of what you have too play attention to, and getting better at the game rewards you with being much more efficient at time management. This game is also chock full of secrets and things to discover, even if they may not be too groundbreaking, it’s always nice to discover a use for something or figure something out, you will want to keep them in mind. This is doubly so by the amount of free updates the game has. And speaking of, props to the dev for the free updates and overall positive demeanor leading to the games loving reputation.  

[h3] sounds and graphics [/h3]  
There is enough variety in music to keep things from getting repetitive, at least 3 pieces per season on your own farm for example, there is a lot of retroesque sound effects to the game as well alluding to the fact the game is sprite based, so it matches as if you were playing an SNES game. The sprites in the game is also pleasant to view fitting for a top down farming sim game that doesn’t require much detail to look pleasant.  

[h3] criticisms [/h3]  
The game doesn’t do anything TOO groundbreaking, and you will experience your average farming sim with life sim elements, all of which can keep you on your toes, but if you are looking for something innovative that may shake up the formula, this game may not be for you. Though in spite of that, it could be the point, why change what isn’t already broke? The combat is also not very good to say the least, as there is no depth to it. The timings of when to get things done such as daily when you have to reach your bed, with a lack of mobility options can be quite strenuous which DOES add to the game having a skill curve. For those looking for a cozier time, where you can do things at your own pace, it could be a tad restricting in freedom, and possibly stressful such as closing times for some businesses forcing you to wait it out, and you may have to keep track of them often.  

[h3] conclusion [/h3]  
High recommend, no questions asked, even if you think you do not like farming sims, give this a try and see, the 15$ price tag makes it pretty worth it as it is as the gameplay loop while debatably repetitive, is still satisfying due to the learning curve of the game, and ease of getting into. There is a lot of what to discover about Pelican Town and the surrounding environment has to offer. It might not be the best farming sim I ever enjoyed, but due to its practicality, and the amount of content already in the game, you will get a pretty good bang for your 15$ bucks, plus the dev is fantastic.

13 hours in, and this game has already surprised me more than most AAA titles.

The core gameplay of this game is to experience a farmer's life tucked away on the outskirts of civilization. I expected a casual farming game. Instead, I accidentally spent thirteen hours forgetting the real world existed.

What makes this game so captivating is the amount of freedom it gives you. You're never forced down a predetermined path or rushed to complete objectives. Whether you want to spend the day tending your crops, exploring the mines, fishing by the river, or simply talking to the townsfolk, the game lets you progress at your own pace.

Despite its simplicity, every day feels meaningful. Small accomplishments gradually build into larger ones, making even the most ordinary tasks surprisingly rewarding. It's the kind of game that constantly leaves you saying, "Just one more day," until you realize hours have passed.

If you're still debating whether it's worth buying, I'd wholeheartedly recommend it. It offers a relaxing yet incredibly engaging experience that's difficult to put down, and it's easily one of the most enjoyable games I've played in a long time

What I really love about it is that it’s incredibly relaxing and cozy, but at the same time it has much more depth than you might expect at first. You can just chill, build up your farm, go fishing, take care of animals, make friends, and explore the world. But if you want more, there are also plenty of challenges.

That balance is what makes Stardew Valley so great. Some things can be difficult in the beginning, but through grinding, better equipment, planning, and preparation, you can make things much easier for yourself. Progress always feels rewarding without the game ever feeling unfair.

You can play Stardew Valley in a completely relaxed way, but if you want to, you can also min-max everything, plan the perfect daily routine, optimize your profits, and get the most out of your farm. The game gives you total freedom to play however you like.

For me, Stardew Valley is an absolute masterpiece: charming, motivating, relaxing, and deep enough to keep you entertained for hundreds of hours.

So I feel I should write a review for one of my favorite games since its the time of its launch. Originally I overlooked Stardew Valley, thinking I would not like it. However I fell in love with this game. My steam hours do not account for the time I have played on my Switch or PlayStation consoles or the time that I've used SMAPI - which is a modded launcher and for a bit didn't count toward my play time. 

Since Stardews launch the game has received so many updates, additions and quality of life addons its honestly insane that all of this was from a Solo Dev. ConcernedApe did a superb job with this indie game. So the original draw for me was the art style and farming simulation of it all. A call back to top down 2d games like A Link to The Past that i grew up with.

Stardews' story, which is itself rather simple, young lad or lass gets a farm from their Grandpa, moves from the city and their corporate job and begins a new life. Along the way they get introduced to the townsfolk and through interactions and gifts they unlock story bits with the NPCs. Some of which can be romantic. You do have to option of dating no one or everyone, marrying your chosen spouse and having children with them.

Farming takes place over seasons and weeks within game and the plants themselves go through various cycles. Spring through Fall are your main growing seasons with Winter being your off season to explore or do quests or gather stuff for the community center (if you are choosing that quest) or my favorite, a lot of mining and fishing.
However since a few patches and updates you can now grow winter crops to add income if youd like to farm during winter, farm animals still produce and if you progressed enough to unlock the greenhouse then you can farm any crop all year long within it. With newer updates you also got Cindersap Island that added island specific crops to farm there, and a whole plethora of new enemies and quests and npcs.

Originally the game only allowed one specific farm type now there are multiple, like the Forest version which gives you access to more Hardwood, Lakes/ponds which allows fishing on the farm, a variant of the original that allows monsters to spawn at night on the farm etc. Multiplayer was added as well allowing 4 players to go off and do as they please though you can either pick shared or individual money pots. So you can play with friends (if you have them) and family. Often play with my kids.

As mentioned there is fishing in the game and it is difficult at first and rather annoying until you unlock better rods and get better fishing lure and level up your fishing skill (there are a few actual skills you can progress and every 5th or so level you are able to choose a skill like increased fish selling prices or chest spawn rates etc) Various fish spawn at various times and conditions and even seasons. Same goes for fruits and foragables in the game.

NPCs also have their own schedules doing different things during the week and even during each season. There is mining and combat as well and a lot of secrets to uncover and explore. I could go on about this game for a long time, needless to say I am not going to. Hopefully this review helps a few gamers out. If you are a fan of Harvest moon you will like this game. If you also dont like something theres a good chance there is a mod to help or change it. there are a ton of good ones out there.

Stardew Valley is one of those games that feels like a second home. It starts as a simple farming game, but the more time you spend in Pelican Town, the more you realize there’s so much more to do than just grow crops.

The freedom is what makes it special. You can spend your days farming, fishing, mining, exploring, decorating your farm, raising animals, or just getting to know the villagers. The characters are probably one of the best parts. Every villager has their own personality and story, and getting to know them makes the town feel alive. The little events, seasonal changes, and small details make it feel like an actual place instead of just a game map.

The amount of content is honestly crazy for a game made mostly by one person. There’s always something to work toward, whether it’s improving your farm, completing collections, unlocking areas, or just making your perfect little life.

The only downside is that the beginning can feel a bit slow, and if farming or relaxing games aren’t your thing, it might not hook you immediately. Some systems also take time to understand.

But once it clicks, it’s hard to put down. It’s relaxing when you want it to be, but it can also become surprisingly addictive when you start optimizing everything.

Chapter 1: Game Basics & Opening Preparation
Farm Type Selection

There are 7 farm types in the game. New players should prioritize the Standard Farm, which has the largest tillable area and accommodates planting, animal husbandry, and automation layouts with the highest tolerance for mistakes. Other farm types each have their own characteristics: River Farm has more water areas suited for fishing builds, Forest Farm is rich in lumber resources, Hill-top Farm has mineable ore veins, Wilderness Farm spawns monsters at night suited for combat builds, Four Corners Farm is ideal for multiplayer co-op, and Meadowlands Farm comes with a pre-built coop and 2 chickens for a quick start to animal husbandry.

Once the farm type is selected, it cannot be changed — you'll need to start a new save file.


Basic Controls & Settings

After entering the game, switch to an English input method or enable Caps Lock first; otherwise, keyboard inputs may not register. Core keybindings: WASD to move, E to open the menu/inventory, M to open the map, F to view the quest log, C/X to use tools or interact, and right-click is the universal interaction key (opening doors, harvesting, planting, opening chests — all use right-click).

Recommended settings adjustments at the start: enable "Show Tool Range" to help plan your操作 area, disable "Auto-Run" to avoid accidental movements, and adjust keybindings to your preference.


Day 1 Core Routine

Clear weeds, branches, and stones around your house. Weeds have a chance to drop Mixed Seeds, branches drop Wood, and stones drop Stone — all essential early-game resources.

Open the chest by your door and take the 15 Parsnip Seeds given by the mayor. Use your hoe to till 15 plots of land, plant all the seeds, and water them with your watering can. Parsnips mature in 4 days and are the fastest crop to recoup your initial investment.

Use your remaining energy to chop trees and stockpile Wood (keep at least 50 for crafting your first chest), and pick up wild leeks and wild berries on the ground to restore energy or sell for gold. Go to bed before midnight to save — sleeping past midnight reduces your energy the next day, and passing out past 2 AM forces you to sleep and causes you to lose items.
Chapter 2: Core Gameplay Modules Explained in Detail
Agriculture & Planting

Season & Crop Rules
The game has four seasons — Spring, Summer, Fall, and Winter — each lasting 28 days. Most crops wither when the season changes, so always calculate maturity time before buying seeds. Every morning, watch TV first: the Weather Forecast tells you if it will rain tomorrow (no need to water on rainy days, and it's the ideal time to send your watering can for upgrade), the Fortune Teller shows daily luck (good luck is great for fishing and mining, bad luck is better for chopping trees and gifting), the Queen of Sauce teaches new recipes, and The Wicked Witch's Flying Castle (Living off the Land) teaches useful tips.

High-Profit Crop Recommendations by Season

Spring: Parsnip (4-day maturity, quick return on investment), Potato (6-day maturity, chance for bonus harvests), Strawberry (must-buy at the Egg Festival on Spring 13, multi-harvest crop — plant in Year 1 and harvest again in Year 2 Spring, extremely profitable).

Summer: Hops (11-day maturity, then harvests daily, core ingredient for brewing, highest-earning crop in Year 1), Blueberry (high yield per harvest, great for early-game gold), Melon (stable returns).

Fall: Cranberry (multi-harvest, great for jelly), Pumpkin (good juice returns), Grape (excellent brewing ingredient).

Winter: Only greenhouse crops can be planted, or forage for winter-specific items (Winter Root, Snow Yam, etc.).

Tool Upgrades & Automation
The Watering Can, Axe, Pickaxe, and Hoe can all be upgraded at the Blacksmith. Each upgrade takes 2 days (including the day you submit it). The best timing is the day before rain or the 27th of each season — water your crops that day, then hand over the tool. When the season changes, fields clear out so nothing is wasted. After upgrading the watering can, holding the button waters multiple tiles at once, greatly improving efficiency.

Sprinklers are the core of late-game automation: Farming Level 2 unlocks the Basic Sprinkler (covers 4 adjacent tiles), Level 6 unlocks the Quality Sprinkler (covers 8 tiles), and Level 9 unlocks the Iridium Sprinkler (covers 24 tiles). Paired with an Iridium Watering Can, you can achieve nearly fully automatic irrigation.


Animal Husbandry

Build a Silo first — this allows you to use the scythe to cut grass into Hay for animal feed. Without it, your animals will starve in winter. Then build a Coop for chickens; eggs made into Mayonnaise double in value (regular Egg sells for 50g, Mayonnaise for 190g). Later, build a Barn for cows to make Cheese, raise sheep for wool, and process wool into Cloth for even higher returns.

Pigs are the core of late-game high income: pigs roaming outdoors have a chance to dig up Truffles. Regular Truffles sell for 625g, and Truffle Oil sells for 1,065g. With the Artisan profession, it reaches 1,491g — one of the most stable high-income sources in the game.

Remember to pet your animals daily and feed them on time. The higher their friendship, the higher the quality of their products. Gold-quality animal products sell for 50% more than regular quality.


Mining & Combat

The mines unlock on Spring 5. Floors 1–30 have Copper Ore and Iron Ore for tool upgrades, floors 40–79 have Iron Ore, floors 80–119 have Gold Ore, and floor 120+ is where you can farm Iridium Ore. Remember to activate the elevator at floors 5, 10, and other milestone levels for quick access later.

Leveling up the Combat skill increases your HP. Monster drops can be crafted into equipment — start with the Wooden Sword and Copper Sword, upgrade to the Steel Sword and Gold Sword in the mid-game, then head to the Skull Cavern to farm Iridium Ore or craft the Galaxy Sword (requires three Galaxy Souls).


Fishing

Fishing is the most stable way to earn money in the early game. The Catfish in Spring, the Sea Cucumber in Summer, and the Sturgeon in Fall are all very profitable. The higher your Fishing skill, the easier it is to catch high-quality fish. You can also unlock Crab Pots, place them in the ocean for passive income from seafood.

The 1.6 version added the Trout Derby and SquidFest, where you can exchange for rare rewards. At Fishing Level 5, choose Fisher (+25% fish sell price) or Trapper (-25% crab pot materials). At Level 10, choose Mariner (crab pots don't need bait) or Angler (+50% all fish sell price).


Social & Quests

Greet villagers daily. Giving a gift on their birthday increases friendship by 8× the normal amount. High friendship unlocks rare gift returns and special storylines. There are 12 marriageable NPCs — gender doesn't affect marriage eligibility. Same-sex couples can only adopt children.

Gifting rules: you can give a maximum of 2 gifts per week (birthdays don't count). Never give NPCs items they hate (most NPCs despise Trash, Sashimi, etc.). Giving a Loved gift grants +80 friendship, Liked gives +20, Neutral gives +10, Disliked gives -20, and Hated gives -40.
Chapter 3: Community Center vs. Joja Route
Community Center Bundles Route (Recommended)

Trigger Condition: On or after Spring 5, on any non-rainy day between 8 AM and 1 PM, enter Pelican Town from the bus stop to trigger a cutscene with Mayor Lewis. Enter the Community Center and click the glowing plaque in the bottom-left corner. The next day, you'll receive a letter from the Wizard. Go to the Wizard's Tower to complete the cutscene, and the bundle system officially opens.

Bundle Rooms & Rewards

Crafts Room: Complete 6 Foraging bundles (Spring/Summer/Fall/Winter Foraging, Builder's, Exotic), rewards: repair the bridge to the mountains, unlock access to the Desert.

So I bought Stardew Valley thinking I'd relax for an hour.
That was January 2026.
I have no idea what year it is anymore.
The game starts innocently enough. You inherit a charming little farm, meet friendly townsfolk, pet some chickens, and think, "I'll just water my crops and then go to bed."
That, my friends,  was the first lie.
Every in-game day ends with:
"Okay, just one more day."
Then suddenly you're optimizing sprinkler layouts like you're managing a Fortune 500 company. You're carrying seventeen different crops, twelve jars of mayonnaise, three mysterious artifacts, a fish that only appears every third Tuesday during a thunderstorm at exactly 6:40 PM while Mercury is in retrograde, and somehow you're still late to Pierre's before he closes.
Meanwhile, real life has completely fallen apart.
My laundry has become an archaeological dig site.
My dishes have formed diplomatic relations with the mold.
My family checks on me by sliding food under the door like I'm a dangerous zoo animal.
I haven't seen the sun in so long that I flinched when Windows switched to light mode.
Inside Stardew, however?
Millionaire.
Married.
Two kids. (I think I have 4 IRL, but I honestly can't remember)
An ancient wine empire.
A fully automated farm that NASA would be jealous of.
Best friends with an actual wizard.
Saved the community.
Own an island resort.
Outside the game?
I celebrated my birthday because my Steam friends wished me happy birthday before my actual family remembered.
The worst part is how Stardew rewires your brain.
I'll walk outside and see a dandelion and instinctively think:
"Nice. That's 40g."
It starts raining and my first thought isn't "I should grab an umbrella."
It's:
"Sweet. I don't have to water the crops."
Then reality hits...
I don't HAVE crops.
I have a mortgage.
The soundtrack has become my internal monologue.
I hear birds chirping and immediately wonder where Linus is hiding.
Someone mentions mayonnaise and I instinctively calculate artisan profit margins.
At this point I'm convinced ConcernedApe didn't make a farming simulator.
He made the most polite hostage situation ever created.
No explosions.
No violence. (Well except for serpants flying at your face at mach 286.
No dragons threatening the kingdom.
Just one tiny little sentence that has consumed thousands of hours of my life:
"One more day."
Final Verdict:
Graphics: Cozy enough to erase responsibilities. ★★★★★
Gameplay: Accidentally invents time travel. ★★★★★
Difficulty: Explaining why it's suddenly 3:47 AM. ★★★★★
Impact on Social Life: "Your friends have forgotten what you look like." ★★★★★
Would I recommend it?
Absolutely.
Would I warn people first?
Also absolutely.
Because Stardew Valley isn't a game...
It's a legally purchased black hole where weekends, responsibilities, and entire seasons disappear without a trace.
Now if you'll excuse me...
I just need to harvest one more crop.
...and that's definitely where I'll stop.

To analyze this game on its technical points would just be repeating what everyone else has said about it for the last decade, so I'm not going to do that, and write more about what it means to me.

I picked up Stardew Valley almost ten years ago, a couple months after it was first released and the hype has built up enough for me to splurge on the purchase. At the time, I had no idea how much I needed this game, and how much it would add to my life. It's an immersive, wholesome escape for me whenever things get rough, and will always be associated with comfort and fun. Over the years, I bought it on four more platforms and logged over 1,000 more hours on the Switch alone, starting new saves whenever I feel like I need to return to the digital village, to friendly characters and forest magic. When the soundtrack was released on Spotify, I'd listen to it at my desk job, and for that time I wouldn't feel like I was just rotting away; I could bring some of the game's comfort back into my life when everything else felt crushing. The pixel art is so beautiful and detailed that it's easy to imagine the world in different forms, so I couldn't help but make some fanart in my own style. Great art always inspires other artists, and so does the story of a single dev creating one of the most beloved games ever made because he wanted to share his music. It has overwhelmingly been a force for Goodness in the world, and we wouldn't be the same without it.

My experience is not unique, as you can tell from all of the other reviews singing its praises. I'm just adding to the choir here.

Stardew Valley is one of those games that you keep going back to, it’s got so much to do and such variety it’s hard to be bored. There’s so many ways to play. You can optimize your farm by the numbers and meticulously plan out the best crops to make the most money, or you can completely drop all of that and build a farm filled only with animals. There’s a lot to do, which makes it the kind of game I keep coming back to, it’s just very cozy and comforting.

It's a calm game play loop, it prioritizes efficient time and energy usage in the game(You have an energy bar for each day and when you go to sleep its recharged the next day, and well time). How? Well, you only have so much time in the day to do your tasks(plant seeds, talk to villagers, explore the caves), and energy per day is limited. Also, staying up late punishes you with half the energy for the next day. It's a good lesson on using something finite and limited with care. Is it boring(yes.), but that's the thing, the "boring" of the game is what makes it good, to sit down and put your brain to rest, to allow work without distraction makes even the boring work, clean and satisfying.

Probably my number one sandbox game of all time. It allows for creativity without forcing it, it has a story without having a convoluted main quest that gets forgotten after a week without playing, and it's one of the easiest games I own to pick back up and figure out what I was doing without having to restart after every break. Compared to things like Minecraft and Skyrim (which still hold a special place in my heart) it has enough direction to keep you engaged without stifling your own story, so if you like to rp in games like these, you're in for a treat.

I think the only thing I could suggest is either custom pronouns, or a gender neutral farmer option. Other than that, I think mods help fill the space for any extra locations or more technical menus, and considering that I have over a thousand hours at the time of writing this review and still haven't reached perfection (yet), I think it goes to show just how much there is to this game on its own. I highly recommend this to people who enjoy a nice farming game that has more to offer than insane wait times and a constant grind to make any progress.

As of June 18th, 2026: it's been exactly five years since I bought Stardew Valley on my Steam profile. I can't exactly phrase how I might feel about that. It's technically the first Steam game I ever decided to buy (I'm excluding Don't Starve Together because it was something my sibling paid for since they thought it would be fun if me, them and our other sibling played the game together). I'm getting off track. What I want to say: this game means a lot to me.

I still remember how much time I sunk into that first summer of me having that game. And even coming back to it now, I still love it as much as ever. Saying this game has been through thick and thin for me would be an understatement. 
It might be a weird comparison, but whenever I think of my first savefile on this game, I think of who I was at that time, and what kind of situation I was in. I won't share too much about the situation, but I will talk about who I was: taking the first steps of being transgender. Barely budding out by asking my mom if I can get my hair cut shorter, deciding to more openly write my name as the name I chose, opening up to people.
How it went from a little sprout, to a vast garden of beauty that can never wilt away.

To say how much this game means to me, it's not the easiest thing to try to compare; but it is pretty much made a home in my heart. I know it probably sounds like I'm the most plain slice of white bread in a bakery when I say: "le farming sim means so much to me!!"
But this game had always been something I could turn to. It was the game that truly was there with me along every step of the way; that went alongside me as I discovered more and more things about myself and who I am. 

While it has taken me five whole years to finally write a simple Steam review that will more than likely get lost in the sea of many others. I wouldn't of had it any other way: Even if it took me five long years of fighting to be who I am, and find the proper words to even begin to describe my attachment to this game.

There's something in a previous review that I wrote that was: "People always say life and the world can be cruel, but you rarely ever hear someone say that the world can be kind as well." And if you're reading this, I hope the world will be kind to you: Because you belong to be in it.

I bought Stardew Valley expecting a cute farming game.

Instead, I got attached to an entire town of weird little people, spent hours decorating my house, stayed up until 2 AM saying "just one more day," and somehow became emotionally invested in whether a pixelated man liked my gifts.

This game is cozy without being boring, relaxing without being shallow, and packed with more content than games that cost three times as much. Farming, fishing, mining, romance, decorating, secrets—there's always something to do, but it never feels like it's forcing you to do it.

But what really makes Stardew Valley special is that it lets you play however YOU want.

I currently have 748 mods installed, and I am absolutely not playing the game the way it's "supposed" to be played. I've added new maps, new dialogue, new mechanics, new crops, quality-of-life changes, and turned the game into something uniquely mine. The modding community is incredible, and the fact that you can customize this game to such an absurd degree without paying for expansion packs or endless DLC is honestly amazing.

I'm a former Sims player who's been there since the beginning, and I got tired of feeling like every new feature came with a price tag. Stardew Valley feels like the complete opposite philosophy. It doesn't feel like it's trying to squeeze every dollar out of me. It feels like it was made with love, and maintained with love.

And somehow, after hundreds of hours, that feeling never goes away.

The fact that so much of this was created by one person is honestly mind-blowing.

I've played hundreds of hours and I'm still discovering new things.

Stardew Valley isn't just a game.

It's a comfort game.
It's a second home.
And maybe this sounds silly, but after years of games trying to monetize every little thing, Stardew Valley makes me feel appreciated as a player instead of exploited as a customer.

If you're thinking about buying it, stop thinking and start planting parsnips.

It's interesting to play such a slow paced game that makes you pause and reflect on things. My time in Stardew Valley was strange for sure. Early on, I wandered aimlessly since there's not much of a tutorial. Even though I've played Harvest Moon and similar games I still had no idea what I was doing. All of a sudden I'm in a cavern fighting slimes and wondering what this is all about. By hour 30 I wished I hadn't made my character a clown with male pattern baldness and named him after the clinical name for chicken pox since I didn't know just how long this venture would be. 

Eventually I just started looking things up because this entire game is based around random statistical number probabilities, and if you don't look things up you will just waste time. I had to raise heart ratings with the townspeople, so I stood outside of an elderly couple's house until 9:00 AM I could get in there and forcefeed a geriatric some spaghetti. Eventually I learned how to get married. I just kept giving someone coconuts over and over until she fell in love with me, or something. Anyway once she moved in the relationship changed quite a bit, since she kept forcing eggs and hashbrowns on me which I promptly threw in the garbage.

Really, I just needed the inventory space. Speaking of which, the main character is a hoarder. This man picks up every bundle of grass, every seed, broken glass, pieces of wood, after a while I started to wonder what his problem was. Some woman I befriended kept mailing me sea urchins and some guy kept mailing me a dish called "pepper poppers." Nobody in Stardew Valley eats land animals but they love fish for some bizarre reason. To increase my luck, I had to create a farm of sixty sea cucumbers who appeared to be very happy, according to the game, though unbeknownst to them I was going to chop them into a salad to prepare a "lucky lunch."

Well, this is supposed to be a farming game, and at this point I've done everything but farm. I just assumed pumpkins were profitable, and they were, but according to the achievements 10% of players were able to earn 10 million dollars, which, by my estimates, would have taken several real life years to finish by simply farming pumpkins. Oh, but there are sprinklers, and this guy can go to sleep as much as he wants, kind of like time traveling. At this point I had already had two children with my wife and it was getting to be a real chore constantly handing her coconuts, so I found out that no matter how awful of a spouse you are in this game, she will never leave you. 

Thus, I decided to go on a wine making venture by creating a wine that takes 60 game days to fully mature. Now, that is a lot of time, but fortunately, I could just immediately walk right as soon as I wake up and force him to go to bed. My wife became increasingly upset, even as we were raking in millions and millions of dollars. She started shaking, stopped giving me breakfast, and would lay in bed all day. My children remained perpetually young for years. In fact, by the end of the game, my wife remarked that we were working on all of this for thirty years. I had been sleeping for roughly 27 of those years, so I didn't even notice! 

I loved decorating my little house. I found a cursed mannequin that truly scared me when it started appearing in different parts of the house. The blobfish is truly the most beautiful fish in the entire game, so I made several dozen aquariums and farmed them so I could surround myself with blobfish. There's also tons of clothing and accessories to find, like a skull mask and fake muscle tee. My only real issue is that this game's combat isn't very good, though I guess people just like that combat even exists in this sort of game. The real joy is just boxing and packaging all the little pieces of the systems, like catching a flounder to make "seafoam pudding" which must be truly as disgusting as it sounds. Sometimes a witch will curse your farm, and you can make sinister mayonnaise for no apparent reason. There are quite a few accursed items, I put skeletons, demonic statues and broken alien containers in my child's bedroom for no apparent reason, as I'm sure many other players did.

By the end I had so much money I could pretty much ruin the entire town. I put hundreds of lobster traps all over and just left them for days, with broken sunglasses and garbage piling up all over the place. I flooded common areas with trees that spontaneously exploded when NPCs spawned on top of them. You can even poison the governor by putting a toxic mushroom in the communal soup. 

The true joy of this game is the comedic jankiness combined with the unbound creativity and freedom to do things at your own pace, so while it's not really a great game, it's a great experience, kind of like a living painting that reacts to your actions. It's inspiring, strange and impressive, especially for a game that was made by only one person (in the beginning at least).

I've played Stardew Valley for over 1,000 hours, reached perfection, and started more farms than I can count. Somehow, after all these years, I still find myself coming back.

There are games that you enjoy for a while, and then there are games that quietly become part of your life. Stardew Valley is the latter for me.

The music has a way of calming me down no matter what kind of day I've had. The world feels like a place I can always return to, whether I want to build something new, chase a goal, or simply spend a peaceful evening tending crops and talking to villagers.

What makes this game even more special is the person behind it. Seeing one developer continue to pour so much love into a game through free updates, years after release, is incredibly rare. Every update feels like a gift from someone who genuinely cares about the community that formed around their creation.

But more than anything, Stardew Valley holds some of my favourite gaming memories. I've spent countless hours playing alongside my best friend, and many of those moments are memories I'll carry with me forever. When I think about Stardew Valley, I don't just think about farming, fishing, or reaching perfection. I think about laughter, late-night sessions, and a friendship that became intertwined with this little pixelated world.

It's difficult to put into words how much this game means to me. All I know is that after more than 1,000 hours, I'm still here.

And I suspect I always will be.

Stardew Valley is actually such a good game to play with your partner.

It is chill, cute and very easy to get hooked on. You can farm together, decorate your house, raise animals, go fishing, explore the mines and slowly build your own little life in the game.

What I like most is that both of you do not need to be doing the same thing all the time. One person can be planting crops while the other is fishing, mining or randomly cutting trees. Somehow it still feels like both of you are working towards the same goal.

It is also quite funny as a couple game because you might argue over where to place things, who spent all the money, or why one of you passed out in the mine again. But that is also part of the fun.

The game looks simple, but it has a lot of charm. The music is relaxing and the gameplay is very satisfying. You do not need to be a serious gamer to enjoy it, which makes it perfect if your partner does not usually play games.

Overall, Stardew Valley is cozy, wholesome and really nice to play together. If you want a game that lets you relax, laugh and build something together, this is a very solid choice.

**Title: A Slice of Paradise in Stardew Valley**

Stardew Valley has completely transformed my gaming experience, and I feel compelled to share just how special this game truly is. From the moment I stepped onto my grandfather's farm, I was captivated by its charm and depth.

The first thing that strikes you about Stardew Valley is its beautiful pixel art. The landscapes are breathtaking, from the rolling hills and lush forests to the quaint town bustling with life. Each season brings its own vibrant palette, and watching the world change around me with the passing months adds a touch of magic to everyday activities. The attention to detail is incredible, with each character and location meticulously crafted to create an immersive environment.

The gameplay is a perfect blend of simplicity and complexity. At first glance, it may seem like a farming simulator, but Stardew Valley offers so much more. There’s a unique mix of farming, mining, crafting, and social interactions that keeps the gameplay fresh and engaging. Planting crops, raising animals, and expanding my farm are incredibly satisfying, especially when I see the fruits of my labor come to life. Managing my farm allows for creativity; I can design it however I want, making each player's experience unique.

What truly shines in Stardew Valley is the sense of community. The townsfolk are well-developed characters with their own stories, quirks, and routines. Building relationships with them, participating in festivals, and learning their secrets adds depth to the game. There’s something heartwarming about helping them out or just stopping by for a chat. The diverse cast ensures that there’s someone for everyone to connect with, and I genuinely found friendships with characters like Abigail, Harvey, and the wise old wizard.

The music and sound design also deserve a mention. The serene and soothing soundtrack perfectly complements the gameplay, creating an atmosphere that is both relaxing and enchanting. Whether I'm working late into the night on my farm or exploring the forgotten mines, the melodies enhance the experience and make even the simplest tasks feel rewarding.

The game’s progression system is rewarding without ever feeling punishing. There’s no rush, and players can progress at their own pace. Whether you want to focus on farming, mining, fishing, or engaging in the local economy, the choice is yours. The game encourages exploration and experimentation, which kept me engaged and excited to discover new aspects of the game.

Additionally, Stardew Valley excels in its multiplayer capabilities. Playing with friends adds a new dimension to the experience. We could work together on the farm, tackle some of the more challenging aspects of the game, or simply enjoy the company of each other as we go about our rural lives. It’s a delightful way to bond over shared goals and objectives.

Overall, Stardew Valley is a masterpiece that brings together engaging gameplay, charming aesthetics, and a warm sense of community. It’s the perfect escape from reality, allowing me to step into a world where I can unwind, explore, and create. There’s a peacefulness in tending to crops and making new friends that I never want to end, and I wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone looking for a rewarding and heartwarming experience. Simply put, Stardew Valley is more than just a game; it’s a home away from home. 🌻🍓✨

This is the coziest of cozy games, and one of my favorite games.  I don't typically enjoy games like this, but ever since I've played it, and again, and again, I've tried looking for other games like it.  I think the closest one would be Graveyard Keeper, but it still doesn't hold a candle.

I think I've done 3 farms at this point, and it seems like each farm is ~150 hours.  Legitimately do not know how I've accumulated that much time.  I mean, I do, because the hours just melt away when you're playing this, but it's astonishing at how fast that happens.

I've never tried mods for this, but I have heard the modding community is quite massive, and there are a ton of amazing mods out there... maybe my next farm I'll look into it.  But I'm pretty sure the game has a native way of creating/adding mods, and whenever a developer does that, you know they care about their product.

The only faults I'd find in this game would be feature requests.  I almost want this to be more like Zelda style combat, castles, and more equipment, but then you'd come back to your farm, take care of your animals, brew potions, maybe temper your equipment, whatever... then back out to the castles, or just stay on the farm doing your thing.  You could extend that to full randomization, and maybe there was a certain win condition or something, but at that point, this would be an entirely different game.

Now that I've gotten that out of the way, I am really looking forward to the Haunted Chocolatier because that might be my feature requests above.  And if not, the creator clearly puts in his best effort and creates quality products, so I'm sure it'll be even cozier.

I have some problems with Stardew Valley in general, but that isn't for my to get into a bunch of rambles about.  Ultimately it is a fun life/farm sim game where you get to enjoy growing your crops and animals.  The townsfolk are entertaining enough, but I do wish more of the romanceable characters were interesting.  A lot of the character arcs are less arcs and more so things happening, which may be par for the course for these kinds of games.  However I still would have liked more.  In spite of this, I find the gameplay quite fun and the music is absolutely gorgeous.  My personal favorite track is "Nocturne of Ice."

Actually, I'll go on one ramble.  I'll never get to say this anywhere else ~

A lot of players do not like the winter season.  I have heard a lot of these people say that winter is the most boring part of the game.  However I think we should be real here.  Winter is Not for growing crops, it is special time for you to explore the entire rest of the game.  Winter, especially the first winter, is a really good opportunity to get further in the mines, upgrade all your tools one after the other, and upgrade buildings while also focusing on your animals instead of your crops.  Winter is also a great time to do fishing, and there are quite a few birthdays to give gifts for.  This all to say, Winter is a fun season.  Maybe it isn't the bread and butter of the game but it is the delicious homemade jam on the side.  And I do quite like the jam.

I expect most of the people reading this review are probably people who have already played the game.  However, if you're interested in Stardew Valley, I suggest trying it out on whatever platform you prefer.  I also suggest checking out a Story of Seasons game, as well as Fields of Mistria.  Stardew might turn out to be your favorite, but these games are good as well, and sometimes you want something Like Stardew, but not quite like it.

Time moves very quickly, and it can sometimes be hard to judge whether you have enough time to get somewhere (especially shops before they close). Stardew Valley: The game that never stops giving!

I don't really know what to say about Stardew Valley that hasn't already been said before. I would imagine that pretty much everyone that is into cozy games has experienced this game. Heck, I imagine for a ton of people, this game started their cozy game enjoyment journey. For me personally, Stardew Valley is the ultimate culmination of a cozy game, and I personally don't think many other cozy games come even close. There is a reason this game is a continual money printer. Every aspect of this game is either addictive or inviting. (Sometimes both!)

And to be quite honest, I don't really see much of a point in talking about the gameplay mechanics. I feel like most people already know about them by now. What is important to me, is telling people why I think Stardew Valley is so special, why it hold so many special places in so many people's hearts. From my perspective, that has to do mainly with the game's charm. There are many cozy games that have tried to ape Stardew Valley's success, and while a bunch of them get the mechanics right, most of those games feel like they are missing something and that would be the charm. There is a charming ambiance around almost all aspects of this game. Whether you are farming, fighting, relationship building, exploring, or puzzle solving. This game is built to be almost like a friend, and I feel like it has for many people including myself.

And the best part? This game has received numerous updates over the years that can either be considered QOL (quality of life) updates, or content updates. Because of that, this game has an incredible variety of gameplay and locations. So much so, that I still have not done everything this game has to offer. I am consistently leaving this game for a while, and coming back later to continue my farming life. That is something that I cannot say about most of the video games I play these days. For most games, it is a one and done type of affair. but not with Stardew Valley. Not with this charming game that I can never seem to get enough of. I typically get full on Stardew Valley vibes, then let them slowly dissipate, then come back for more.

Everything I said above are only small bullet points on how I feel about Stardew Valley. I could go on forever, but instead of you continually reading this review (if you can call it that), how about you instead go and play this game if you have not already?

Stardew Valley is somehow considered one of the most relaxing games ever made, but after playing long enough you realize it’s actually just an anxiety simulator disguised as a cute farming game.

People say:
“Just chill and enjoy the farm life.”

Meanwhile the game has you speedrunning your entire existence every single day because apparently 14 in-game minutes pass every time your character blinks.

Wake up.
Water crops.
Feed animals.
Check machines.
Collect eggs.
Talk to villagers.
Mine rocks.
Fish.
Forage.
Donate museum items.
Upgrade tools.
Rush home before 2 AM or collapse like a Victorian child dying from exhaustion.

Very relaxing.

The game constantly pretends to be cozy while secretly turning players into optimization addicts. Nobody starts Stardew Valley saying:
“I need maximum sprinkler efficiency and ancient fruit wine profit margins.”

But 30 hours later people are calculating crop rotations like they’re managing an agricultural hedge fund.

And the stamina system in early game is torture.
You chop down three trees and your farmer already looks ready for hospice care. Want to clear your farm?
Too bad.
Your character gets exhausted faster than someone climbing stairs after eating an entire pizza.

The villagers are also weirdly overrated.
Everyone talks about how “deep” and “heartwarming” they are, but half the town acts rude until you bribe them with vegetables twice a week.

“Oh wow thanks for giving me this random flower.
Now I no longer hate your existence.”

Groundbreaking social design.

And somehow every villager has the same schedule complexity as a CIA operative. Miss someone by 10 minutes?
Congratulations, now they’ve vanished into another dimension until tomorrow.

Fishing is another crime against humanity.
People either love it or want to throw their monitor through a wall. Why is catching a tiny fish harder than landing a spacecraft? Early-game fishing feels like wrestling a possessed bottle cap using pure disappointment.

Then there’s the mines.
Which are somehow:

* repetitive
* stressful
* grindy
* and weirdly mandatory

Because eventually the game stops being:
“cute farming adventure”
and becomes:
“industrial resource extraction simulator.”

Your beautiful little farm slowly transforms into a capitalist machine full of kegs, furnaces, preserve jars, crystalariums, and enough automation to concern labor unions.

And don’t even get me started on Pierre.
The entire community collectively agrees that Pierre sucks, and honestly that’s probably the most emotionally united the playerbase has ever been.

The calendar system is pure psychological warfare too.
Forget one birthday and suddenly an NPC dislikes you for the next century because you didn’t hand them mayonnaise on exactly the correct Tuesday.

The game also pressures you constantly with seasonal timing:

* missed crop season
* missed event
* missed fish
* missed recipe
* missed bundle item

Oops.
Guess you wait an entire in-game year now.

Fantastic.

And despite the cute graphics, the gameplay loop becomes disturbingly repetitive:

* wake up
* harvest crops
* refill machines
* organize inventory
* sleep
* repeat until real life seasons change too

The soundtrack is amazing though.
Which honestly feels intentional because the music is probably the only reason players don’t realize they’ve spent 6 real-life hours optimizing blueberry production.

The craziest thing about Stardew Valley is that it successfully convinces millions of people that doing farm chores after work is somehow a form of relaxation.

You’re not escaping responsibilities.
You’re just replacing your real responsibilities with pixel responsibilities.

[h1]"Just one more day..."[/h1]
[hr][/hr]

I bought this game thinking, "Oh, a cute little pixel-art farming simulator. I'll play it for twenty minutes to unwind after a stressful day."

Next thing I knew, it was 4:00 AM. I had three spreadsheets open on my phone, a fully optimized automatic sprinkler system mapped out, and I was genuinely angry at a fictional pixelated blacksmith named Clint for closing his shop at 4:00 PM when I desperately needed to break open some geodes.

This isn't just a game; it’s a beautifully crafted escape from reality.

[h4]The Good Stuff:[/h4]
-The Gameplay Loop: It is absolute perfection. Wake up, water crops, check the weather, pet your chickens, forage, fish, or head into the mines to fight monsters. Every single day feels productive, and just when you think you're ready to log off, you realize tomorrow is a festival or your crops are about to harvest. You will get trapped in the "one more day" cycle.
-The Value: For the price of a fast-food meal, you get hundreds of hours of base-game content, massive free content updates that could easily have been paid DLCs, multiplayer co-op, and a massive modding community if you ever somehow run out of things to do.

[h4]The Cons:[/h4]
-Time completely ceases to exist in the real world while playing.
-Your real-life relationships might suffer because you're too busy trying to figure out what purple items to put in the Mayor's soup.
-Meeting your crush at the Flower Dance in Year 1 just to have them say "Ew, no." hits harder than any Dark Souls boss.

[h4]Final Verdict:[/h4]
If you are stressed, burnt out, or just need to feel something wholesome again, buy this game. It will heal your soul, steal your time, and teach you how to love raising a virtual duck named Howard.

This game surprised me a lot. At first, I wasn’t fully sure if I would enjoy it, but after playing it over several days, I started to understand why so many people love it. It begins very simple, almost humble, but the more you play, the more it opens up.

The gameplay is easy to understand but has enough depth to stay interesting. Progress can feel slow sometimes, but the game is very good at giving you something new right when you start to feel bored. New enemies, challenges, unlocks, achievements, and relationship systems keep the experience fresh.

The controls take a little time to get used to, especially with a controller, but once they click, they feel smooth and comfortable. The story also starts simple, but there are hints of something deeper, especially with the strange nighttime voices and slightly creepy atmosphere.

What I liked most is how much content is hidden behind such a simple-looking game. It does not try to look big or flashy like many AAA games, but it still manages to be just as engaging, maybe even more in some ways.

Overall, this is a simple but surprisingly deep game that keeps getting better the longer you play. It is easy to lose hours in it, and that says a lot.

Before I played Stardew Valley, I never thought pixel art could captivate me. I always gravitated toward modern, realistic graphics, the kind that try to impress you with detail and fidelity. But Stardew Valley changed that completely. Its simplicity isn’t a limitation, it’s a kind of magic. The pixel art feels warm, nostalgic, and alive in a way I didn’t expect, and it opened my eyes to an entire style of games I used to overlook.

I love this game so much that I actually own three copies, one on Switch, one on PC, and one on mobile. Even though I haven’t played much on PC or mobile yet, my Switch farm has over 500 hours poured into it. It’s perfected, polished, and complete… and yet, I still feel the pull to go back. There’s something comforting about stepping onto that farm again, hearing the soft music, and slipping back into the rhythm of planting, harvesting, mining, and connecting with the townsfolk.

What makes Stardew Valley special is how personal it becomes. It doesn’t rush you. It doesn’t demand anything. It simply invites you to build a life at your own pace and somehow, that quiet freedom becomes deeply meaningful. Whether it’s the changing seasons, the relationships you build, or the satisfaction of watching your farm evolve, the game creates a sense of home that’s rare to find.

Even after “finishing” it, I still want to revisit it often. That’s the mark of a truly great game: one that stays with you long after the goals are completed.

Stardew Valley is honestly one of my favorite games ever. I keep coming back to it again and again and can spend countless hours playing without even noticing how much time has passed.

What I love most is that it’s not just a farming simulator. Of course, building your farm and making it beautiful is amazing, but the game feels so much deeper than that. I really enjoy talking to the villagers, building friendships, learning their stories, and feeling like the whole world is actually alive. It makes Stardew Valley feel cozy, meaningful, and special in a way very few games do.

The only thing I truly feel is missing is an official Ukrainian localization.

I’m definitely not the only one waiting for it. There are so many players in Ukraine who love Stardew Valley and would be incredibly happy to experience this wonderful story in Ukrainian.

Right now, many Ukrainian players have to play in English, which means some people can’t fully understand or connect with the story. Others switch to Russian because it’s easier for them to understand, but because Russia started a full-scale war against Ukraine, this language has become deeply uncomfortable and painful for many of us. Most of us would much rather play in our own language.

We would be truly grateful if Ukrainian localization could be added someday. It would mean a lot to a huge number of players here.

Awesome game! I was wondering at first if I would get bored with a farming game. Turns out it is quite addicting and there is lot more to do than just that. I just started and am loving it so far.

Last night my cows and goats stopped producing milk and egg outputs were down.  As I am an artisan farmer quality is also paramount, but you cannot generate 5-15k a day without any supply at all.  I quickly asked them what was wrong by petting them, they indicated the problem was not me so I looked outside the barn and realised that my gentle approach to woodland management was not working for them or me.  Saplings had taken over every available bit of space, meaning that they could not get in to obtain fresh grass.  I spent about a week in game time clearing out all the saplings and establishing twisty routes through the woodland croft I had established, and not only did milk production treble, egg production more than doubled and the truffle pigs were also delighted.

For someone to put this level of finesse into a game, they can only be described as an artist.  Not only that, from now seeing what everyone was raving about, I see there are many routes to playing this.  I prefer a tiny garden, fruit trees, mushrooms and high quality produce that pretty much takes up mornings apart from the autumn season.  I see others go for a high volume approach or even join the corporation.

All I can say is wow, this is the most outstanding piece of work I have played since Farmer's Life, on the basis of storyline, and Guild 2 Renaissance, on the grounds of understanding of European history.

"250 Hours, 87% Achievements, and Still No 'True Perfection'."
Year 5 on my farm and I spent the whole day just redecorating. No rush, just vibes.

If you look at my profile, I’ve clocked over 250 hours and unlocked 86% of the achievements, yet I still haven’t officially "beaten" the game. Honestly? I love it.

The best thing about Stardew is the absolute freedom. There’s no "right" way to play:

*Play Your Way*: You can play it super cozy just decorating your farm and foraging in the rain or go full capitalist tycoon mode, min-maxing crops to make millions by Year 1. Zero pressure, zero punishment.

*Endless Content*: 250 hours in, and the gameplay loop never gets old. From the mines to Ginger Island, there’s always one more secret to find or one more friendship to max out.

*Vibe & Visuals*: The 16-bit retro aesthetic is gorgeous, and the seasonal soundtrack is the ultimate stress-reliever.

*Based Developer*: Massive respect to ConcernedApe. Free massive updates (shoutout to 1.6) with zero microtransactions is a rarity nowadays.

Whether you want a cozy escape or you're a completionist chasing 100% Perfection like me, this game is worth every single second.

My Dream of Being a Farmer

Being a farmer is something that I would truly enjoy because I like nature, animals, peace, and hard work. In my opinion, the life of a farmer is not easy, but it is honest and meaningful. A farmer works every day to grow food, take care of animals, and help people live better lives. That is why I think being a farmer would make me feel proud and useful.

First of all, I really like the countryside. The fresh air, green fields, forests, and quiet mornings make me feel calm and happy. Life in the city is often noisy and stressful, but on a farm everything feels more natural. I imagine waking up early in the morning, hearing birds singing, and watching the sunrise over the fields. I think this kind of life is healthier and more peaceful.

Another reason why I would enjoy being a farmer is because I love animals. Farmers spend a lot of time caring for cows, horses, chickens, sheep, and other animals. Animals are important because they give milk, eggs, wool, and other products. I would enjoy feeding them, cleaning their shelters, and making sure they are healthy. I think animals can also teach people responsibility and patience.

I also like the idea of working with the land. Farmers plant vegetables, fruits, wheat, corn, and many other crops. It must feel amazing to see plants grow from small seeds into healthy food. Although farming requires a lot of effort, I think the results are worth it. A farmer can look at the fields and know that all the hard work helped something grow. That feeling must be very satisfying.

Modern farming is also very interesting because today farmers use tractors, machines, and technology to make work easier and faster. I would like learning how to use farming equipment and how to take care of crops in a smart way. Farming is not only physical work; it also requires knowledge, planning, and problem-solving skills.

Of course, being a farmer can sometimes be difficult. Farmers often work in hot weather, rain, or cold temperatures. They must wake up early and sometimes work long hours. Bad weather or diseases can damage crops and create problems. However, I think these challenges make farmers strong and hardworking people. Success in farming comes from patience, discipline, and dedication.

Another important thing is that farmers help the whole world. Without farmers, people would not have food to eat. Every bread, vegetable, fruit, or glass of milk comes from the hard work of farmers. Because of this, I believe farming is one of the most important jobs in society. Farmers deserve respect because they work every day to support other people.

In the future, I would love to own a small farm with animals, fields, and a beautiful garden. I would like to grow healthy food and live close to nature. I think this kind of life would make me happier than living in a busy city. Even though farming is difficult, it can bring a lot of satisfaction, freedom, and happiness.

In conclusion, I would enjoy being a farmer because I love nature, animals, peaceful places, and hard work. Farming is a difficult but important profession that helps people every day. I think a farmer’s life is simple, honest, and meaningful, and that is why I would be proud to become a farmer one day.

This game has gotten me through some really hard times and it's honestly hard to beat for just £11 you can get yourself one of the coziest games ever made.

You quit your dead end job and inherit your grandfathers old farm, you fix it up, meet the locals, get married and you can easily spend thousands of hours doing this.

The whole game is made by 1 person and it's genuinely impressive.

Don't be afraid if you get stuck, Stardew Wiki can help you with absolutely anything from timetables of villagers to most profitable crops.

You can spend the day unwinding, listening to the relaxing music, Farm, Construct new buildings, go into the mines to kill enemies and get stronger loot, and tons more.

Did I also mention that this game has an insane modding scene? Theirs full blown mods which convert the game into Baldurs Gate, some that add a dozen new expansions to the valley and mods which change the aesthetic entirely and even ones that add some nice extra QOL. And it's incredibly easy to do.

If you're someone like me who plays a fair amount of intense Competitive games like Overwatch and want something to mellow out to and you've never played Stardew then you're seriously missing out.

I bought Stardew Valley because people kept calling it a relaxing farming game. What nobody told me is that it would completely take over my free time.

You start out thinking you'll just plant a few crops and clean up your farm. A few hours later you're fishing at midnight, trying to finish community center bundles, talking to villagers, decorating your house, and somehow planning your entire next in-game season.

What I love most is that the game lets you play however you want. You can focus on farming, mining, fishing, making friends, raising animals, or just turning your farm into something you're proud of. There isn't really a "wrong" way to play.

The pixel art is charming, the soundtrack is amazing, and the amount of content is honestly ridiculous for the price. Even after dozens (or hundreds) of hours, there's still something new to discover.

It's one of the few games I can recommend to almost anyone. Whether you want a relaxing game after a long day or something you can sink hundreds of hours into, Stardew Valley delivers.

Stardew Valley isn't just a farming simulator; it’s a digital sanctuary. Developed by the legendary solo creator ConcernedApe, the game starts with a premise that resonates with almost everyone: escaping a soul-crushing corporate job to inherit your grandfather’s overgrown plot of land. From the moment you step off that bus into Pelican Town, the game wraps you in a warm blanket of nostalgic pixel art and one of the most soothing soundtracks ever composed. Whether you’re clearing weeds, planting your first batch of parsnips, or just listening to the rain fall on your farmhouse roof, the game provides a sense of peace and purpose that is genuinely rare in the medium.

What makes Stardew a true masterpiece is the incredible depth hidden beneath its simple surface. What starts as a game about watering crops quickly evolves into an intricate web of social relationships, cave exploration, and industrial optimization. You can spend your days courting the local villagers and uncovering their surprisingly deep (and sometimes dark) personal backstories, or you can go full "min-max" mode, turning your farm into a massive ancient fruit wine empire. The sheer amount of post-launch content added over the years—ranging from new festivals and endgame islands to a massive 8-player multiplayer mode—is staggering. It is a game that grows with you, offering new secrets and goals every time you think you’ve seen it all.

Ultimately, Stardew Valley is the rare game that manages to be "no-brainer" relaxing while still being deeply rewarding. It respects your time and your pace, allowing you to be as casual or as hardcore as you want. There’s no ticking clock forcing you to finish the "main quest," and the community-driven goals like restoring the Community Center provide just enough structure to keep you motivated without feeling stressed. It’s the perfect game to play while listening to a podcast, chatting with friends, or simply decompressing after a long day. It didn’t just revive the farming sim genre; it perfected it.

Stardew Valley taught me that a video game can be better than any pill. The creator put real care into every part of his world. As you immerse yourself in everything he has prepared for you, you realize that at least one person—or one team—poured their heart into building a sanctuary just for you.

If most of human suffering comes from our environment, then constructing a virtual world that feels authentic—and using it to reduce your contact with the real environment (since our bodies are inevitably tied to reality)—can greatly ease your pain. No matter how much of a failure you think you are in real life, in Pelican Town, someone will always need you. We human beings need that feeling of being truly needed — just you.

Every time I play until my body gives out and I have to go offline to sleep, I feel completely drained—my mind has been fully absorbed into that world. If you’re going through a really tough time, to the point where you feel like leaving the real world behind, please don’t go just yet. Stardew Valley is the door. Only here can you connect with the kind of real world you wish existed.

I have the game on pretty much every platform it has been released on and I have to say mouse and keyboard beats joysticks or touch screens any day, though all those platforms are very playable. As the player progresses more means of transportation are unlocked and it makes sense to not introduce all that stuff at once because it'd be overwhelming for new players but as a returning player getting through the early game without access to things like the return scepter or totems feels rough but unlocking them still feels great. For new players I'd strongly recommend just using the original farm layout, the forest and hills ones have great benefits but the irregular shape and loss of farmable tiles isn't worth it when you're learning the game.

When I first played this game in May of 2016, the only thing anyone would say was that it was an amazing, outstanding game and I needed to put down whatever I was doing and give it a go.

I absolutely hated it. I went through over 2 years of in-game time before uninstalling it out of frustration, wondering how anyone got ahead in this game with so little help, and I had made almost no progress due to being grossly uninformed about how to play the game.

There are no in-game gui tutorials or mechanical explanations of anything in the entire game, and you are very much dropped into the thick of it, up a certain creek without an oar. Townspeople seem arbitrarily cold, dismissive, and harsh until you remember that you are a stranger in a town of no more than 40, and they don't really have much to say to you to start with. Your tools suck. You went from being an office worker to a farmhand, so your stamina sucks. You have almost no starting capital. Seed is expensive, and working the farm is hard work. You'll find that in the first week, you barely have the energy to turn over a frighteningly small amount of soil, plant seeds, and water your crops, much less talk to anybody and get on their good side. Your seeds routinely die at the season's turn, and you will need to start your farm plot over. You need to turn around your farm from a rotting cabin in an overgrown and refuse filled starting area to an economic powerhouse and pillar of community. How do you do it? I'll give you a secret that I wish I had when I had started.

THIS IS A WIKI GAME. You will miss out on a lot of information and mechanics if you don't have someone to tell you or walk you through getting on your feet. Exploration is rewarded, and there are a LOT of secrets and niche to-do lists that can easily escape your notice in your already difficult routine. Answers are hard to come by, but there is literally no time pressure. You could make like SCP-7179 and play this game for an extraordinarily long time before finding something new and interesting. There's a lot to love, so I would encourage people to either play unaware or look up answers to their standard of enjoyment. If it's grown stale, you could well be missing something.

Give it a chance, do not be afraid to look up answers, whether they be townspeople's routines, their favorite gifts, what they do on certain days, where to get items (and when!), and the nuances of various game mechanics. Unfortunately, one of the most helpful ways to approach the game is to get a mental head-start by watching someone else play it, either in tutorial fashion online or getting your wife to walk you through it. This is not my preferred way to induct myself into games, but I enjoy the game anyway. I now have the Perfection achievement, and I plan on doing so again in my newly modded version.

It's daunting, it's big, and as of writing it's all for a very respectable price. One of the means by which I judge a game as being "worth my time" is whether it can meet a bare minimum of 1 hour of enjoyment per dollar USD that I spent on it. I've achieved that milestone by an order of magnitude, and I likely will twice over, as have many other people. Give it a chance, and don't give up like I did all those years ago.
