Just little things like that, and you can pet animals :3 the story isn't really that deep at first, but as you progress each character has unexpected nuance and development even if that doesn't go as far as I might like but still very nice and a bunch of visually dazzling cutscenes here n there. Apparently the next update, whenever it comes out (1.7) will add more depth to a bunch of areas, which will be interesting I hope. This is a lovely game. Is helping me get through a major deppressive episode, frfr. 8/5/10. Loses points because the story is not as deep/long as I want it to be, and when you get to the endgame, it feels like there isn't really anything to do besides farm endlessly and just gather resources. The rewards for perfection are cool, but by the time you get them they aren't particularly useful. More big quests would be cool. The yearly events that happen are fun, but after your 3rd or 4th year, they get kinda repetetive. You only need so many squid paintings and trout trophies. Minor complaints, still a great game, worth the price.

Stardew valley is a near perfect farming sim game, I'd give it 9/10.

The graphic style and soundtrack are my favourite out of the other popular farming sim games that I've seen, and the intro that shows your character escaping the rush of modern life to live on the farm can really resonate.

There are so many different aspects and systems to this game that it makes you feel like whatever you're doing, you're always making progress or money for your farm.

There's a huge variety of crops, plants and trees to grow and harvest, animals to look after and fish to catch which you can of course sell but also use for cooking a huge variety of meals. One of the games goals it to cook them all, other goals that yield great rewards including catching every fish and selling one of every item in the game, giving completionists something to strive for.

One thing I would like to state though is that this game is not "relaxing", despite it's appearance and what some people may say. 

In the early game you will be rushing around to accomplish your tasks each day before bedtime or before you run out of stamina, and in the mid to late game there are some difficult areas with tough enemies that require a lot of preparation to navigate. 

I don't mind this, but this game may not be what some people are looking for because of this. The rushing around diminishes as you progress through the game thankfully, as you become faster, unlock fast travel and special items for teleportation.

That's not why I gave 9/10 instead of 10/10 though. The reason for this is because of the relationships system, I feel it doesn't hold up to the other main systems of the game in terms of quality and rewards.

I feel like the relationship system would be a lot better if it was less one-sided. Relationships are of course optional, but the gifts and rewards you get aren't really worthwhile for the amount of gifts you have to give and the money it costs to get married and have children. It would be great if each marriage candidate could bring something unique to the farm to help you. For example Maru could build gadgets that help you farm more efficiently since she's into tech and inventions.

It would also be better if there were more ways to increase the heart metre for the characters. Currently I believe the only way to do this outside of a few specific quests is by giving gifts and talking to them, but it would be cool if you could take people out on dates, bond over farming activities and play games with your children.

My criticisms of the relationship system aside, this game is a near perfect farming sim and is worth it even at full price for the amount great content available.

Wiki-game. Look up everything.
Punishes your ignorance rather than rewarding your curiosity.
Frustrating rather than relaxing.
Induces "fear of missing out" while pressing deadlines over your head.

I would recommend the game due to the general fun there is, but it feels like a game you’re supposed to have a wiki next to you to enjoy, despite me trying to avoid that until I get too tired of the pressing ingame deadlines and dates to keep up with to have more than just watering my crops.
Simply put- there’s too many "gotcha, try again next year" moments and small annoyances to make this game relaxing and not just annoying to play.

Want an example? A small assignment, get 20 copper ore.
Earlier assignments allow you to use items you found before, but for this specific job you can’t use the 80 copper ore you had mined before. You need NEW copper ore. Could’ve been worded better or been very explicit rather than "bring 20 copper ore".

Another example? Giving villagers gifts is a pain in the ass too. They don’t like a gift? They’ll take it anyway, say "I hate it! Don’t give me gifts!" like a toddler having a tantrum and practically speaking, throw it on the ground to spite you rather than to say no thanks and refuse it.
Why can’t I straight up slap the fucker after that level of disrespect? The relaxing baby game feels more like a drama town simulator.

Also, long term saves will not make much sense because the villagers will never change or age.

Another, different criticism is about villagers never bothering to initiate conversation with you- except for business owners trying to sell you shit.
"Come buy new seeds! Buy my furniture!"
I like Willy at least. That guy gives you a free fishing rod and just shares with you his love for fishing.

The villagers are realistic in a sense, but moreso boring and the lack of interaction makes not only the characters feel shallow but the social game as well, as they will only say the same lines everyday.

Like I get it, Penny works as a teacher, Shane works a depressing job at Joja and hates you and so on- they will never bother to get to know you, they only care if you, the new guy showers them in gifts they specifically like (which you would never find out about without trial and error, hence the wikipedia game label)

Let me start by saying that Stardew Valley has firmly placed itself in the Top 3 of my favorite games of all time. I do take breaks from time to time, but I ALWAYS end up coming back to start a new farm and try out something I haven't done before in other playthroughs.
I'll start out by going over some dislikes I have, all be it very few, then we can move on to the good stuff.

Dislikes:

1. Clint. Look I know it's a meme to hate on this guy, but it does come from reason. There is something about his personality that just comes across, to me, as a whiney man baby, that just doesn't sit right with me. His constant obsession with Emily, as an adult, is weird. Its like an elementary school kid having a crush, as an adult its just weird. Then, what is this guy's hours. He closes at 4pm. What else does he have to do all day? He literally does nothing besides a blacksmith, which is a huge part of the game, yet this dude closes at 4pm. 
2. Harvey/The Clinic. I understand the need for this location from a gameplay perspective and a in-world perspective, but same issue as Clint but worse....what on earth are these hours. I feel like I NEVER interact with the clinic yet Harvey AND Maru work there. Every time I ever see Harvey he's just standing around not even in the clinic and Maru isn't even behind the desk 50% of the time. On top of that its only open from like 11am-3pm. Why? It doesn't help that Harvey as a character is so dull and boring. I wish there was more of a purpose for The Clinic as a whole.
3. Some of the Farm choices. This is a very small nitpick, but some of the farm types I find to be confusing on why I would ever choose them. Hilltop is significantly smaller than any other farm in map size but also WAY less space to even build or farm in. Its a cool idea for a farm, I just wish it had more room to breathe. The Wilderness farm is also a weird one to me, mostly because there's an option in game to turn on or off Monster Spawns on any Farm type.

Likes:

1. The Progression. I've never played a game with a progression system as satisfying. Throughout all the types of skills, the slow burn of tiering up weapons and gaining XP in each skill to become more efficient, I don't know its just super satisfying. 
2. The Characters(as a whole). The sheer amount of character lore and growth and amount of interactions and dialogue, its stunning someone came up with all of this and has it all work together so well. I will never begin to understand the Dark Magic that Concerned Ape was able to conjure to map out this many NPC's individual schedules that are ALL dependent on what season, character progression, weather, etc. Its emaculate. 
3. The Art style. This game is the king of 2D Pixel Art. Everything about the way this game looks is just iconic. As a Pixel Artist myself, its so fun to see all the ways things are made to look like, from the shaping to the shading, etc.
4. Gameplay Variety. A lot of the time with games like this, players are mostly locked into a certain playstyle. However, with Stardew, you can be a casual gamer who's just trying to play the game as it comes. You could be an absolute chad and minmax the entire game. You can even play it entirely as a dating sim game with the NPCs. There's so many ways to play the game, which add to its replayability.

Conclusion(for now):

As of the time of this review, I have admittedly, not had the ability to explore much of Ginger Island, so I can not speak on that edition to the game. However I have watched my wife play through a lot of it, and I can say its impressive how much extra has been added to the point it feels like a whole seperate game that most companies would be charging full price for, and its just a free update. 

Overall, I think any type of gamer or even non-gamer, should give this game a try. I have recommended this game to a bunch of people over the years, that come from different walks of life, and I have yet to find someone who didn't have a blast playing this game in whatever capacity they had played it. 

If you have EVER considered trying the game, just get it. Don't wait for a sale or anything, its worth every bit of the cost and more. We still get FREE major content updates. Just do yourself a favorite and join the millions of us who have forever made a special place in their soul for this game.

Stardew Valley is a gold standard for farming sims. It’s got that perfect "just one more day" vibe that works whether you want to chill out or go full try-hard with your farm's efficiency. It’s got this retro Zelda feel when you’re diving into the mines for loot.

The story hits home too. You play as a tired corpo slave who ditches the corpo life for chill farm life, eventually choosing between saving the local community or letting a big corporation take over. The NPCs aren't just cardboard cutouts either. They’ve got real depth and deal with heavy, relatable stuff, which makes befriending or romancing them feel way more meaningful. Plus, the whole thing looks like a gorgeous 16-bit dream and has a soundtrack that’s absolute fire.
Stop reading reviews, buy this game and farm some parsnips. Enjoy life.

[h2] The gold Standard of Cozy Gaming [/h2] 
​It is genuinely mind-blowing to think that Stardew Valley was created by just one person. When you compare it to other titles—which I won't name—that stay stuck in Early Access for years despite having entire studios behind them, Eric Barone’s achievement is even more impressive. This isn't just a farming sim; it is a labor of love that has become the definitive blueprint for what a "cozy game" should be.

​The beauty of Stardew is that the pacing is entirely up to you. You can play it as a chill, relaxing escape where you just enjoy the scenery, or you can go full "hard-grind" mode and try to complete the Community Center challenge in a single year. Whether you want to min-max your profits or just spend your days fishing, the game never forces a specific playstyle on you. With the variety of seasons, festivals, unique crops, and hidden secrets, there is always something new to discover. You are never limited to just farming; you can be a miner, a combat specialist, or a master socialite.

​Especially after the massive 1.6 update, the endgame and progression feel unmatched. There is a deeply satisfying arc to going from a struggling farmer who uses all their energy just watering a few parsnips, to becoming the "Overlord of Stardew Valley" with automated systems and total freedom. You can customize your farm to your exact liking, maximize your millions, or simply focus on building your dream life—getting married, having kids, and becoming the heart of the town.

​Honestly, it’s a massive time sink where the "just one more day" feeling hits harder than almost any other game I’ve played. It’s a masterpiece on every platform, and while it’s incredible solo, it’s especially fun if you have a group of friends to run the farm with. If you haven't played this yet, you are missing out on one of the greatest gaming experiences ever made.

I have poured more hours into Stardew Valley than I can honestly count, and not once did it feel wasted.

The first time I arrived in Pelican Town, it felt small and almost insignificant. A run-down farm, a handful of townsfolk, a few parsnip seeds in the ground, but that is the quiet brilliance of it. You build everything from almost nothing. You clear the land one stone at a time (maybe a little too difficult for a beginner). You watch the seasons turn. You begin to recognise the music that plays on a rainy morning in spring. Slowly, that tiny patch of land becomes yours.

What makes this game so important to me is how it shields you from the harshness of real life without pretending problems do not exist. When the outside world feels overwhelming, Stardew is there to protect you with its coziness. Wake up. Water crops. Check on the animals. Maybe head to the mines. Maybe just fish until sunset. There is comfort in that routine. The relationships are another reason Stardew Valley stays with me. The villagers are not just quest dispensers; they struggle with loneliness, depression, expectations, alcoholism and family pressure. Their stories unfold slowly and earning their trust feels like an accomplishment.

I also love how the game respects different playstyles. You can optimise every tile of your farm and chase profit, or you can grow flowers, decorate and take it slow. You can focus on friendships. You can disappear into the caves. There is no single correct path and that freedom makes every play session enjoyable.

Stardew Valley It is a place I go when I need to breathe and I know I will keep coming back to that valley for years to come. Thank you ConcernedApe for creating such a masterpiece and for helping so many humans through their struggles with your game!

P.S. If you picked the Joja route, shame on you! There is no other way to see this T_T!

Happy 10th Anniversary, Stardew Valley.
It’s hard to believe this is my sixth year playing this game.

I don’t know if you’ll ever see this, ConcernedApe, but I need to say it anyway. Thank you for saving my life.

Over the past six years, during countless moments when I felt like I couldn’t go on, when I wanted to disappear, your game healed me. It gave me warmth, strength, and a sense of connection.

When I was disappointed in the world and in myself, Stardew Valley accepted me. It gave me belonging. It gave me a home.

I saw myself in the villagers of Pelican Town, their loneliness, confusion, quiet pressure, and small hopes mirrored my own. The music comforted me through breakdowns more times than I can count. It calmed the parts of me that wanted to vanish.

Sometimes I watch your interviews. Hearing you talk about the pressure, the self-doubt, the anxiety, and the perfectionism you faced while creating this game made me feel less alone. When I was writing my PhD dissertation and drowning in my own doubt, I felt understood.

Your pure love for what you created reminded me that doing one thing with sincerity and idealism still has meaning.

Because of you, I truly understood what games can be.
They can cross time and space and reach a desperate soul.

I have graduated with my PhD, but new challenges have followed. I immigrated to a new country. The language, the culture, and the life here are all unfamiliar. Even the PhD degree I worked so hard for sometimes feels like it has no place here. I feel like I have lost my ability and am even afraid to go out and face people and the world. I trapped myself in my room day by day. I miss my family and friends on the other side of the earth. I feel lonely again.

So I opened Stardew Valley once more.

I started a new save file, just like my real life, beginning from nothing and slowly rebuilding.

I know Pelican Town will flourish again.
I know I’ll go from stranger to family with its villagers.

Maybe that means I will build a home here too, one day.
Little by little. Season by season.

That is what I hope for.
And I’m still trying.

Thank you, ConcernedApe.
I don’t think my gratitude will ever fit into words. I really wish that one day I could tell you this in person.

Thank you for showing the world that loving something purely, and doing it with your whole heart, is enough to give it meaning.

Stardew Valley, thank you for the joy and hope you have given me.
I believe you’ve saved countless people like me.

Happy 10th anniversary.
Here’s to twenty, thirty, forty more years. 🌱

Now that I've spent a few years in the Valley, I'm ready to share my thoughts. 
I have to admit, this game did not immediately grab me. I spent a lot of time trying to figure out how things worked since it doesn't tell you anything, and I even wondered if I should get a refund and just go back to Story Of Seasons: Trio Of Towns. But I spent so much time looking things up on the wiki while playing that I passed the 2 hour mark. So I kept pressing on. I tried things and made mistakes because I knew nothing. I contributed forage to the potluck soup and ruined everyone's day. I took my time and decided not to hurry about completing anything. Whatever didn't happen this year, there was next year. I still haven't finished the community center because there's one thing I still need for one bundle. (On that note, how stupid is it that I can't retrieve hay from the silo or the hopper if the feeding bench is full? I can always retrieve fodder in SoS. I should always be able to access all my resources!) 
Also, it kind of annoys me that using the seed maker isn't very straightforward - I never know how many seeds it will make, and sometimes I get wild seeds or something, and I just lost a crop I could have sold or used. In SoS I can make seeds from anything in my storage, one to one, and ask for a specific amount. Much more reliable than deciding whether to play seed lotto or just go buy more. Sprinklers are a lifesaver, though. 
Even making money is more nuanced here. In SoS I can use high quality ingredients to cook dishes to sell, and I'm raking in millions. Here I'm running around processing all sorts of things and bringing in a few thousand a day, and apparently cooking or processing some items will actually lose money. I'm still figuring out what is actually profitable, and how to scale it to make it worth it. 
Over time, though, I started to see the appeal. The story is simple and sweet, just right. The art is adorable, and the music is calming. There's always something to do, and it's open ended enough that you can grind hard or take it slow, specialize or be a Jack/Janet of all trades. The NPCs are kind of bland and I often forget to talk to them, but that's NPCs for you. They have made me laugh a few times, though. (I found out where the purple shorts are...) It's getting a little better as I bribe them with gifts, but I feel like SoS often has characters with more personality from the get go. On a related note, I'll probably be staying single.
I do appreciate that my horse stays put when I dismount - my horse in SoS always wanders off, LOL. And having a dinosaur in my livestock is pretty unique. Livestock that let themselves in and out is much easier than in SoS where I literally have to push them in or out or carry them. 
The fishing, though... I hate that fishing mini game. Hate it. I tried it all spring and lost so many fish and finally said heck with it. For the first time, I modded a game and I took that sucker out. Don't miss it at all. SoS doesn't waste my time like this. 
I also added a mod so I can actually see what things are worth before I ship them. How am I supposed to know what's profitable or not if I don't know the price of anything? Another thing this game won't tell you, at least not for free. It turns out there's a book you have to buy for that feature. Nope. Again, SoS gives you this basic information right from the start without any extra steps. 
As I enter my third year, I'm still finding things to explore, and there are more surprises, which is great. This game really leans into exploration - it expects you to just jump in and try things, and will wait around until you discover everything on your own. I think an optional tutorial could be useful for first time players who just want to know how the heck basic farming works, something like a bookshelf in the house they can consult if they want, and players who hate hand holding or are starting their 20th farm can safely ignore it. Having the wiki pulled up on your phone is a must while playing, at least for me, but it is an extra step. 
Overall though, I see now why this game is so popular. It's truly a sandbox where you can go in almost any direction, and I can see myself trying different kinds of farms in the future. Maybe even joining Joja Mart just to see what happens. It does start pretty slow, but that's how it is with farming games. If you keep showing up, you get rewarded, and it looks like there is still more to be unlocked. 
That being said, sometimes I miss my SoS farm and go there instead. But Stardew Valley is an excellent offering on the farming sim menu, even if it does take longer to chew sometimes.

I never played any farming games before. I didn’t grow up with Harvest Moon, so I had zero nostalgia when I started Stardew Valley. I honestly didn’t expect much.

But this game completely surprised me.

First of all, the fact that it was mostly made by one person ConcernedApe is insane. He handled the coding, art, writing, and even the music. And the music is actually one of my favorite parts. It’s so peaceful and perfectly fits every season. I even listen to the soundtrack when I’m trying to relax or sleep.

The game looks simple at first. Just farming, right? But it’s so much deeper than that. You build relationships, uncover the townspeople’s stories, explore mines, fish, decorate your farm, and play however you want. There’s no pressure. No rush. You set your own pace.

What I love most is how relaxing it feels without being boring. There’s always something to do, but it never feels overwhelming.

For someone who never played a farming game before, this became one of my all-time favorites.

Be me in 2017. Freshly in university and meeting other big gaming fans. So far, I have only really played Pokémon or other creature collector games, or straight up JRPGs like Dragon Quest. I have never really played Farming Sims, or Simulators over all, maybe a bit Sims and Animal Crossing New World for the DS when I was very young
Then my friend recommends me this game for the Switch, that she just hasn't been able to put down. Stardew Valley.
I like the art style but I am not really convinced. This isn't the type of game I usually play. But I trusted her and bought the game for my Switch (at the time it even was on sale and costed like...5€ or smth?). 
Skip forward a whole week and there I am sitting in my lecture, not being able to put down my Switch and completely focusing on my farm.

Stardew Valley started my love for farming simulators. Here on Steam I have roughly 200h (at the point of this review) and on my Switch around 150h.
In the meantime I have checked out a whole lot of different Cozy Farming Sims but I always come back to Stardew. The artstyle, the music and the gameplay overall just keep me hooked and even 9 years later, I will always recommend this game to someone, who never heard of it or is hesitant to play it.

Also, whenever a new Update comes out, it will be fully functional and playable. No unplayable state or making existing systems worse. It is sad that this is something that needs to be mentioned nowadays but it is part of why I still love this game to this day.


[h3] ~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^ PC REQUIREMENTS ~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^ [/h3]

My beefy PC nowadays can run the game without a sweat and roughly 8 years ago, when I bought Stardew Valley for my PC back then, that wouldn't be really able to run a lot of modern games, I never experienced any stutters.


[h3] ~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^ PRICE & PLAYTIME ~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^ [/h3]
In my personal opinion, the 14€ for this game are more than worth it. If you are big into Farming Sims, you will easily reach over 100 hours (or 1000), so 14€ for a one time purchase? No brainer. In case you don't have enough money, the game does go on Sale pretty often and I think you can easily get it for half the price or less.
And in the case that you will get bored and think that there should be more content? Just look into the Modding Community and your playtime will easily double or triple, OR there are so many stupid challenges people have done over the years, that maybe something tickles your fancy


[h3] ~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^ AUDIO ~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^ [/h3]
Absolutely beautiful pieces. I have studied for various exams just listening to the soundtrack and it's just such a comfy vibe. Music always fits the season/situation, except maybe the mines but I still like the calmer vibe of the songs in there, it makes the mine runs just a nice experience.


[h3] ~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^ GRAPHICS ~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^ [/h3]
Nice pixel art style that has captured my heart. Personally I really love the villager portraits, they way no one looks the same and isn't just straight up perfect. Filled with enough details but also a very unique and charming fantastical look.


[h3] ~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^ GAMEPLAY ~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^ [/h3]
The gameplay. The bread and butter of every cozy farming sim.
The loop is fairly simple. You wake up at 6am and can do whatever you want until preferably 12am, or at the latest 2am.
You can fish, grow veggies, take care of your farm animal, clean up your farm, hang out with the villagers, do a mine run or just run around the village exploring. There are a lot of small details and other things you can do but I don't want to spoil these, since I think that they will be a nice and pleasant surprise. Just know, that the game can go deeper than you may think at first.
Really, you can play the game however you want and in the speed you want.
If you are a min-maxer, there are tons of ways on how to optimize your farm and get a lot of money as quickly as possible.
If you just want to vibe, make your farm look pretty and take it easy, you can also just do that.

There are a bunch of customization features available and if you look up farms online, you can see how many possibilities there are to make your farm and house look absolutely stunning.

The overarching story isn't really a lot of content and you will see it all during a normal run normally. Where most of the story is, is in the heart events. Personally I think every villager is worth getting to max hearts, because everyone is nice and charming, having their own unique quirks (except maybe one but oh well).
Still there are certain goals that you can work towards but you aren't forced to do it. Over the years, more and more goals got added and they will help you to get deeper into certain parts of the gameplay features.

Difficulty wise I would say, that it's overall a very easy game but you do need to understand the core mechanics, like keeping track of your crops and not letting them wilt. Some friends of mine struggled with the fishing minigame, while I didn't have any problems at all and would even say that it's one of my favourite mini fishing games ever. It will get easier tho, when you get better equipment.
It can be hard to keep track of all the villagers and where they are at certain points in the game. Most people just look it up online, just wait until they naturally meet them or have learned over time where to look for certain NPCs.

I can see why some QoL features might be wanted for new players, that I don't necessarily need (for example a tracker on the map to see where each NPC is at the moment) but fear not. The Stardew Modding Community is big and even if you (sadly) can't just install the mods over Steam, there are a lot useful guides online on how to set things up to start your modded Stardew journey.


Have fun farming! And don't forget: we say [u] no [/u] to Joja!!!

This nails just about everything you'd want in an immersive pixel art farming game, from the gameplay, skills, crops, exploration, customization, furniture, to the art style, music, sound design, and dialogue. The sheer amount of content in this game will keep you entertained for days on end. It's also just a pleasant, relaxing experience when you want to just take it easy and forget your troubles.

As an avid collector in video games, it hits all the right spots. All the upgrades you make and the progression you get through hard work and patience is extremely satisfying. Achieving perfection requires you to explore every inch the game has to offer. Perfection is quite a prestigious journey, and I would suggest anyone who is a fan of this game to try it at least once if they haven't already.

I've shared but a fraction of what I enjoy about this game, but I'm sure enough has been said by others, considering at the time of this review, Stardew Valley is the 2nd highest rated game on Steam, right behind Portal 2. It also consistently reaches around 80,000–100,000+ concurrent players every single day. So if you ever needed a scope on just how much of a juggernaut this game is, there you have it.

Stardew Valley is genuinely one of my favorite video games ever made, and it has been such an honor to have been around for a good majority of its time. I've seen it grow in many ways and I can tell it has been treated with the utmost passion and care. To everyone who worked on this game, I cannot thank you enough. The impact it has made on me is inexpressible and ConcernedApe has my full support in his next project.

Stardew Valley is a game for a very particular time.

It's not that the game is for a specific person, but a time in every person's life that it kind of hits and makes sense.

I got this game ages ago on a crazy steam sale, probably a winter sale, I booted it up and didn't get the appeal. I had Terraria and it did all the things I liked better.

The mining, exploration, and combat were much better in Terraria. At the time those were the features that I was drawn to in the game, though ofc I love farming in general, I tend to gravitate to that sort of thing in Minecraft and other titles because I find it peaceful.

Needless to say I didn't play the game long, I didn't really get the hype and ethos that believers have for this game.

However I think the place that ConcernedApe was in when making the game is the perfect example of when to play Stardew.

He labored over the game while out of a job and dealing with a lot.

I hit some hard times and found myself with a large bank of freetime and was trying to comb through my bloated steam library when I came back across the title.

If you spend a little time with the game it will draw you in. Building a cozy little farm and managing the local townfolk and filling out your fishing portfolio between delving deeper into the mines becomes second nature.

Once you get into the flow, the world vanishes and it's just Stardew. It's a wonderful little title that is perfect for what it's trying to be. It's a great little indy game that I think everyone should pick up. And I ask only that even if you dislike the game, leave it in your library and circle back to it.

It will pay off in a big way.

TL:DR - Stardew is for you, the only question is if now is the time.

Stardew Valley offers a wide range of activities such as farming, gathering resources, expanding your business, fishing, exploring, getting married, having kids, and decorating your house. Yet none of these systems are overly layered or mechanically complex. Even the skills you level up retain their simplicity from beginning to end, which I see as a major strength because it keeps the game accessible to any player. Visually, it is vibrant and full of small details that bring the world to life. The seasons dramatically shift the color palette and the town’s atmosphere, and while the main premise is simple, the characters’ backstories explore themes such as family abandonment, depression, alcoholism, introversion, and not belonging.

What I enjoy most is the methodical, relaxing rhythm of tending my farm. The variety of seasonal crops, their planting and harvesting times, the range of animal products, and the different ways to process them create a steady sense of challenge as production grows and management becomes more demanding. Since the game tracks everything I have harvested, crafted, and sold, there is strong incentive to diversify rather than settle into repetition, especially if you are a completionist. Even when routine sets in, each new day feels full of quiet possibilities, small goals, and relationships waiting to deepen.

If you're looking for a chill, cozy farming game with character stories and some dating, this is for you. If you want to go fast, you can go fast, and if you want to go slow, you can go slow, it's truly for every playstyle.

This game is a masterpiece. Art, music, humor, secrets, quirks, and an excellent balance between challenging and cozy. 

Your first week in game will be slow - meeting villagers, getting to know the different game mechanics, swearing that you will fish as little as possible in this game (yet once you figure it out you'll miss the Stardew fishing in every other game you play) and chopping lots of trees to build a few storage chests. 

But soon after you'll have more things to do than you know what to do with (hint: pick one activity per day, pack lots of food, and you'll be fine) and occasionally dying in the mines or passing out from exhaustion. But it's part of the fun. 

You will laugh and cry with the villagers stories, you'll discover secrets that change your first impressions of people, and you'll be deep-diving in the wiki to optimize your time and farm layout. 

Also, this game continues to get major updates 10 years after release, which is insane - and a testament to how much love and dedication ConcernedApe puts into his work.

I've been playing Stardew since it first came out (along with trying many other games along the way, but I always wind up coming back to Stardew).  I noticed one review mentioned it was for all players/audience (except Grandma).  Well, I am a great-grandma and I still love the game!  I have about 2,660 hours in it and I always come back to it because other games tire me after a time.
I'm free to make up different scenarios to play.
I usually don't like pixel games, but this one isn't overdone...sprites are easy to see what they are without stressing the eyes.
I like that the people and animals are realistic in looks and personalities, not faded, washed out, odd-looking, blown up like balloons, or people looking like animals of some type (cutesy games).
I like that the game has land/town/water/stores/mines/etc. that are easily accessible, not hidden at all.  I hate running into awkward, dead-end spaces, too many hills, or towns on multiple levels that you constantly get lost in.
I will say that I never could manage to get into the second part of the game though...I got stuck and couldn't figure out how.  Also, I've only played in the main mine; I don't like the others.  I'm not a 'completionist' either.  So ALL of my time has been spent on the main island and I'm STILL not tired of it...and this is with NO MODS.
I'm forever grateful to the developer for this game for my entertainment!  If I live a few more years I'll probably be a great-great grandma and STILL playing Stardew!!!
Note:  I've spent many years playing multi-player games too, from the first one that came online and almost every one that came out after that until a few years ago.  But Stardew is my favorite overall.  I'd like to see a good new farming game, but they all fall short somehow.  Long live Stardew Valley!

There are so many things that I could say about this beautiful game which I've enjoyed on and off for several years now.  It truly is a labor of love and the ultimate comfort food for me.  Designing and building a viable farm from the harvestable resources that are available to you is incredibly fun and engrossing and there's something down right magical about how the cycle of the year is depicted and the way that the seasons change the Valley.  In revisiting this game recently, I was surprised to rediscover how dark some of the side storylines are as you get to know more about the villagers and their troubles.  I somehow had forgotten that alongside the cozy, feel-good plot about helping apple-shaped forest sprites restore a run down community center, this game also tries to tackle themes of poverty, homelessness, alcoholism, suicide, and abuse, basically the darker parts that come with living in a small, economically stressed town.  Stardew Valley, as in the setting itself, may be an escape from the tedium of modern life that the player wants and embraces but the same isn't so for some of the other townsfolk who grew up there, particularly the younger and poorer ones who dream of escape in the other direction, leaving the Valley to move into the city.  So all that to say I think an important component of this game is that amidst raising chickens and building beehives, it does try to grapple with some more mature themes, though the storytelling is very simple and sometimes clunky.  It's not just mindless escapism and I respect this game all the more because of that.

Stardew Valley is what happens when you trade fluorescent office lighting for golden pixel sunsets and somehow come out richer for it. You inherit a run down farm, a handful of parsnip seeds, and a town full of people who feel surprisingly real for 16 bit sprites. From there, the game quietly unfolds like a well loved journal.

At its core, it is a farming simulator. You plant crops, raise animals, fish in glittering rivers, and dive into monster filled mines. But that description is like calling pizza “bread with stuff.” The real magic is in the rhythm. Wake up, water crops, talk to the locals, maybe give someone a gift that reveals a little more about who they are. The days move quickly, yet never feel rushed. It is cozy without being shallow.

Pelican Town is packed with personality. Each character has their own struggles, secrets, and little heart events that turn simple conversations into emotional snapshots. You can build friendships, start a romance, get married, and even raise kids. It feels like tending to a garden of relationships, not just crops.

The gameplay loop is addictive in the quietest way. “Just one more day” turns into three in game weeks. There is always something to improve. Upgrade tools, decorate your farm, restore the community center, automate with sprinklers. It scratches that progress itch without turning into a grindy treadmill.

Visually, it leans into charming pixel art that feels nostalgic but intentional. The seasonal changes are especially beautiful. Spring is soft and hopeful, summer hums with energy, fall glows like a campfire, and winter feels peaceful and reflective. The soundtrack ties it all together with gentle melodies that somehow make watering digital turnips feel profound.

If there is a downside, it is that the open ended nature can feel overwhelming at first. The game does not hold your hand. It hands you seeds and says, “Figure it out.” For some players, that freedom is bliss. For others, it may take a few in game weeks to find a groove.

Overall, Stardew Valley is a masterclass in cozy design. It is not about winning. It is about growing. Crops, friendships, skills, and maybe even your own patience. It turns simple routines into something quietly meaningful.

Final verdict: A pixelated sanctuary that proves sometimes the best adventure is planting potatoes and watching them thrive. 🌻

[h1]Stardew Valley – The Game That Brought Me Home[/h1]
[b]Game:[/b] Stardew Valley
[b]Developer:[/b] ConcernedApe
[b]Genre:[/b] Farming Sim / Life Sim / RPG

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Introduction – A Return to Something I Thought I’d Lost[/h2]
Growing up, I spent countless hours playing Harvest Moon: A Wonderful Life on the Playstation 2. It wasn’t just a farming game to me—it was routine, comfort, and quiet progression. Feeding animals after school. Watching crops grow day by day. Slowly building a life.

Over time, I drifted away from farming sims. They either felt simplified, rushed, or missing something intangible. Then Stardew Valley appeared—and somehow it didn’t just revive the genre. It revived that feeling.

It reminded me why I loved these games in the first place.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]The Farming – Simple, Deep, and Perfectly Paced[/h2]
At its core, Stardew Valley is about tending to your land. Planting crops, watering them, upgrading tools, raising animals, expanding your farm. But it never feels repetitive.

The loop is satisfying because progression is tangible:
• Early game: scraping by with basic tools and limited stamina
• Mid game: sprinklers, expanded barns, artisan goods
• Late game: efficient layouts, gold-star harvests, optimized production

It captures that same steady growth that A Wonderful Life did—but with more flexibility and player freedom. You can min-max, or you can casually grow pumpkins and fish all day. The game supports both.

And that’s beautiful.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Pixel Art – Warm, Timeless, Emotional[/h2]
The pixel art in Stardew Valley is nothing short of charming. It’s colorful without being overwhelming. Soft without being dull. Seasonal transitions feel magical.

Spring feels alive.
Summer feels vibrant.
Fall feels cozy.
Winter feels quiet and reflective.

There’s a warmth to the visuals that makes the town feel lived in. You don’t just see Pelican Town—you feel it.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Characters – Small Stories That Feel Real[/h2]
One of Stardew Valley’s greatest strengths is its writing. Every character feels like they have layers.

• People struggling with identity
• People stuck in routine
• People grieving
• People chasing dreams
• People learning to open up

The heart events aren’t just cute cutscenes. They explore loneliness, depression, family tension, ambition, insecurity. It’s subtle, but it hits.

Building relationships doesn’t feel transactional—it feels gradual and human.

That’s rare.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Music – Pure Nostalgia, Pure Comfort[/h2]
The soundtrack is unforgettable. It balances calm melodies with uplifting seasonal themes.

Some tracks feel hopeful.
Some feel peaceful.
Some feel nostalgic before you even realize why.

There are moments in Stardew Valley where you’re just standing on your farm at sunset, music playing softly, and it hits you: this is what relaxation feels like.

The soundtrack carries emotion without demanding attention.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Freedom – Play Your Way[/h2]
Stardew Valley doesn’t force you into one playstyle.

You can focus on:
• Farming
• Fishing
• Mining
• Animal raising
• Artisan goods
• Relationships
• Community Center completion
• Exploration and secrets

It never punishes you for going at your own pace. There’s no urgency. No ticking clock pushing you forward. It respects your time.

That design philosophy makes it timeless.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]How It Brought Me Back[/h2]
After years away from farming sims, Stardew Valley felt like coming home.

It carried the spirit of Harvest Moon: A Wonderful Life—the slow growth, the emotional warmth, the routine—but refined it with modern design, deeper mechanics, and player freedom.

It didn’t just modernize the genre. It reminded me why I loved it.

That’s powerful.

I came in as a lost individual who didn’t know the difference between a parsnip and a potato. I left as a man who understands routine, patience, and the emotional weight of gifting someone the wrong flower on their birthday.

This game taught me discipline. Waking up at 6am every day to water crops I willingly planted? Character development. Passing out at 2am because I needed to fish one more time? Real-world consequences.

Stardew taught me relationships are built on consistency, kindness, and occasionally handing someone a mayonnaise jar until they love you. I learned that trust is earned… and that Pierre cannot be trusted under any circumstances.

I now measure time in seasons, money in gold, and self-worth in how efficiently I organize chests. I fear thunderstorms because they mean lightning rods, not weather. I see rocks and think “resources.” I see grass and think “wasted hay.”

Before Stardew, I was weak.
Now I am emotionally attached to pixels, deeply judgmental of JojaMart, and fully convinced I could survive off the land if given a farm, a town full of oddly intimate strangers, and infinite retries.

This game didn’t just make me relax.
It made me responsible.

To finish, Stardew Valley is definetely a game that will always make story, even if it stops updating, because the creator made possible that it receives a fanbase of love and respect.

✅ Maximum chill – perfect game to relax and reset your brain.

✅ No pressure gameplay – play your way, always.
✅ Insane replay value – every save feels like a new life.

Cons:

❌ Honestly? Almost none.
❌ Only downside: you lose track of time 😄

a quiet Sunday
a warm coffee in the morning
a peaceful walk with no destination

Look, on paper, you’re just inheriting your grandad’s old, weed-choked farm and trying to turn a profit. But calling this "just a farming game" is like calling a 5-star meal "just calories." It’s really about having the freedom to do whatever you want at your own speed.
The game thrives on that "just one more day" itch. Days only last about 15 or 20 minutes, so you’re constantly thinking, I’ll just wake up, check the melons, and then I’m done—and suddenly it’s 2:00 AM in real life.
There’s so much to do besides watering plants, too. You can lose hours to the fishing minigame, head into the mines to fight monsters for ore, or just forage through the woods. Plus, the people in town actually feel like neighbors; you can build friendships, and get married, which makes the whole world feel alive.
Toss in a soundtrack that perfectly matches the vibe of each season, and you’ve got this incredibly cozy, nostalgic escape that’s hard to put down.

Ok, so its been about 4 lifetimes since I've reviewed a steam game and looking back over the 3 games I did review, its clear I have an extraordinary talent for reviewing and i've become somewhat of an ambassador for the people who use a "joypoad" and as a result of high demand and much begging, I feel obliged to direct this god given talent towards a little gem known as starjew valley.

In recent months I've become a steam deck gamer, after basically retiring from gaming several years ago and starjew valley is a game I would frequently see recommended by other deck users, to other deck users, and other deck users multiplied by other deck users divided to the power of ten gives a square root of ok I'll decide for the people if this is fake news biased undeserved hype, or some kind of low level, don't answer the door, eat your KFC off the floor while playing bingo with your feet hands type genius.

I'll be honest, i was 90% sure this games praise was pure deck user "you gonna eat that cornbread?" type bias, and 37% there's potential, but I'd rather do homework even though school is a myth. However, much to my surprise, this game actually is one of the finest examples of "cosy" gaming there is.

From the minute I booted it up I was pretty charmed by the retro style graphics and music, and as I began to play the hours just started to fly by. The 61 hours at time of writing this masterclass in literature were actually accrued over a two day period. I played it hard, and found it hard to stop. I'm not going to breakdown the game, how it works, why it works, cause I can't be bothered tbh, but there's a beautiful balance and lack of pressure and demand on the player, and instead you're simply given the keys to your own little paradise to shape as you see fit.

What you can do in Starjew (apparently)

Want to be unemployed, single, and eat potatoes every day like real life? Starjew's got your back baby.

Want to simp for that little blonde chick Haley? Starjew gives you the keys to raid her bin broseph.

Oh, whats that? She likes Alex and seems to follow him around and he seems to not even make any effort but still wins her over? Unfortunately there's no option to jar your farts and mail them to him, but you can give Haley flowers and give Alex a broken CD you fished out of the lake, and any other literal trash you find.

Eventually you can cut him out the picture pretty much and now I can raid Haleys bedroom and check through her furniture for souvenirs and hang around in there until I literally collapse from exhaustion.

When you're not simping you can milk your chickens, or try to, i'm not giving up on my dream of starting a chicken milk product line and cutting an absolute mother of a deal with Pierre and one day in the future my goal is me and Haley live together, we make babies, I upgrade the chicken milk command centre, or home as other people might call it, and I just waltz around the town with a top hat an monocle while Haley holds my cape and my posse of chickens surround me like Kim Kardashians bodyguards, suited and booted while excreting milk as they strut and eyeball Alex and any other threat to Haley.

Overall verdict

I went into the game pretty skeptical tbh, almost wanted to hate it so I could tell people to stfu about it, but credit where it is due, this is a finely crafted slice of gaming that caught me by surprise, and maybe its not for everyone, but if you need something in your library for just kinda chilling, that's easy to play and you need somewhere to escape to, there's not really anything like this, not that I've played tbh. It made me think of animal crossing, but I think this is better tbh. How you say? Cause. That's how.

Steam Deck notes (specific points)

I also want to add some specific points worth noting for deck users.
I have the LCD deck an run the game at like 3 TDP, which is basically the deck is in a coma, a vegetative state, and it obviously handles it no problem and I don't know if there's a game that could possibly sip the battery anymore gently than this does. You're looking at 8-9 years off of a single charge.

With that in mind and the other benefits of the deck, the portability, sleep mode, steam and everything that brings, this is indeed a great deck game.
And the install size, its a diabolical 600 odd megabytes. Ooft.

Final conclusion

So my final conclusion is should you own this? Probably.
Will you play it? Dunno.
Is it right for you? You won't know until you've heard the dry squeak that comes from trying to milk your chickens or until you're raiding some chicks bin.
Is it a good deck game? Yes, but only if you have a deck. If you don't, then you may have difficulty running this on the deck.

there are several fun mechanics in Stardew that keep it feeling dynamic. The farming, fishing, mining/combat, helping the neighbors foraging/exploring, they all work together well to keep things moving along. You can choose a relaxed or more intense playthrough by choosing a couple or all of the challenges. I've chosen to focus on a few of those things in my first playthrough where as my wife plays to beat her perfection record. Choosing the perfection route and completing all the tasks and upgrades is not for the casual player though. The day/night and season cycles become more stressful the more challenges you choose. The feeling of accomplishing your goal for the day is really satisfying.

Some of the controls could be a bit better. I often pick something up and its in my hands when I don't want it there. Half the time I end up eating something I didn't want to or giving something to someone that negatively affects friendship levels. The selection box shouldn't stay on an empty inventory spot. The combat could be a bit more fluid if the weapons didn't take so long to swing before you could move again. It makes combat very sticky and inflexible. There doesn't seem to be a way to beat the game unless you're set your own time limit or goal such as completing all the quests given by townsfolk or perfection. I guess that's another thing to choose in the game. I still haven't decided what that is. Overall its a well made game with a lot of fun for those that enjoy the survival, crafter, adventure style.

I recommend this game if you have a special interest in farming games or are new to gaming as a hobby. But I didn't like it much. Let me explain why. 
-----
While playing I would have waves of enjoyment and boredom. I would do everything i could do, and then like an in-game week later will unlock a new thing that opens up the world a whole lot more. Having the world open up so often is a really awesome feeling, but it could have better pacing so I'm not bored waiting for the next new thing to get me hooked. I played on keyboard and it was a pretty awful experience control-wise. You gotta like, point vaguely at a direction to interact in that direction, but it's all vibe-based and sometimes just doesnt work at all. I'll be aiming left and my character smacks up. or have my cursor directly on a chest but it opens the chest next to it for no reason. These problems are especially exacerbating to the combat system. At first, the combat was fine for the first 80-90 levels of the Mines as its not taken seriously, the monsters are all cute creatures that hardly hurt you, but the later floors, and also the Skull Cavern you unlock later-- just take themselves too seriously. The combat system was not made for anything difficult to be implemented but the developer did so anyway. Another issue I had was that I wished the role-playing elements were stronger. The game starts out as you making your character. I made the character to be a self-insert, but I had very little control over my character's decisions or how I truly present myself as to the other characters. I want to be a homewrecker and date older gentleman >:). but no, the cast is almost entirely college-aged. Sure, theres like, Harvey, but he suspiciously has quite the baby-face going on. I just feel like I'm not the target demographic for the dating pool. Which is okay, but knowing beforehand how queer this game was I was expecting a lot more diversity (Not just talking about age) like for one, I dont think there's a single Asian in the game. and only one descriptively non-Caucasian dateable character? It's a shame. That's actually not completely true based on technicality, but would require spoilers to explain. This next issue may be a bit of a personal issue as I talked to my friends who have played this game, and while they have had issues, never to the extent of I had. but i had TONS of glitches in my playthrough. My save file got corrupted like 4 times in my 80 hours of playtime. Luckily, the game keeps yesterday's save as backup when-needed, so I never lost too much. It shouldn't have ever happened though, especially more than once.
+++++
To list out some positives: I think the level progression with skills and crafting and new abilities are all very well paced; the game is extremely QoL friendly, one example I'd like to shoutout is that despite normal chests and big chests being completely different items, you can just place a big chest ontop of a normal chest to upgrade it, keeping the inventory. Absolutely stunning thoughtfulness and every game needs to do this.; The mini-games, while being brutal in difficulty, were very fun to play.; Should be expected since it is majority a farming game, but the farming gameplay loop was fun, and trying to make your farm as optimal as possible can strike the fancy of a lot of people. All the characters have pretty distinct personalities, all of them had reasons to love them, and reasons to hate them with their character flaws.

Overall, I found the game to be mid and not for me. Still, I might come back to it someday to try out some of the most popular mod(pack)s to see if that makes the experience any bit more enjoyable for me. But mod support isn't native into Steam so I'm not factoring it into my review. 5.5/10

What begins as a simple farming simulator quickly reveals itself to be a profound, therapeutic, and deeply engaging experience that feels less like playing a game and more like coming home.

The "Just One More Day" Phenomenon
The premise is a classic trope: you inherit your grandfather's old farm plot to escape the soul-crushing drudgery of a corporate office job. However, the execution is flawless. The core gameplay loop—clearing land, planting seeds, watering crops, and harvesting the fruits of your labor—is incredibly satisfying.
There is a unique rhythm to the game that hooks you immediately. You wake up, check the weather, tend to your animals, and then decide how to spend your energy. Do you want to brave the depths of the mines to find rare ores? Do you want to spend a lazy afternoon fishing at the beach? or do you want to forage in the secret woods?

 Note: The genius of Stardew Valley is the lack of punishment. If you miss a harvest or forget to talk to a villager, the game doesn't punish you. It waits for you. This creates a stress-free environment that is purely motivated by your own desire to improve your farm.

A Living, Breathing World
Visually, the game is a triumph of 16-bit pixel art. The changing of the seasons is not just a gameplay mechanic but an aesthetic shift that changes the entire mood of the valley. From the floating pink petals of Spring to the cozy, melancholic snow of Winter, every screen is a painting.

Accompanying these visuals is a soundtrack that can only be described as iconic. Composed by the game's sole creator, Eric Barone (ConcernedApe), the music perfectly encapsulates the feeling of the season. The upbeat tunes of Summer make you want to work, while the gentle piano melodies of Winter encourage introspection.

Heart and Soul
Perhaps the most surprising depth lies in the villagers of Pelican Town. At first glance, they appear to be archetypes: the jock, the prep, the grumpy old man. But as you build relationships with them through gifts and conversation, you uncover genuine human struggles. You help characters deal with depression, alcoholism, PTSD, and family abandonment. The writing is empathetic and real, making the town feel populated by friends rather than NPCs.

The Verdict
Stardew Valley is a labor of love that respects the player’s time and intelligence. It is a game about connections—connecting with nature, connecting with a community, and reconnecting with a sense of peace that is often lost in modern life.

Whether you are a hardcore gamer looking for efficiency and optimization, or a casual player looking for a cozy escape, this game has something for you. It is, quite simply, pixelated perfection.

Pros
• The game never pressures you, and encourages you to be free of what you do as you please. You can just abandon a quest and never get repercussions for it. Losing random items from your inventory from collapsing at 2am/dying in the mines may be the harshest thing it can do. 
• The game is subject to many mods, allowing you to have experience beyond what SDV vanilla can offer
• The ambience and great music
• You can have as many pets as you want!

Now to the cons. Honestly, they're more of "I want these to be updated" rather than saying these are forever bad.

Cons
• Stardew Valley's writing, as of 1.6, for me, is weak. I've seen more headcanons/theories because there is little to no canon plot to discuss about. I've wanted to explore more story about the magic, or the Junimos. I would've loved it if there are more canon lore.
• Kids do not contribute to anything, except probably for the Steam achievement. 
• The only difference between marriage candidates after you marry them is their room, and their heart events. After that, they all function the same, watering crops, feed your pet/s, and fix fences.
• The characters' dialogues are repetitive, and you can only talk to them once a day. My pet peeve is Kent—I drop by to say hi, only to be [spoiler]trauma-dumped by how he lost his friends in battle.[/spoiler]
• Customizing buildings' colors may give you the satisfaction of "oh hey I can color it whatever I want!" only to find out that you can't, because you can't create pastel and everything other than red or brown comes off neon-ish.
• Barely any clues on what to gift to all the villagers. Difficult to do when you don't look up online/ask other players. I'm aware of the [spoiler]Secret notes[/spoiler], though they only cover a small amount of the villagers.
• No heart meter. I don't mean the 8/8 at the corner of their portraits, but a meter that describes how far am I from leveling up friendship with a villager.
• Community Center has no use after completion. The only impact it has is to deprive me of accessing Clint every Friday.

I was quite excited to play at first due to loving all the Stardew Valley games, Stardew Valley 1 being my first. I love the Stardew Valley universe, I am especially loving the new show on prime as well. Unfortunately after giving Stardew its fair shake and then some I can now write a fair review. For starters Stardew Valley first is heavily pushed onto you via limited stash space, without it the game becomes more of a storage organizer simulation.

Stardew Valley first grants you unlimited junk, ammo and medicine storage and without it you cannot consistently stockpile anything due to the stash limit of only 1200 lbs. Everything has weight from the lightest seed and foods and even just misc items. Also to sell anything in your player owned vendor each item while on sale also still takes up storage space at the same time. So everything you sell to other players eats up storage space at the same time, there is no split at all so unless you sell items fast they weigh you down. Even plans carry a weight of .25 lbs and there are hundreds of plans, they add up quickly.

You also get a survival tent and a private server with Stardew Valley first, the tent is like a small portable camp that you can place down to be able to scrap and repair items when needed. Without it you are stuck fast travelling back to camp every time, can't fast travel when overweight without specific perks. The private servers are almost a necessity when trying to farm items, public servers all share the same spawn points for items. If someone beats you to that item you have to switch servers or go through hoops to get what you need. A private server negates this, all items are just for you without having to fight anyone for it.

These are just a couple ways the creator of Stardew Valley pushes you to spend 13$ a month for honestly basic functionality in most other MMOs. Speaking of $$ the shop is disgusting, primarily full of re-skins for the same items over and over again. The creator of Stardew Valley just loves to get you with FOMO then nickel and dime you for another backpack skin that is exactly the same mesh as another. Items are overpriced with certain packs costing upwards of 1800 coins, which is almost 20$ for a small selection of similarly themed items. I can go on about the atom shop but it's just complaining at that point.

The story is disjointed and poorly written with quest chains ending abruptly or being nonsensical. The latest "huge" in game update 1.6.15 wound up being around 4 quests total with a new area added. At the point I was in the game, lvl 1500 at the time, I managed to clear the entire update and explored the new area in about 2 days. Once you hit a level plateau of about 300 the game becomes just a grind for levels for legendary perks. Lvl 300 is easy to get to very quickly and with little effort, cursory Google searches will guide you to hit that fast.

All in all I feel you can probably get a few months of quality game time in with this then it just becomes a repetitive slog all the way around. Game balancing is a joke as well, the meta changes constantly due to harsh nerfs to weapons. They nerf certain weapons into the ground instead of making less used weapons more desirable by buffing them, once you experience it a few times it becomes a huge annoyance.

If you want to play Stardew I say go for it, maybe it will click with you who knows. God knows I really really wanted to love it but after playing as much as I have the polish that once seemed great now is just so lackluster. It's supposed to be an MMO (lite) so the point is to pour gametime into an evolving world that feels alive. Stardew feels hollow, relies too heavily on FOMO and the nickel and diming with the shop just sink it lower. Once the initial wow factor wears off there's really not much to do in the game. Content is lacking and the daily concurrent player numbers are sad proof of that. Even with a highly rated show to tie into it it can't even muster better numbers than other single-player farming sims. At the end of the day I'd give it a 9 out of 10. A lot needs to change with the creator of Stardew Valley but the way things have been going I don't expect it to get any better. Cheers.

I've put hundreds of hours into Stardew Valley between console and PC and I can confidently say that this game is pure comfort in video game form. It takes the simple idea of farming and turns it into a deeply satisfying, endlessly charming life sim that somehow feels both relaxing and addictive at the same time.

From planting your first crop to building a thriving farm, every small victory feels meaningful. The gameplay loop is perfectly balanced: farm, fish, mine, explore, socialize, repeat—but it never gets boring. There’s always one more day you want to play, and suddenly it’s 2 a.m. (both in-game and real life lol).

The characters are where the game truly shines. Pelican Town feels alive, with villagers who have real personalities, struggles, and growth. Building relationships, attending festivals, and uncovering backstories makes the world feel warm and personal. You’re not just managing a farm, you’re becoming part of a community.

The pixel art is gorgeous and timeless, paired with many soundtracks that are soothing, nostalgic, and emotionally resonant. Each season feels distinct, and the game’s gentle pacing lets you play exactly how you want: min-max like a pro, roleplay a cozy farmer, or just vibe.

On top of all that, the sheer amount of content is amazing; secrets, quests, upgrades, romance, multiplayer, mods, etc. And it’s all crafted with obvious love by a single developer.

Stardew Valley is a masterpiece of cozy gaming. It’s relaxing without being shallow, deep without being stressful, and endlessly replayable. Whether you’re a hardcore gamer or someone who just wants a peaceful escape, this game is amazing! 1000% Recommend!

In this cozy game, you have to make sure you are managing you time. 20 minutes in real life is the whole day in Stardew Valley. And if you aren't in bed by 2 or 3 in the morning (I can't remember which one, I'm usually in bed by 1am) you lose some of your day and risk passing out in a random place and losing items on you.

I find myself constantly coming back to this game and trying out new farm types, play through styles and even making myself challenges while playing this game. Not to mention there are tons of mods to sort through to play as well, keeping the game feeling fresh and not boring while increasing the replayability. In a world filled with sprawling open-world epics and competitive online shooters, sometimes all you need is a quiet escape to the countryside. Stardew Valley offers just that, and it's an experience that’s nothing short of a modern classic. While it's not without a small flaw, the game delivers an incredible, heartwarming, and unforgettable journey that fully earns its place among the all-time greats.

Let's get the one minor gripe out of the way. Stardew Valley can be, at times, a "wiki game." There were countless moments where I found myself pausing the game, pulling up an online guide, and searching for a specific item, quest detail, or character preference. While a sense of discovery is a wonderful thing, the game’s lack of in-game direction can occasionally feel more confusing than challenging. This is a common issue with a certain genre of sandbox games, but it’s still a valid point of critique.

Despite that one issue, every other element of Stardew Valley is a masterclass in game design.
First and foremost, the music is simply phenomenal. The melodies are charming and catchy, perfectly capturing the peaceful, rural life and embedding themselves in your memory long after you’ve stopped playing. The fact that this, along with every other aspect of the game, was created by a single person, Eric Barone (ConcernedApe), is absolutely astounding and a testament to his talent.

In terms of value, Stardew Valley is an incredible deal. For a price of around $15, you can easily sink well over 100 hours into a single save file, and many players push that to 150 or more to achieve 100% completion. The hours-to-dollars ratio is off the charts, making it one of the most worthwhile purchases in gaming.

The art style is another triumph. The beautiful, detailed pixel art is a joy to behold. The character models, items, and environments are all meticulously crafted. What truly stands out, however, is the dynamic art for each season. The way the game's surface level completely transforms with the changing weather from vibrant spring greens to crisp autumn oranges to a gentle winter blanket of snow is a true artistic feat.

What truly gives the game its soul are the characters and their stories. The villagers of Pelican Town are far more than simple NPCs. They are a collection of diverse and complex individuals, each with their own personal struggles, from PTSD to alcoholism, and their own secrets. Earning their trust and watching them slowly accept you, an outsider, into their community is an incredibly rewarding experience. These emotional arcs, often culminating in deeply moving moments, give the world a rich, human depth that few other games can match.

Finally, the gameplay loop itself is an exercise in satisfying prioritization and planning. The day-to-day rhythm of tending crops, raising animals, and mining for resources is perfectly paced into short, digestible days. This bite-sized structure makes the game easy to pick up and hard to put down. It presents a constant challenge of balancing time and resources, making every successful harvest or crafted item feel earned.

Stardew Valley is a loving tribute to the indie genre and a shining example of what a single, passionate developer can achieve. It's an approachable and engaging entry point for new gamers and a profound experience for veterans. While it may rely on outside resources for some guidance, its beautiful art, unforgettable music, deep characters, and addicting gameplay easily make it one of the greatest games ever made. For its singular issue and five overwhelming positives, Stardew Valley receives a 9/10. You owe it to yourself to play this game.

Stardew Valley changed my life in ways I honestly never expected.

I am a 38 year old divorced woman with 2 kids. My life wasn’t crashing all at once—it was decaying slowly. My husband and I didn’t have explosive fights. It was worse than that. We argued about nothing. Dishes left out. Money. That awful silence at dinner where no one wants to be the first to speak. They say communication is key but we had none of that.

One night, after another pointless argument about groceries, he went to sleep on the couch. I stayed up, scrolling. That’s when I saw it.
Saw her.
Haley.
She looked so pretty. So feminine. So rude. I thought, Sure. Why not.

I named my farm after my biggest goal of the game; Haley

That’s where it all went wrong.

I started waking up early—not for work, not for my kids—but to water parsnips. I knew the villagers’ schedules better than my own family’s. I remembered birthdays. I listened. I helped. I mattered. I. MATTERED.

No one yelled at me in Pelican Town. No one judged the way I used to water my seeds everyday before I knew sprinklers even existed.

My husband asked why I was smiling at my screen at two in the morning. I didn’t answer. He wouldn't understand anyway. I was fishing. Willy needed me. My crops needed me. The community center needed me. Haley needed me.

Weeks went by.

My marriage didn’t survive the winter, but my farm did. Even though I didn't have a greenhouse, I used that as a chance to get to know the game more. A break from farming, but more foraging, mining and fishing.

When the divorce papers arrived, I felt strangely empty. I had just unlocked the greenhouse. My kids asked why I seemed distant. I told them I was “working on myself.” That wasn’t a lie. I had hit level 10 farming.

Now I live alone. My house is quiet, but my barn is full. I have truffle oil money. I have a wife who lives in my computer and loves me no matter what. I have a cat and a dog that never judges me.

Do I miss my old life? Sometimes.
Do I regret it? No.

Because when I lie in bed at night, listening to the soft Stardew Valley music, I know one thing for sure:

Haley would never treat me like that.

10/10.

My favorite farming sim that I consider a 10/10, this game is a wonderful anomaly because despite being developed by one young solo dev with a dream, he made a hit game that is both simple and extremely deep. You can play as you like and play blindly or min/max with guides and the stardew fandom wiki, with both paths being viable. A very good pick up and play game. What makes it so easy for me too is you can drop the game for a while and come right back in and pick it up, and just chill out. Stardew Valley is the epitome of the cozy game genre, and easily one of the most well-known entries in it. At its core, it is enjoyable. It delivers exactly what it promises: a classic farming loop mixed with mining for ore and gems, light combat in the caves, and the constant pressure of making it back to bed before midnight.

The world is rich with charm, and it’s obvious how much time and love went into crafting the story and its characters. Pelican Town feels lived in, and the game offers an enormous amount of content for players willing to sink dozens—if not hundreds—of hours into it.

That said, Stardew Valley isn’t particularly welcoming if you try to return after a long break. Jumping back in without starting over can feel disorienting, with systems, goals, and routines that assume you remember exactly where you left off. While that may be a personal issue, it does make the game less enjoyable to pick up years later, especially if you’re no longer as invested in the farming-and-mining style of cozy games.

Ultimately, Stardew Valley is a lovingly made classic, but it shines brightest when experienced continuously rather than revisited after time away.

[h1]Stardew Valley — A game that calms and delights[/h1]

I first heard about Stardew Valley from an old friend back in school, and at the time, I never could’ve imagined that such a simple-looking pixel farming simulator would completely hook me. Its slow pace, simple tasks, and freedom of choice pulled me in right away: every day on the farm brought small, but genuine joy, and the world around felt alive in its own quiet way.

Gradually, I started discovering everything the farm had to offer. At first, it was just planting seeds, watering them, and harvesting crops. But over time, new plants, animals, building upgrades, cooking recipes, and secrets kept appearing, and I wanted to uncover them all. What I loved most was the freedom: you can focus purely on farming, or dive into the mines, fishing, or building relationships with the townspeople. Every choice feels meaningful, and every little bit of progress — no matter how small — feels like a personal victory that keeps you coming back for more.

What really stands out is how alive the world of Stardew Valley feels. Every character seems like a real person with their own habits, joys, and problems. Town events, festivals, small quests — it all creates a sense of life you can genuinely care about. The music is soft and unobtrusive, and the pixel art, simple as it may seem, actually creates a cozy, immersive atmosphere where you just want to linger and watch the days unfold on your farm.

Whether you want the governor to taste the mayors shorts or ignore some forest spirits and power fund your way to restoring the community center, stardew valley is filled which amazing characters, interactions and gameplay. Level up 5 skills such as: Farming, Foraging, Fishing (you're telling me this salmon is void??), We yearn for the mines, and combat.

Meet the local townspeople such as:
- Lewis, shorts guy

- Pam, drunkard, BUT also drives
- Jas (Child #1)
- Vincent (Child #2)
- Haley, lover of the rainbow rock
- Pierre, hider of 'secret stashes' 
- Abigail, quartz consumer

Each villager feels uniquely crafted with their own experiences, especially with their own heart events that allow you to understand them more than just a as a pixel art-styled fictional character with only a unique set of clothes in winter. You can even date/marry some people in this game! 
Don't like interaction? Doesn’t matter, some of them will appear at your doorstep.

Well, you can focus on your farm instead! Gifted by grandpa on his state-of-the-art bed, by the time you arrive the farm is full of weeds and debris that you can clear with your starter tools. Make sure to visit the local blacksmith (too late he's closed) so that you don't spend your life knowing that it takes 8 swings to mine gold ore with a basic pickaxe. Decorate your farm with paths, fences, general decor and rarecrows! Make sure to plant some crops, craft some useful items and have fun at your own pace. I like hows there's not much rush to get things done, and that there's things to be done until almost the endgame where you buy a clock for 10 million. 

I'm genuinely baffled how this almost 10 year old game is made by one person, coding, art, music and all, and is still getting updates (1.7 woohoo!). Thank you epic bologna for making this, and I will treasure this game forever.
