Stardew Valley is my favorite game of all time, and it's not even close. The beauty of this game is that you can play in any way and at any pace you want. You can be and do whatever you want. Sure, it's a farming sim if you want it to be, but every day you wake up you could also choose to go mining and fight interesting monsters, roam the forest and forage, go on a fishing trip to the ocean, river, or lake, build relationships with the village NPCs (and marry them!), raise and care for animals, organize and decorate your farm, collect materials to restore the Community Center, attend village festivals and see marvels such as the moonlight jellies, and so much more. Your progress is rewarded, too. The more you progress, the more you can automate and make easier, allowing you to get more done in a day. You can race to unlock things, level up, minmax your farm, make quick profits, finish all the achievements, and achieve perfection, or you can play slow and do whatever you like each day. The Wiki gives you all the info you could need, and the online community is great. Just the sheer range of fun things to do each in-game day has kept this game forever fresh for me, and I'm learning and encountering new things even 1100 hours in. I highly recommend this game, and I think it's got something for everyone to enjoy.

Stardew Valley is a masterpiece of cozy gaming that manages to be both a relaxing farm simulator and a deep strategic RPG. You inherit your grandfathers old dilapidated plot of land in Pelican Town and leave behind a soul crushing office job to start a new life. What follows is a beautifully crafted experience about community growth and the simple satisfaction of a hard days work.

The core gameplay loop is perfectly balanced. Your days are spent clearing land planting crops and managing your limited energy levels. As the seasons change so do the challenges and rewards. I found a deep sense of peace in the routine of watering my parsnips and checking the weather report but the game never feels stagnant. Just when you think you have mastered farming the world opens up to reveal fishing mining and a surprisingly dangerous combat system in the local caves.

The inhabitants of Pelican Town are the heart of the experience. Each villager has their own schedule likes dislikes and personal struggles. Building relationships through gifts and conversation unlocks unique heart events that make the characters feel like real friends. Whether you are helping the local museum recover its lost artifacts or deciding between the corporate interests of JojaMart and the restoration of the Community Center your choices shape the future of the valley.

Visually the pixel art is timeless and vibrant. Each season has its own color palette and musical score that perfectly captures the mood from the hopeful chirps of spring to the quiet melancholy of winter. The level of detail is staggering with secrets tucked away in every corner of the map and a massive amount of end game content that keeps the story going long after the first year.

10/10. It is a rare game that feels like a warm hug. It respects your time allows you to play at your own pace and offers a level of depth that many big budget titles fail to achieve. 

Whether you want to be a master winemaker a legendary fisher or just a good neighbor Stardew Valley is a place you can truly call home.

 There are many different types of activities to do in the farm and in the village, and that allows you to play the game in whatever way you prefer. There is a task for every player, and every mechanic works harmoniously with one another (which is surprising, considering the insane amount of things you can do).
 The game doesn't teach you everything, only the basics. It's helpful to follow a guide or read the game wiki if you want to take the most out of it right away. However, there isn't a story and you could play with the same character and farm forever, so I don't think it's necessary to rush or stress too much about playing in the "optimal way". the base game does have flaws that usually would ward me off from playing. no option to play as a nonbinary farmer, while also only having one notable nonbinary NPC; the town being an idealised rural southern americana translates into a noticeable lack of ethnic variety; ginger island's colonial undertones as the player builds over an island where the only "ethnic" variety comes from the local pirates and anthro animals - these issues have been around for a long time, and discussed to death long before i started playing.

luckily, i knew about these issues going into the game and was able to find mods that address them. mods that enable playing a nonbinary farmer, and diversify the cast (both with new characters and the originals), have enabled me to feel comfortable with this game's world, and consequently discover just how rich the gameplay is. seriously, even just the base game has so much to do and explore, which is made obvious by the chase for Perfection when you get into lategame stages of your farm.

of course i didn't stop at just installing a few mods; instead, every one of my playthroughs has been on a [i]megamodded[/i] farm, such that the volume of things to do skyrockets far beyond the base game's scope. choosing whether to explore the ridgeside village forest, or check on the crops passively growing on the meadow farm by east scarp, or figuring out where to catch all the new fish - having all of these extra activities means i am almost never bored from running out of tasks.
maybe my complete lack of experience with vanilla rubs some stardew purists the wrong way. but even without megamodding i'd still have to use at least [i]some[/i] mods, so as to address the game's first-mentioned flaws. this is also why i'd never consider playing on console - or even android, since that platform is less reliable with running mods - the PC version is [i]the[/i] go-to, by far.

it might seem a bit strange then, to base so much of this review on my entirely modded 800 hours of playtime (which, spoiler: [spoiler]a good few hours were spent idle overnight on the stardrop launcher, oops[/spoiler]). but since megamodded is all i've known, this is what i have to say.
i think it's fair to say that this game has incredibly robust modding frameworks and a passionate modding scene that continues to breathe more and more life into this already well-blossomed game. and the absolute freedom to create more content for this game, without worrying about a company breathing down the necks of both modders and players (good time to throw shade at dinkum hehe), is an important part of what makes this game special. whenever there's a fun NPC event, or some wild luck in the caves, or i figure out a new method to make that dough, i think to myself: "damn, i love this game."

At 46 hours, and on "Year 2" of the game, I think I am in a good place to review this game fairly. This game is great in so many aspects of its design. It's a much-improved version of other chill farming / community games, like Animal Crossing and, more directly, Harvest Moon. The gameplay and progression is excellent, and the visuals age like wine, but the real thing that keeps you invested is the characters and the writing. Every single character in the game, from the kids playing under the tree, to the town mayor to the shopkeeper, all have a character arc. They all interact with the other characters. There are dialogue options in which characters remember previous choices. And the characters can address some pretty adult themes, such as alcoholism, mid-life crisis, homelessness, war, and so on, but the game does this with with class and isn't obnoxious about it. 

The vibes are like Mr. Roger's Neighborhood meets Bob Ross. It's very laid back and positive and is very aware of why YOU, the player, are playing it. The premise is that you are working at a job you dislike, in the city, and that the world is slowly draining your life's light with a constant barrage of bad news, monotony, and social isolation. So your character (you), decide to start over in a small community to take over your grandfather's farm. This is probably close to the real-life reason of why you are attracted to this game.

I recommend you give it a try, even if you normally aren't into this kind of game. You won't regret it, and you may end up re-evaluating your own life and priorities because of it.

As a spiritual successor to the classic Harvest Moon series, Stardew Valley delivers on all fronts. From cultivating fields and expanding your farm, to exploring underground mines and engaging with village life, the game elevates every core mechanic to a new level. This is achieved through heartfelt storytelling and numerous gameplay additions that enrich the overall experience.

From the very beginning—when you clear your first fields of wood, stone, and bushes to plant your initial crops—the familiar Harvest Moon feeling immediately sets in. After just a few in-game days, harvesting your first produce, planting new crops, and steadily increasing your profits to unlock additional content becomes highly addictive. The progression through the seasons further enhances this loop, as each season introduces new crops and visual changes to the environment, keeping the gameplay fresh and engaging.

The parallel storylines of the individual villagers, while entirely optional, greatly contribute to the game’s cozy and comforting atmosphere. Activities such as gathering resources, fishing, or mining for materials are equally addictive and constantly motivate the player to keep going. If it were not for the day–night cycle forcing the player to go to bed at night, it would be very difficult to stop playing at all.

The expansion of the mines, the addition of the desert area, and the extensive endgame content—including a newly unlockable island with additional farmland, crops, and quests—all have a very positive impact on the overall gameplay experience. There is always something to discover, something to do, or some aspect of the farm to optimize. As a result, the enjoyment only begins to decline after well over 100 hours of playtime.

If I were asked to name a negative aspect of the game, I could only point to the enforced bedtime mechanic, which occasionally pulls me away from the fun when I would rather continue playing. Aside from that, Stardew Valley is, in my view, a clear 11/10. It stands as a perfect game and a truly worthy successor to Harvest Moon, earning its place among the all-time greats. I highly recommend this game to anyone who is still undecided.

Stardew Valley is the kind of game that looks simple at first—plant crops, water them, go to bed—but it slowly turns into a whole routine you start caring about. It’s a calm “new life” fantasy that becomes surprisingly hard to put down once you’re invested in your farm and the people in town.

The day-to-day gameplay loop is incredibly satisfying. You’re constantly choosing between farming, fishing, mining, foraging, or just improving your property, and almost everything feeds back into progress. Even small upgrades—better tools, a bigger backpack, sprinklers—feel like real quality-of-life wins that change how you play.

What makes the world feel alive is the town and its characters. Building relationships isn’t just a checklist; it’s a steady drip of little scenes, gifts, and stories that make you feel like you belong there. Some characters grow on you over time, and the seasonal festivals help break up the routine and make the year feel like it has its own rhythm.

The mining and combat side adds a nice contrast to the peaceful farming. It gives you a reason to gear up, plan your day, and take risks for better resources. Combat isn’t the deepest system in the world, but it’s good enough to keep the caves feeling tense, especially when you’re pushing for one more floor before heading home.

Progress can be as relaxed or as optimized as you want. You can min-max profits and plan crops like a spreadsheet, or you can spend an entire day decorating your house and wandering around. The game supports both styles, and that flexibility is a big reason it appeals to so many different kinds of players.

It’s not flawless, though. Early game can feel a bit grindy before you unlock the tools that speed everything up, and inventory management can be annoying until you expand it. Combat can also feel a little rough compared to the rest of the game’s polish, and late-game goals sometimes turn into “collect a lot of stuff” rather than truly new experiences.

Overall, Stardew Valley is a cozy, addictive time-sink with a lot more depth than it first appears to have. If you like games where small daily decisions build into a bigger story you create yourself, this is one of the best in the genre. It’s easy to recommend—especially if you want a game that’s both relaxing and quietly absorbing.

Stardew Valley – A Game That Never Truly Ends

Stardew Valley is not just a farming game; it’s a peaceful escape, a second life, and one of the most beautifully designed indie games ever created. At first glance, it may look simple, but the depth hidden beneath its pixel art is absolutely incredible.

I’ve played over 100+ hours, and even after all that time, I still haven’t fully completed the story — and that’s the magic of Stardew Valley. The game never rushes you. It lets you play at your own pace, whether you want to farm, fish, mine, build relationships, or simply enjoy the calm atmosphere of Pelican Town.

Every villager feels alive, with their own personalities, struggles, and stories that slowly unfold over time. Building relationships isn’t just about gifting items — it’s about understanding people, their pasts, and their emotions. This makes the world feel deeply personal and real.

The gameplay loop is incredibly relaxing yet addictive. One more day turns into one more season, and before you realize it, hours have passed. There’s always something new to discover — hidden events, secrets, festivals, upgrades, and long-term goals that keep pulling you back in.

What truly makes Stardew Valley special is how it makes you feel. It’s calming without being boring, deep without being overwhelming, and emotional without forcing drama. Even after 100+ hours, the fact that the story still isn’t fully complete shows just how much content and heart this game has.

Stardew Valley isn’t about finishing everything quickly — it’s about enjoying the journey. And that journey feels endless in the best way possible.

When the fatigue of concrete jungles seeps into your bones, a call emerges from between the pixels—not an escape, but a return.

Stardew Valley is a love letter to the earth. It lets you touch not just soil, but the very texture of time itself. You lift your hoe at dawn, when the dew still clings to the grass, and return under a moon-washed sky as twilight bleeds into night. The seasons turn in gentle 16-bit hues: spring with its drifting cherry blossoms, summer alive with fireflies, autumn thick as maple syrup, and winter warmed by the crackle of a hearth. Here, time is not a whip at your back but a stream you can sip slowly.

Yet beneath this land runs a vein more precious than any harvest—the people, each carrying their own scars and stories. The veteran drinking alone in the bar corner, the old curator mending fragments of memory, the one-eyed boy staring at the sea from the pier… Every conversation quietly knits back the frayed threads of the community. Until one festival evening, you find yourself laughing by the bonfire, truly home.

The game’s deepest magic lies in turning labor into poetic meditation. You plant not just seeds, but days of anticipation; you catch not just fish, but the breath of an entire world beneath the waves; in the mines, each swing of the pickaxe echoes against the hidden chambers of your own heart. When your first jar of pickles matures, when a chick pecks free from its shell, a primal satisfaction stirs within—an ancient covenant between humanity and the land, diluted by modern life but never forgotten.

More astonishing is how this seemingly simple pixelated world holds quiet depths. The abandoned Community Center’s silent plea, the blue shadow of Joja Corporation, the dreams within the Wizard’s Tower… the game gently asks: as traditions fade and connections thin, how do we rebuild a sense of place? Every choice you make becomes part of the answer.

Here, success is not measured in gold, but in the laughter that returns to Pelican Town because of you—in the vintage aging in your cellar, in the coat your partner drapes over your shoulders on a rainy night. It heals not by offering an illusion, but by reminding you how to sink roots into the earth, and how to turn passing days into a life worth savoring.

So if you ever hear the rain tapping on leaves outside your window, if you still remember the scent of wet soil—then the train to Stardew Valley is arriving. Bring the parts of you that still yearn for something real, and claim your rusty hoe. A life meant to be lived slowly awaits.

I bought this expecting a relaxing farming game to play for maybe an hour here and there. Next thing I knew, it was 3 AM and I was frantically trying to finish the Community Center bundles before Winter started.

Why you should play it:

The Loop: The "just one more day" syndrome is real. Since days are only ~15 minutes long, it's impossible to put down.

The Vibe: The music is incredible and the pixel art is charming. It’s genuinely relaxing until you realize you forgot to buy seeds and the store is closed on Wednesdays.

Variety: You can farm, fish, mine, fight monsters, or just run around town giving gifts to people so they will like you. There is no wrong way to play.

Pros:

Super chill atmosphere.

The feeling of progression is perfect.

You get to name your chickens.

Cons:

Fishing takes some getting used to.

Pierre’s General Store is closed on Wednesdays (it’s annoying).

You will lose track of real time.

Verdict: I'm 30 hours in and I feel like I've barely scratched the surface. If you need a game to relax with after work (or to accidentally binge all weekend), this is the one.

Stardew Valley is one of those games that quietly becomes special the more time you spend with it. The pixel art is beautiful in a simple, cozy way, and every season feels alive with its own colors, music, and atmosphere. There’s something really calming about starting your day on the farm, talking to villagers, fishing by the river, or just watching the sun set over Pelican Town.

What makes the game stand out is how much care and personality is in everything. The characters feel real, the music is memorable, and there’s always something meaningful to work toward without the game ever feeling stressful. Whether you’re farming, mining, decorating, or just relaxing, Stardew Valley makes you slow down and enjoy the moment.

It’s a genuinely beautiful game — not just visually, but emotionally. Easy to recommend to anyone who wants a peaceful, rewarding experience.

So I bought Stardew Valley thinking I'd relax for an hour.
That was January 2026.
I have no idea what year it is anymore.
The game starts innocently enough. You inherit a charming little farm, meet friendly townsfolk, pet some chickens, and think, "I'll just water my crops and then go to bed."
That, my friends, was the first lie.
Every in-game day ends with:
"Okay, just one more day."
Then suddenly you're optimizing sprinkler layouts like you're managing a Fortune 500 company. You're carrying seventeen different crops, twelve jars of mayonnaise, three mysterious artifacts, a fish that only appears every third Tuesday during a thunderstorm at exactly 6:40 PM while Mercury is in retrograde, and somehow you're still late to Pierre's before he closes.
Meanwhile, real life has completely fallen apart.
My laundry has become an archaeological dig site.
My dishes have formed diplomatic relations with the mold.
My family checks on me by sliding food under the door like I'm a dangerous zoo animal.
I haven't seen the sun in so long that I flinched when Windows switched to light mode.
Inside Stardew, however?
Millionaire.
Married.
Two kids. (I think I have 4 IRL, but I honestly can't remember)
An ancient wine empire.
A fully automated farm that NASA would be jealous of.
Best friends with an actual wizard.
Saved the community.
Own an island resort.
Outside the game?
I celebrated my birthday because my Steam friends wished me happy birthday before my actual family remembered.
The worst part is how Stardew rewires your brain.
I'll walk outside and see a dandelion and instinctively think:
"Nice. That's 40g."
It starts raining and my first thought isn't "I should grab an umbrella."
It's:
"Sweet. I don't have to water the crops."
Then reality hits...
I don't HAVE crops.
I have a mortgage.
The soundtrack has become my internal monologue.
I hear birds chirping and immediately wonder where Linus is hiding.
Someone mentions mayonnaise and I instinctively calculate artisan profit margins.
At this point I'm convinced ConcernedApe didn't make a farming simulator.
He made the most polite hostage situation ever created.
No explosions.
No violence. (Well except for serpants flying at your face at mach 286.
No dragons threatening the kingdom.
Just one tiny little sentence that has consumed thousands of hours of my life:
"One more day."
Final Verdict:
Graphics: Cozy enough to erase responsibilities. ★★★★★
Gameplay: Accidentally invents time travel. ★★★★★
Difficulty: Explaining why it's suddenly 3:47 AM. ★★★★★
Impact on Social Life: "Your friends have forgotten what you look like." ★★★★★
Would I recommend it?
Absolutely.
Would I warn people first?
Also absolutely.
Because Stardew Valley isn't a game...
It's a legally purchased black hole where weekends, responsibilities, and entire seasons disappear without a trace.
Now if you'll excuse me...
I just need to harvest one more crop.
...and that's definitely where I'll stop.

Stardew Valley is one of those rare games that feels nearly perfect across every category of gameplay. No matter what kind of player you are, there is something here that works.

If you enjoy combat and exploration, the different types of mines offer plenty of opportunities for challenge and discovery. If fishing is more your thing, the fishing system actually requires skill and timing, making it far more engaging than the usual “press a button and wait” approach found in many games. On the creative side, you can customize your character’s clothing, decorate your farm, and carefully design the layout of your buildings, all while still enjoying the core farming mechanics that define the game.

When I first played Stardew Valley years ago, shortly after it was released, I assumed it was just a relaxed farming simulator with little depth. I was very wrong. The game is packed with interesting storylines, surprising plot twists, and genuinely funny moments. The villagers feel alive, and building relationships with them adds emotional weight to the experience. You can even get married, which makes for a fun and rewarding side goal.

The achievements are another strong point. Most of them progress naturally over time, which feels fair and satisfying. At the same time, they are challenging enough that completing them actually means something. Some are difficult enough to show real skill, especially the Prairie King mini-game, which I still have not managed to beat. That challenge alone says a lot.

Overall, Stardew Valley is an incredibly impressive game. Even after years of imitators and so-called “cozy farming” knock-offs, none have come close to matching its depth, charm, and balance. Stardew Valley sets the standard, and it remains unmatched.

A timeless comfort game

Stardew Valley is one of those rare games that you can always come back to, no matter how much time has passed.

What starts as a simple farming game slowly opens up into something much deeper: building relationships with villagers, exploring mines, decorating your farm, fishing at 2am because “just one more day,” and constantly finding new little goals to work toward. It’s relaxing when you want it to be, and surprisingly engaging when you dive deeper.

The freedom to play at your own pace is what makes it special. You can min-max everything, or you can just enjoy tending your crops and living a quiet virtual life — both approaches feel equally valid.

It’s also fantastic in co-op. Sharing a farm, dividing tasks, and slowly growing something together adds a whole new layer to the experience.

Whether you’re new to farming sims or already love the genre, Stardew Valley is an easy recommendation. Few games manage to be this cozy, deep, and endlessly replayable at the same time.

❤️ Highly Recommended

I bought this game because I needed a break from wiping on raid bosses. I thought, "Hey, a relaxing farming game." I was wrong. This isn't a relaxing game. [b]This is an intense economic optimization simulator disguised as a cute pixel cartoon.[/b]

[hr][/hr]

[h2]1. The Gameplay: "The Daily Quests Never End"[/h2]
In WoW, I complain about doing my dailies. In Stardew Valley, I wake up at 6:00 AM sharp, water 400 blueberries, pet 12 chickens, and sprint to the store before it closes at 5:00 PM.

* [b]The Rotation:[/b] Instead of [i]1, 2, 3, 4[/i], my rotation is [i]Hoe, Water, Seed, Water[/i]. If I miss a global cooldown, my crops die. The stress is real.
* [b]The Combat:[/b] The mines are basically a dungeon crawl. The slimes have aggro ranges. I am hitting them with a sword. I feel at home, except the loot is rocks instead of Epics.
* [b]Fishing:[/b] This is the hardest boss mechanic I have ever faced. Forget the Lich King; trying to catch a Sturgeon requires more focus than a Mythic raid.

[h2]2. The NPCs: "Bribing People for Friendship"[/h2]
The social system is weird. In other games, I gain reputation by killing the enemies of a faction. Here, I gain reputation by handing people raw eggs and mayonnaise twice a week.

* [b]The Wizard:[/b] There is a Wizard. He doesn't give me quests to save the world; he just wants void essence. I respect his hustle.
* [b]The Romance:[/b] I decided to marry Abigail because she eats rocks. That is the kind of tank-like constitution I look for in a partner.
* [b]Linus:[/b] He is the best NPC. He lives in a tent and eats trash. I trust him with my life.

[h2]3. The Graphics: "16-Bit Bliss"[/h2]
I have a great gaming PC, and I am using it to play a game that looks like it runs on a Super Nintendo. And honestly? It’s beautiful.
* [b]No Lag:[/b] I can plant 500 pumpkins and my framerate doesn't drop. Take notes, modern AAA developers.
* [b]The Vibe:[/b] It’s charming. It makes me want to move to the country and learn what a "turnip" actually is.

[hr][/hr]

[h3]Final Verdict[/h3]
[b]5/5 Blue Chickens.[/b]

Spoilers below probs. I really liked Stardew Valley, but I didn’t quite fall head over heels for it. I played Coral Island first, which is almost the same game structurally just in 3D instead of 2D pixel art, and I think that shaped my experience a lot. Coral Island won me over with stronger character writing and automation options like conveyors that let you build a full on farm operation, Stardew feels more hands on and as a result you have to do a lot more work.

That said, Stardew Valley does an incredible amount right. I don’t usually like pixel graphics, but for pixel graphics, this game is genuinely beautiful. The Moonlight Jellies festival, the way leaves and flower petals drift through the air in different seasons, and the cozy atmosphere all work together in a way that’s hard to deny. There’s also an absurd amount to do. Easter eggs are everywhere, but even with notes and letters, some secrets are so well hidden that I ended up consulting guides every single play session.

I 100%ed the game, and every achievement felt doable except for Prairie King without dying. That minigame broke me. I hated it. Truly, deeply. I eventually installed a mod just to get through it because my patience had fully evaporated, and I regret nothing.

My biggest gripe is the character writing outside of cutscenes. Most of the heart events are great, but day to day dialogue can feel off. Sebastian calling me 'dear' after marriage grated on my nerves in a way I can’t fully explain. He went from moody programmer to oddly lame husband overnight, and I genuinely considered divorcing him and letting Krobus move in instead. I didn't but I REALLY thought about it and that comes from a person who gets obsessed with my fiction BF's a lot more than I'd like to admit. 

Still, progression in Stardew feels fantastic. Every upgrade matters, every unlock feels earned, and you can really feel yourself becoming more efficient and capable over time. There’s a lot to manage, but the calendar helps immensely if you actually use it. Compared to Coral Island, where the kids never grow out of their cribs, I did appreciate seeing my Stardew toddlers wandering around in little hats (they were so cute!). That was a nice touch.

Overall, this is a great game, and I completely understand why it’s as beloved as it is. Coral Island feels like home to me. I log into that farm between games just to check in. I don’t know if Stardew Valley will be that kind of comfort game for me, but I could definitely see myself doing another playthrough someday, especially with mods, and there are a lot of very cool ones out there.

Stardew Valley – A Cozy Masterpiece That Keeps Growing

Stardew Valley is one of those rare games that quietly settles into your life and refuses to leave — in the best possible way. What starts as a simple escape from city life quickly becomes a deeply personal adventure full of charm, heart, and endless things to do. Whether you're tending crops, mining for rare gems, fishing at sunrise, or getting to know the wonderfully quirky villagers, the game always gives you something meaningful to work toward.

What really sets Stardew Valley apart is the feeling of calm satisfaction it delivers. Days pass at a gentle pace, letting you build your farm and your relationships exactly the way you want. There’s no pressure, no rush — just an inviting world that grows alongside you. The writing is surprisingly emotive, too; each character has their own story, and watching them develop over time feels rewarding.

The game also rewards creativity. Your farm can become anything: a highly automated machine, a cozy cottage garden, or an elaborate vineyard. Every choice feels personal, and no two playthroughs end up the same.

With regular updates, tons of content, and a thriving modding community, Stardew Valley feels more alive now than ever. It’s easy to recommend to anyone who enjoys farming sims, RPGs, or simply a relaxing game to unwind with. This is one of the most heartfelt indie projects ever made — and it shows in every detail.

Stardew Valley has truly earned its reputation as one of the most, if not the most, beloved games on the entire Steam platform. Made by a single individual, it is an undisputed labor of love that continues to receive updates to this day. There is also mod support and a large modding community to help provide players with anything that they may be missing. The soundtrack is so iconic and memorable that Stardew Valley has its own concert on tour. 

The quintessential farming game, Stardew Valley is a story about an escape from the draining corporate job and city life to go out to the countryside to become a farmer. Entirely at the player's own pace, the player can make money, acquire and upgrade tools, acquire new buildings and equipment, make alterations to their home and to the town itself and become more integrated with the town as a whole. Farming, foraging, fishing, mining and combat are the skills that the player can evolve, on top of getting closer to the townspeople (sometimes in romantic ways as well) and delving into the town's more "hidden" mysteries.

Stardew Valley's biggest appeal is the fact that it can appeal to almost every kind of player. Looking for a cozy game to do whatever you want in a nice, peaceful place? Covered. Looking to speedrun and/or micromanage every possible detail to advance and profit as fast as physically possible? Covered. Obsessed with growing weed and looking for a laugh? Covered (through modding). Looking to play solo when you have some time? Covered. Looking to play with friends online and work together? Covered. Looking back at the clock and realizing that you accidentally played for way too long? Covered.

In terms of progression, Stardew Valley is most satisfying in the early and mid-game, while the player is evolving their skills, tools, buildings, animals and bankroll. Since Stardew files can be played continually for in-game year after year, it does eventually reach a point where there isn't much for the player to do (usually when all else is complete and the player is trying to make money to acquire the most expensive endgame items and structures). While going this far is an option is available for those seeking full completion, the option to simply start a new file is also there for you.

Overall, Stardew Valley is the definitive "cozy" game on Steam and anyone who is into that sort of thing should play it. It stole away years of my life and I wouldn't change a thing about it. 10/10.

I've played this game way too much.  I have a kind of love/hate relationship with it.  It is very addicting, but not in a good way, in my opinion. I keep wondering what it is that keeps drawing me back to the game, as it is really simple, has hardly any challenge to it (if you can click a button, you can win the game), and overall has really no satisfying conclusion, and after finishing the Community Center challenge, the game just keeps going on and on without anything really feeling rewarding or satisfying to complete.  In fact, after finishing most tasks, I feel underwhelmed by the rewards, both the lack of narrative impact or satisfaction for overcoming a challenge.   I really can't recommend it to anyone because of this.  It just seems like a lot of the tasks are extremely repetitive without any scale in challenge besides having the patience to keep doing the same thing over and over again.  The systems are overall simplistic without really any complexity or synergy between systems.  For instances, you can work up reputations with NPCs, but why would you even bother?  Besides just generating small blurbs and cutscenes, building this relationship has NO effect on gameplay, unlocks nothing that isn't unlocked naturally by just doing other things in the game.  As such, it is either an extraneous system that could probably be removed entirely, or it is so simple that to complete that it might as well have been given for free at the beginning anyways.

Overall, after unlocking most of the game, I can't help but feel like what was the point of doing any of these things?  The narrative of the game really lacks anything to draw me in and want to care about anything in the game.  Perhaps if your actions and choices had more lasting impacts on the NPCs and the game story, it would be more entertaining.  But as it is, the game is kind of lacking in meaningful impact for all the time and effort you put into it. 

As I kept playing the game, I kept thinking this is a great example of how not to build a game.  So, I guess my time wasn't completely wasted.

I am convinced that Stardew Valley is so great not because someone set out to make a good farming game, or a good life sim game, but instead that the developer made a laser-focused, years-long effort to condense down what these genres [i]could be[/i] into nothing but the best gameplay loops and scrapping all the rest. The farming, fishing, combat, decorating, and the character storylines are all independently top-notch, no-frills video game goodness. That all of these systems weave together so well feels like a miracle. Add to that a ton of easter eggs and events, and one of the best soundtracks in history to boot, and it is very clear that Stardew Valley is by and for people who love games and all they can represent. Deserves its title as one of the best indie games ever.

Easily one of the best Indie games (and punches well above it's weight as an Indie game!). 

If you live Harvest Moon, you'll love this game. It's basically a modern Harvest Moon but with its own story and style. Harvest crops, explore the town, dig in the mine, rebuild the community center, make friends with villagers, marry one if you want, etc. Plus you get to build up your farm with upgrades to buildings, tools, buy animals and harvest their milk/eggs/etc. The story has some quests that will unlock things or make you best friends with the villagers and so on.

Plus there's endless mods if you get bored of the main game. I'm almost 300 hours into the game and I haven't even modded anything yet. Some of the mods are full on expansion packs with new villagers, locations, quests, etc.

The developer is also an awesome Indie dev who has constantly supported the game / community with free updates for years. While developing a new game too. For example, there was a large expansion to the end game with a new area you unlock that wasn't there when I first bought/played Stardew. So I had a TON of fun revisiting the game and exploring the new location. Who knows what a new update will drop; I might end up replaying the game for a third or fourth time if more locations, quests, villagers, etc get added. And I'll absolutely buy the next game that the dev (concernedape) puts out.

This is the game that keeps on giving! Concerned Ape just can't help adding updates, and has yet to charge anything more than the base game price. If you enjoy cozy games with farming, relationship building, exploration and a touch of combat, I highly recommend this game. Just try not to give yourself too many spoilers looking at the wiki - part of the joy is discovering things by accident. :) 
PS My steam hours played are low, but I have hundreds of hours on iOS and Xbox. Yes, I love this game so much I've now bought it 3 times. :D

Stardew Valley is the perfect game to sit back and relax after a busy day.

It is a high quality farming sim with a lot of in-depth mechanics, items to collect, characters to interact with and multiple special events and seasons. There is a reason people are still playing this game after its release in 2016.
Besides farming, there are various other activities to do like fishing, mining, gathering, socializing and fighting monsters in dungeons. The game also supports multiplayer. (Although I haven't tried it myself)

Over the years several free content updates have been released which added more content including a whole new island to explore. If you are craving even more content, there is also an active modding community for this game. The music is also excellent.

While very relaxing for the most part, you do need to be mindful of managing your energy, health and time. Some resources are also only available in certain seaons. So there is at least some risk or time pressure while playing.
At first, I was quite anxious about the rapid day and night cycle and tried to min-max my setups to get all resources for each season in the 1st year. But once you realize that there is really no hard time limit in this game and are able to kick back and relax, the game managed to become a lot more enjoyable to me.

Stardew Valley is a magical little world where you can farm, fish, mine, and somehow still get a full social life… if your social life consists of awkwardly gifting flowers to pixelated townspeople. 

The townspeople are charming… mostly. I now have a detailed spreadsheet of who likes what, because apparently giving someone a bouquet of flowers is more complicated than rocket science.

Farming is strangely addictive. I planted one pumpkin and now I run a pumpkin empire that makes Jeff Bezos look broke. Meanwhile, my chickens are living their best lives, judging me silently for forgetting to pet them.

Mining is fun and dangerous, but mostly dangerous for me. I fall off ladders, get chased by slimes, and somehow leave half my inventory behind every trip.

Fishing? Relaxing, peaceful… and also the single hardest activity in any video game ever invented. I now consider trout a personal nemesis.

The villagers are charming, the festivals are delightful, and the world is so cozy that I almost forget I’m also hoarding 300 potatoes in my barn for some reason.

A charming, chaotic, farm-sim masterpiece where I’ve simultaneously built a fortune, become everyone’s best friend, and been murdered by a single angry slime.

[h1]An enjoyable lack of planning[/h1]

This game is kind of a mixed bag. Overall, I've enjoyed the experience. There are a lot of systems that feel lazily thrown in that can ruin the experience if you're counting on using them. The game's core loop of farming works very well. You start simple with a small farm, interact with the town's people, learn new things you can make to simplify farming, collect materials in the mines and by foraging. You them use these materials to build things that make farming easier.

[h2]The mines[/h2]

Honestly, I'm not a fan of the actual farming. I was really intrigued by the mines at first. I delved into them and was disappointed by what I felt was a lack of depth (gameplay depth, not mine levels depth). The combat isn't challenging, the mines don't actually hold any especially cool secrets. The reward for getting to the bottom is underwhelming, etc. There are several other mine-like places in the games that I enjoy more.

The game relies a lot on the luck system and RNG to give you content in the mines. On one side, this provides variety when delving into these dungeons. On the other hand, my success in these dungeons felt more like it was up to chance than it was something I could control to a satisfying degree.

[h2]Introducing multiplayer to my experience[/h2]

Because I don't much enjoy the farming aspect, multiplayer means my wife and I can enjoy different aspects of the game together. At least, that's what it means on the surface. Multiplayer has some quirks in regards to the mines. In single player, eating food, browsing your inventory, and several other actions all pause the game. The balance of difficulty seems to rely pretty heavily on the fact that doing these things pauses the game. In multiplayer however, the game only pauses if all players are performing one of these pausing actions simultaneously. In the mines, this means that enemies keep moving while you are eating or drinking to restore health or energy. This would be fine, except for how heavily the game relies on the pausing for it to be balanced. Enemies don't just keep moving, this means they all pile on top of you while you eat and do damage the instant you are no longer in the animation.

On top of the increased difficulty of combat, the mines are also balanced around you being able to spend more time there. There are challenges you can choose to engage in that are like "descend x levels in x days in these mines". In single player, time slows down to give you the time necessary to make that descent. In multi-player, the same change applies here as it did to creatures in the game. The game only slows time if [i]all[/i] players are in the mines together. This adds difficulty the game isn't really balanced around.

[h2]Learning the game's secrets[/h2]

The game has a lot of complex systems and a lot of content that isn't immediately obvious how to use, or even how to learn to use. If you just enjoy exploring the mechanics and how they work through trial and error, I don't expect you will have the same trouble with this that I do. I am confident, however, that it will take you a long time to learn of all the locations, secrets, tools, etc. that are available to you. I've had to rely pretty heavily on the stardew valley wiki to learn things about this game. Some systems seem to have limited impact on the game until you reach some unknown milestone. Without a wiki to tell me "Yes, there is a reason you should keep doing that thing" I would have chosen not to care about some systems and missed out on a lot of content.

[h2]In summary[/h2]

Overall, the game still has fun aspects. Depending on how you play, the issues I've encountered might not bother you often enough for you to notice. I do enjoy playing this game, and all my criticism comes from a place of loving it. The game has fun unique characters and systems that give it a lot of charm. Interacting with the characters in this game and learning their stories is a joy. Just be aware that if you're counting on enjoying some of these aspects of the game I've listed, especially in a multiplayer experience, make sure there are other parts of the game you enjoy enough for it to still be fun. Or maybe play with someone who enjoys the same things you do, so you can go to places like the mines together regularly.

Now, I want to preface this review by saying that this is the only game that I have bought multiple times for multiple devices. I have the game through Steam for PC and on my Switch, and I have plans to go ahead and get it for mobile, too.

On to the actual review:

This game is easily one of the best that I have played. I would personally rank it as Third Place, right behind Golden Sun on the Gameboy Advance and Final Fantasy X on PS2 (and Steam). I have at least 400 hours in this game, which isn't fully reflected on Steam due to also playing on my Switch. This may not be the highest playtime on my Steam account, but if you ignore the idle games and MMOs, then I think Stardew Valley would count as my most played game that can be purchased through Steam.

Pros:
- Concerned Ape is still working on the game, improving it and adding more content. His dedication to his creation is truly inspirational.
- The game is very cozy, with a focus on just living your best life on your inherited farm.
- The characters are interesting, and it's easy to get attached to them and their stories. (My favorite is Leah.)
- If min-maxing is more your style of play, this game can also be planned out meticulously.

Cons:
- I'll be honest, I can't actually think of anything that I would consider a con except maybe the tedious nature of a few of the achievements.

Overall, I would recommend everyone play this game. If I was only allowed to play one game for the rest of my life, this game would be the easiest choice.

Stardew Valley is genuinely one of my favorite video games of all time. I first played it way back in 2016 and I immediately fell in love with it, and that feeling has not gone away. I have played it on multiple different platforms since then, and each time I start a new farm it's still so much fun! It has been so cool to see all of the updates to the game throughout the years, and all of the fun stuff that has been added! I really can't recommend this game enough to people.

Also anyone who says that Stardew Valley is ONLY a "cozy game" has NOT been to the Skull Cavern or had to use the Deluxe Speed-Gro fertilizer on all of their crops because they miscalculated by a single day in the month, OR tried fishing lol. But that's a part of what I love so much about this game. There's a little bit of something for everyone, whether someone likes cozy farming games, crafting, fighting in caves, decorating, or, when playing multiplayer, filling their friend's house with random furniture lol.

I could go on and on about how much I love Stardew Valley but, genuinely, I think the game speaks for itself. It is beyond clear that this game is filled to the brim with love, by ConcernedApe and the rest of the team, by the community of players, and by the fact that there are little secrets hidden in the game that few have found (myself included with some of them). The secrets aren't necessarily "game-changing", but the fact that they aren't shows that they are simply there to make the game even more fun and interesting. Stuff like that, something so small and rare that it might not even show up in someone's farm but it was still programmed with the same love and care as the rest of the game, are just another reason why I love this game. Stardew Valley is a game made with a genuine passion for creating, and with a genuine joy for playing. and I think that's really beautiful.

Want to go buy seeds? Sorry, it's Wednesday and the shop is arbitrarily closed today!
Want to go and see the blacksmith? Sorry, we're setting up for one of the dozens of festivals today, so you just can't visit half of the map!
Want to visit the desert? Bus driver isn't here today. Or tomorrow, probably. And the day after that, there's another fucking festival, so you can go and eat shit.

JUst a calming, relaxing experience, y'know. You can go at your own pace, as long as the game doesn't decide to just say no to everything you want to do on any given day.

The game is jam packed with arbitrary restrictions and schedules that will constantly stop the player in their tracks, saying "nope, not today". Then there's the constant cutscenes you're forced into with no warning when you just want to do what you were doing. Incredibly wordy, incredibly bland cutscenes. They all go on for far longer than they need to because that's just every game these days, wanting to talk you into a coma. Cause more words is more "content" I guess. More playtime, and more playtime = more value. Apparently.

The characters are all extremely shallow. There is nothing interesting about any of them, so there's no need to bother with talking to them or build relationships other than to check something off a list. To make matters worse, relationship levels decay over time so anyone wanting to keep them high is forced to spend hours running through town throughout a playthrough just finding each one of them and talking to them to hear the same lines of dialogue over and over and over again.

Combat is also shallow and a horrible experience that feels extremely inprecise. Brain-dead easy at times and needlessly punative at others. There seems to be little regard for balance.

I normally love fishing in games. It really sucks in this. Players are foced to spend hours leveling their fishing skill because some fish are quite literally impossible to catch at lower levels. Stardew Valley is a simple game on the surface, but somehow it holds a quiet kind of magic—the kind that feels stronger when you’re not playing alone. I started the farm for myself, but it became something much bigger once my friends joined me. We watered crops half-asleep at dawn, sprinted into the mines together, got lost in the forest at night, and laughed over the most ridiculous mistakes. None of it was dramatic, yet every moment felt warm.

What Stardew teaches you is that happiness is often found in routine—planting seeds, tending animals, watching the seasons change—but the joy doubles when someone shares those small moments with you. When we built our first barn together, or sat by the beach during the in-game summer festival, it didn’t feel like pixels. It felt like a memory.

The game never pushes you. It simply gives you a place to breathe, to slow down, and to appreciate the people beside you—both on the farm and in real life. Stardew Valley isn’t just relaxing; it’s a reminder that comfort can be grown, just like a crop, as long as you have good friends to grow it with.

Stardew Valley was responsible for reigniting my love for cozy games. When I was little, I played a lot of Animal Crossing, and Stardew comforts and relaxes me in a very similar way. I have played a lot of different farming sims, but I still come back to this one every once in a while, especially co-op with people who are important to me.

The core gameplay mechanics are simple but effective, and there are a lot of different ways to enjoy the game, like fishing, taking care of animals, exploring the mines, and befriending the townsfolk. Pelican Town feels like home, with so many people to meet and things to do, as well as small fantasy aspects mixed in with the rural atmosphere.

Even though it has always been a fun game, the 1.6 update brought many new things to experience, and it shows that even after all this time, ConcernedApe still cares about the players. However, there is a huge and very active modding community for Stardew. It's super easy to mod and there are countless options for different visuals or extra mechanics to add and breathe new life into the game. 

Is it perfect? No. I personally dislike some of the characters and their arcs, ESPECIALLY Shane. I think some areas could be explored more, since we barely have anything to do in the Desert and Ginger Island. The arcade achievements will definitely keep me from getting 100% since I don't think they're fun or worth the time and effort. Even with its flaws, Stardew will always have a special place in my heart and I will keep coming back to it whenever the world feels too heavy.

I definitely recommend the game if you're looking for something comforting that you can play for countless hours. Beware, though! It might spark a new obsession for you, just as it did for me!

The main strengths of Stardew Valley lie in its well-conveyed story and solid gameplay. In its current state, I would regard the game as having appreciably good replay value and great potential to be improved upon in the future. Because ConcernedApe (the developer) is still working on the game, it occasionally receives content updates that are generally more positive than negative. Some of the content added in the 1.6 update detracts from the immersion of the game and at times feels generally out of place; however, I imagine these additions are less jarring to players who only started playing after the 1.6 update. Playing Stardew Valley with multiple people is awful because there is no reliable way to pause time; however, due to the way Stardew Valley handles time, I can understand why fixing this issue would be difficult. Ending on a high note, there are thousands of wonderful mods for this game, and many more still being developed. The modding community has done a stellar job of maintaining old mods in newer game versions while still consistently releasing new, original, quality content, which is absolutely fantastic. I would unreservedly recommend this game.

I started playing Stardew Valley “just to see what the hype was about.” That was 1 weeks ago. I haven’t seen sunlight since.
What was supposed to be a relaxing little farming sim has completely hijacked my life. I told myself I’d play for an hour before bed. Next thing I know, it’s 4 a.m., I’m in the caves again. My crops are perfectly watered, my animals are brushed and loved, my spouse brings me coffee every morning, and somehow this pixelated valley has become more real to me than my actual responsibilities.
The addiction is unreal, I cry real tears when my favorite chicken gets eaten by a wild animal because I was too busy fishing at 2 a.m. 
There is no endgame. There is only perfection percentage slowly creeping toward 100% while my real-life social skills atrophy. My friends text me and I reply “sorry can’t talk, it’s the night market.” I’ve spent actual money on multiple copies just so I can co-op with myself on different devices. Send help. Or more cauliflower seeds.
10/10 would abandon all adult responsibilities again. Grandfather’s ghost knew exactly what he was doing leaving me that cursed farm. Best worst decision of my life. If you value your free time, run. If you're wondering if it's still worth it to pick this game up when it's older now and so many new games have come out I'd day overwhelmingly yes. For myself as a long-time player picking it up again feels a bit like home and the modding community is HUGE if base game ever starts feeling a little stale. Stardew is overwhelming a labor of love and it shows in the best way.

The game is quite open ended even as farm sims go, especially in the very beginning. Some people find the lack of direction overwhelming, but I love the freedom of focusing on what I want to do when I feel like doing it, so keep in mind what kind of gamer you are. As an older game it lacks some of the really clean QOL features some newer cozy games have but never in a way I've found to be imperative.

Stardew valley is a relaxing game with no clear goals or directions
The game is very clearly an analogy for real life with all it’s systems mimicking a farm life
So if nothing interests you in it just for the sake of doing that something then the game won’t interest you
The one thing that stood out to me the most are the really short days and the even shorter shops opening hours
Which makes it so you kind of have to plan what you’re going to do the next day because often times if you don’t do that then you just won’t be able to do it because of the time constraints
Days being very short also makes it so you have to constantly be making new plans every few minutes which gives you a sense of constantly achieving something

The game also has a strong social element where you can literally marry and kiss some npcs (only those that are marked as single) and even player characters if you aren’t playing alone
For me the enjoyment would have to come from figuring out how to get as much money as quickly as possible which I didn’t get to experience since I was playing with someone who already had 150 hours in this game
I can name the following main gameplay reasons to play this game:
Figuring out how to get as much money as possible (and all the systems associated with this process, so treating the game kind of like Factorio)

“Social” element (interactions with 28 unique villager npcs which include but are not limited to talking, trading, helping, dating)
Collection/completionism (I have heard that the steam achievments in this game are among the hardest to complete due to how long that would take, and there is a museum with relic items you can find in the game)
You private property building/decorating (explanation probably not needed, I can note that this was the first time when I didn’t feel overwhelmed by my options)

Fishing (You may snicker at me for making this into it’s own category, especially since this doesn’t really offer anything objectively unique - this is part completionism, part money making and part helping npcs.
Yet I have seen fishing in almost every game I have played recently I start to suspect that there really is a demand for specifically “fishing” being in the game, which by the way while seems odd to me should be understandable. 
The fishing minigame in stardew valley itself is similar to other fishing minigames you have played, for example the Genshin one.) 

And lastly the cave/mining gameplay (it is the familiar loop of breaking blocks and killing enemies and finding valuable items from time to time, with the cave changing enemies and scenery every so often, making the player curious what the next biome will be like. This cave gameplay is fairly different from rest of the game which made it stand out to me.)
There were other gameplay loops like the incredibly challenging arcade minigames but I just didn’t consider them being a big enough part to include as a reason to play the game 
But yeah if you end up not liking any of these in the context of the time management element + the interactions with npc then you have no reason to like the game
But you will more likely end up enjoying one or more and enjoy this game!

One lovely golden autumn day I felt like playing something cozy for a change from action roguelikes and such. Stardew Valley was already in my library, but frankly I tried it before and at that time it didn't grow on me and I quit in less than a couple hours. But this time the mood was just right for countryside escape and do farming.

Needless to say that the game is charming and quickly sets you to the country life daily routine loop. I enjoyed the early game progression. Learning farming tricks and optimizing your returns was fun. I wanted to get sprinklers so bad, that became my motivation to go caving to get crafting materials. Fishing is lots of fun too when you get a grasp on that mini game.

The game unfortunately breaks the spell of peaceful country life, at least for me, and offers you industrial scale farming development as you get over a certain threshold of gold on your account. The crops yield enormous incomes, forcing you to do something else or don't, because you have all you need. Except new resources that you can find in new caves, which is the opposite of what I wanted when coming to play a cozy game.

One thing that bugged me the most in the game was the time limit. You have so much you can do during an in-game day, so as in real life. But it always kept me frustrated that I cannot fit farming, foraging and social quests in one day. So I eventually gave up and focused just on farming, occasionally going to caves and fishing, and I totally neglected all the social life aspect of the game. Though somehow I got married on that hippie artist girl.

Despite a few negative sentiments, I would say it's a great game. The endless sandbox game is not for everyone, but if you want to take a break an explore cozy games and some cottage-core aesthetics, you'll be treated with at least 40 hours of great time. I spent a bit over 80 hours in it, and lived up until mid-fall of the second in-game year. Built a huge farm, built max size house, got married, finished all quests in community center, became millionaire. But after I achieved all that I didn't have motivation to wait for certain someone to get to see me and evaluate my achievements. But it doesn't mean the game is bad, it's just the thing about sandbox games, you play it for as long as you need it.

I've only played Stardew Valley for a couple of hours, and it's already been a journey! The game is incredibly charming, but I'm clearly a natural disaster when it comes to farming life. My first night, I lost track of time, got caught in the rain, and just... passed out right there on the ground. The next morning, I got a letter informing me that "unconsciousness is dangerous" and a bill for the emergency services that found me! I didn't even know that was possible. On day two, I was determined to clear the land around my house. I got a little too enthusiastic with my axe, chopped one too many trees, and collapsed from exhaustion right on my own doorstep. The fact that the game has these funny, forgiving consequences for failure makes it feel alive and lighthearted. I'm learning to manage my energy and time, and the loop of "work, nearly die, get a bill, repeat" is weirdly addictive. Ingredients For the Pumpkin Pie:

    ▢ 1 9-inch Homemade pie crust , or store-bought, deep dish, unbaked
    ▢ 3/4 cup granulated sugar
    ▢ 1 teaspoon ground cinnamon
    ▢ 1/2 teaspoon salt
    ▢ 1/2 teaspoon ground ginger
    ▢ 1/4 teaspoon ground cloves
    ▢ 2 large eggs
    ▢ 15 ounce can canned pumpkin or fresh pumpkin puree
    ▢ 12 ounce can evaporated milk

Instructions
 

    Preheat oven to 425 degrees F.
    In a large bowl beat the eggs and pumpkin together.  In a separate bowl, combine the sugar, cinnamon, salt, ginger and cloves, and add to pumpkin mixture.
    Gradually stir in the evaporated milk. Carefully pour mixture into unbaked pie shell*.
    Bake at 425 degrees F for for 15 minutes. Reduce temperature to 350° F; bake for 40 to 50 minutes longer, or until the pie is set. Check for doneness by giving the pie a gentle wiggle. The center may jiggle just a tiny bit. It will continue to set up as it cools. Or, it is done when a sharp knife inserted in center comes out clean.
    Cool completely on a wire cooling rack. Serve immediately with whipped cream and caramel pecan topping, if desired.

Alright, listen up. You're probably burned out from getting teabagged by 12-year-olds in shooters or grinding dailies in some soulless MMO. Your soul needs a vacation. Your brain needs a hug. What you need, my friend, is Stardew Valley.

Forget everything you know about farming sims being "boring." This game is a masterpiece of pure, unadulterated dopamine. It's the video game equivalent of a warm blanket and a cup of hot chocolate.

The Grind is... Actually Fun?

The core loop is genius. You start with a dump of a farm, overrun with trees and rocks. It looks like a scene from a post-apocalyptic movie. But then you get your rusty tools, and the magic begins. "Just one more day" becomes your mantra. You'll find yourself saying, "Okay, just gonna water my crops, pet my chickens, maybe go fishing... wait, it's 2 AM in-game and I'm risking passing out to catch one more carp."

Before you know it, you're not just a farmer. You're a artisanal mayonnaise tycoon, a master angler, a legendary monster slayer in the mines, and the town's #1 matchmaker. The skill progression is so satisfying it should be illegal.

Content for Decades

The amount of stuff to do is absolutely bonkers. This isn't just a farming game. It's a:

· Dating Sim: Can you woo the goth elf boy or the moody writer? You betcha.
· Dungeon Crawler: The mines are no joke! Pack some snacks and a good sword.
· Town Restoration Project: Rebuild the community center and stick it to the corporate Joja Mart. Feels good, man.
· Fishing RPG: The fishing minigame is a whole vibe and I will fight anyone who says otherwise.

The Verdict: 10/10, A Perfect Comfort Game

Stardew Valley has been my favorite farming game for a good five years now. Having played through a new save on Steam and almost reaching perfection again at the time of writing this review, it's just as calming, fun, and open-ended as I remembered. As a gamer with the attention span and general gameplay interests of a caveman, it's pretty crazy that something that appears so mundane and simple at a surface level is one of the most addicting things I've ever played.

This game has been around long enough that the best it has to offer has already been parroted by tons of people, so I'll try to keep the things I love most pretty brief. Progression is perfect and moves at a pace that's simultaneously slow enough that the game always feels relaxing, yet fast enough that all of the seasonal content the game has to offer returns semi-frequently and it's not quite as agonizing if you accidentally forget to/run out of time to do something during a certain season. NPC townsfolk are designed great, having unique schedules and interests and pretty engaging storylines for the most part. There's a ton of ways you can make money, and with the right setup any of them can be extremely profitable, which makes the gameplay fundamentally super open-ended. That paired with the sheer diversity of things you can do in a single year cycle and the (SPOILER FOR ENDGAME AREA) [spoiler]giant distant island with a colossal amount of unique content you can access late in the game[/spoiler] gives this game a pretty insane longevity that provides hundreds of hours of engagement, and ensures that there's a dozen other projects you can focus on if you can't finish something season-specific.

It's been said by many already, but I can concur that this game has something for everyone. Tons of avenues of farming and ranching for whatever playstyle you have the most fun with, well-designed and fun combat that can be challenging but rarely feels like you're unfairly screwed over, open-ended building and different farm layouts that can allow for breathtakingly beautiful farms, tons of varied NPCs of different age groups you can choose to make friends with or pursue romantically (or not, you can be a sigma lone wolf too, with zero consequences), cross-platform co-op if you'd like to play with a friend or partner, Steam Deck compatibility (which I can't comment further on as I don't have one), and some fun lore that you by no means need to care about at all to enjoy the game but also adds some very welcome charm and mystique to the world if it does interest you, all for the frankly stupid price of only $15 USD. There are very few games that provide this level of content and quality with an indie pricetag, and it's fantastic that we have a charming and relaxing life sim in that boat, as a majority of them tend to lean towards being fast, fun, and high-octane action/adventure/platformer titles. 

There's a million other things to gush about, but I'll leave it at that so as to not spoil anything for anyone. It's worth mentioning I don't play with mods apart from a few small quality-of-life things, but a single browse through Nexus will make it obvious there's a pretty wild modding community working diligently to enhance the game even further. This game is an unbelievably good value for $15, even going on sale occasionally, and comes packaged with so much varied content it's highly unlikely you wouldn't enjoy the game (though I think it also does a good job playing enough of its cards in the first two hours that you'll know very well if this game simply isn't for you and you want to refund it). I can't do anything but strongly recommend giving Stardew a try. The amount of positive reception it continues to get almost a decade after release and its stagnant Overwhelmingly Positive rating on this platform says enough; this game is WELL worth your money. Thank you for helping me through some of the hardest times of my life with your funny little farming game, Mr. Ape.

Stardew Valley is one of those rare games that just stays with you. I went all the way and 100%’d it, and for some reason I still open it from time to time — sometimes just to walk around and listen to the rain, sometimes to go fight slimes in the mines like it’s a life-or-death mission. There’s something therapeutic about almost dying to a dust spirit at 2 AM.

But what really sets the game apart is the people. The characters feel like they’ve got actual lives and issues. Abigail? Eats rocks and somehow makes it cool. Haley starts off like she runs a high school mean girl cult, but ends up surprisingly decent. Shane has the emotional range of an actual human being who's seen some stuff. They’re flawed in ways that make sense, and that makes Pelican Town feel incredibly real.

And then there’s ConcernedApe! one person making an entire game of this scale and heart? No cut corners, no cash grabs, no “season pass.” Just layered design, care for the craft, and free updates even years later. The guy’s a workhorse.

Oh, and one personal tip: Don't play it with your spouse. Stardew has a weird power. One minute you're just choosing which crops to plant, next minute you're low-key angry at your partner for messing up the chests. I almost got divorced over a virtual chicken coop. Not kidding.

All in all, it's calm, deep, and has more soul than most games released today. Easily one of the best experiences I’ve ever had in gaming.

I still can’t decide if I’m playing a cozy farming game or slowly building a cult of villagers who love my mayonnaise.

You start off escaping the soul-crushing corporate grind to fix up your grandpa’s old farm—and suddenly you’re knee-deep in crops, fishing at 2 a.m., and crying because you missed the flower dance again. It’s wholesome, chaotic, and weirdly personal.

The magic of Stardew is how every little thing matters. You plant, water, harvest, upgrade, fall in love, mine until you pass out, then do it all again. The seasons change, your farm evolves, and somehow you start caring more about your pixel cows than your real-life responsibilities.

The villagers? Absolute characters. Some are sweet, some are disasters, and all of them will judge your life choices. But over time, you build bonds that feel real—and suddenly, giving Shane a beer every day feels like emotional support.

After 180 hours, I’ve got ancient fruit wine money, a wife, two kids, and still get excited when it rains.

Some people may have told you that Stardew Valley is a chill game about farming and making friends. Someone might have told you that this is an easy going, relaxing game that can be enjoyed by anyone, even those who don't normally play video games. Those people were wrong. Stardew Valley is not really a game at all; it is a mirror, reflecting within it the darkness of the human condition, and my own inability to escape it. 

At the time of this review, I have logged 400 hours into this game across platforms. I have completed the community center in it's entirety, and I have perfectly optimized my farm for brutal efficiency. I make millions of dollars every season, and, for good reason, l continue pushing just to see how grotesque my industrial landscape can become. I have never spoken to a single member of the town who cannot benefit me monetarily in my personal quest for power. 

This game may be relaxed for some, but for me, it is war. There will be no item left unpurchased, no crop left ungrown, and no slime left unslain. I have become Death, destroyer of worlds. If you share a desire for ruthless expansion and power, this game is for you. If you just want to have a cute little farm and role-play a simple but idyllic rural fantasy, this game is also for you. If you value your mental health, or maintaining productivity, this game may not be for you.

Stardew is a lifestyle! I don't think a game has ever had such a hold on me (except maybe Skyrim).

Stardew Valley is THE GOLDEN STANDARD for the modern farming sim/RPG for many reasons: the gameplay, the setting, the story, the characters, the music... I lost myself in Pelican Town a couple of hours every day after work for weeks on end.

I thoroughly enjoyed my progression from a humble gardener to a multimillionaire in my road to perfection in over 4 in-game years. It's filled with small victories, every new fish you catch, every profession you unlock, every build you commission, all the expansions and installations in your fields, your artisan enterprise, your social life, this game rewards you and encourages you to go further all the time.

I have a few nitpicks, nothing deal-breaking, just little "ugh" moments I experienced here and there:

- Forced socialization:
Why do I have to max-heart everyone in town? Plus, the friendship decay (especially with animals) is too punishing in a game aspect that's already too grindy. If that hoe Marnie sold an autopetter, that would be great. And btw, why are romanceables all young adults? We need an option for Zaddy Gus and muscle mommy Robin.

- Inventory clutters too fast:
Especially with the various qualities of fish and forageables. If tools didn't take up inventory space, that would be a huge QoL improvement (in 1.7 Eric, please?).

- The dinosaurs:
Pepper Rex are the only element that broke my suspension of disbelief. They feel so out of place in this picturesque rural setting. An eyesore.

- Unconsequential story elements:
Like the mayor’s affair and his golden statue. Robin's unhappy marriage. Community center re-abandoned right after restoration...

So, after countless farms, achieving perfection twice, unlocking all 49 achievements (I totally didn't mod the 2 cheevos for Journey of the Prairie King), I'm proud to say that Stardew is as close to perfection as any piece of entertainment has ever gotten me.

The game is cute in the beginning but quickly becomes a repetitive slog. 

The game does not explain its mechanics at all, it depends completely on fan made content to make it playable for a new player. 

Fishing is the best example of course, fans of this game lol about how hard fishing is. But it's not only hard mechanically, in the beginning I couldn't understand what I was supposed to do at all. So if you stop fishing completely, Willy comes to you and asks you why you aren't fishing. If you say it's too hard, he gives you training rod, says he will give you a lesson. That just gives you one fishing level for free but still doesn't explain what you're supposed to do. It's like the dev clearly sees that fishing is just a mess in this game but decided to just shrug it off.
And you need to fish to progress the game...
This makes the game unbalanced because you progress all the other skills too fast compared to fishing, 

Then there's making friends with characters... It's mostly giving them gifts, doing their quests and hoping for a cut scene...
And finding these people in time to give them a gift without the wiki is near impossible - and you need to chase them around to give them gifts and finish their quests.
Ah, the mini quests, they start on the day you pick them up and you need to chase the character to close them on the next day, So you need to pick them up early enough to finish them on the same day you pick them up and then chase down the character who requested it the next day. 
There's so much timed stuff to keep track of, it gets stressful very quickly.
  
At least I lucked out with romance, chose Maru on looks alone in the beginning when I knew nothing about her because she's the only one that doesn't look like an anime reject (also funny how most of the romance options look like anime rejects and there's not a single Asian person in this game). Her personality is very pleasant and her story is neat. 

If someone is starting with this game, my one tip is ignore chasing the quests early on. It will only frustrate you.
And to never pick up Robin's hardwood quest before you get a horse. The horse lives in this sad shoddy stable that costs a lot of resources and he makes the game much more playable because you move faster on it. Hail the horsey.

Also, if you upgrade your foraging skills to collect double and then to get highest quality, piggies are the best. 

I'm a completionist, so I will try to restore the community centre but I might give up because of the fishing eventually because after days in game and hours irl of doing the fishing minigame, I still barely understand the mechanics of it, youtube tutorials help very little.
