As a first time player to this game, I decided to wing it. (Experience with a similar game, made me want to avoid getting bogged down simply chasing endless chores).  

This mean't no farm animals, greenhouse or min maxing relationships and money for the first year.  (I did accidentally buy a chicken near the end of Winter while trying to check the price).  

Rosemary farm, more accurately known as, 'The Wilderness' turned out to be quite the adventure.  

One bonus was the gift of a dog early on which was lovely.  She kept me going, despite getting lost in the undergrowth or accidentally watered by a hopeless farmer trying to fill her water bowl every day.  

I didn't focus friendships, but after feeling sorry for one character, I started speaking to him and gifted foraged items.  Then it occurred to me that I was also scraping by for food and money myself, which made it interesting.  The funny thing was, this character would find me if I passed out with exhaustion and see me safely home.  

Thanks go to the Stardew Wiki which helped me understand the festival events or know if items I picked up were safe to sell.  

One festival I was soo pleased to get a hat and THEN I got a green rug !  (no sarcasm, genuinely pleased with this)
My first bit of furniture as I couldn't afford to buy anything.   (The farm has some basic decor, you do have a bed, but it is nice to choose something yourself).

What wasn't so good, especially to start with was fishing ! oh Boy ! 
I nearly quit the game as it was quite hard.  

But,  Reddit, Google and Wiki took me for a drink, listened to my complaints and offered advice. So I put down my fishing rod and took a break (before an npc ended up wearing it) Emptied my purse to buy a crab pot, added bait and plonked it in the sea to get on with it.  

A while later, after fishing was levelled a bit more, using a training fishing rod (bigger bar) and not taking 'Yo yo ing fish' so personally it got better.  I noticed that after a erratic bouncing fish was missed the next one was usually a lot slower and less annoying. (The fish of hope - just kidding)   It is still sometimes a challenge, but my farmer can now eat and get stuff done. 

The game has a 'sleeping' schedule so you need to be in bed before 2am or pass out and lose a percentage of your money.  This was ok for a while as I was near constantly broke, but I did lose 800g one night.  (Yeah thanks a bunch Harvey! mgb) 
However, there are reminders and you get used to the rhythm of the game.  Stuff is also available as you progress to help with this and give more options.

So I have really enjoyed my first year, there is a lot more still left to discover and unlock.  More strange things (with a 0.000not much drop rate) regularly landing in my farm getting swallowed by the grass.  But at least the dog has plenty of things to find and play with :-) 

Despite the long review hope you enjoy reading it and find it useful.

[h3]A review for Stardew Valley:[/h3]

I played Stardew back in 2017 and got to fall of year 1 before I eventually quit. In 2025 I gave it another go, and this time it got me. 

Starting off in Stardew is pretty rough. Your farm is a wreck, you're poor, nobody likes you, you suck at everything and get exhausted after watering a few crops. That's day 1. By Day 15, you've cleared some debris, made some money off turnips, and gained a level or two in farming and foraging. You've probably gone a few levels in the mines and gathered some copper ore. The gameplay loop for me became so addicting because there's always something to do, something to work towards. Sure, the energy meter drains quick and you've got to get to bed at night, but that becomes routine and your energy eventually increases. [i](You can also eat almost everything you can grow for energy, forage for morsels, and soon you'll be cooking all kinds of recipes.)[/i]

So there you are, accomplishing this task and the next, growing your farm, making money, upgrading tools, restoring the community center, fishing, foraging, mining and befriending the townsfolk [i](who are silly, charming, sad, shy, happy, rude, nice, smart, drunk, a dwarf, a hermit, and a creature of the shadows.)[/i] Spring turns to summer, to fall and winter, and before you know it you're on Year 2. Stardew is full of making little discoveries that make life easier [i](Oh, I can do THAT!?)[/i] and constantly improving and optimizing. 

Fast forward several years and now you're a millionaire making truffle oil, aging wine in casks, teleporting to a tropical island, having little spirit creatures harvest your crops for you, collecting rainbow rocks, getting married and pimping out your house and farm. And you're still not done, because getting 100% is a monumental task. [b]THAT is Stardew Valley.[/b]

And all of this, this game loved by so many and that's claimed countless hours, was made by one man. One developer with a dream who struggled for years to make it come true, who poured so much time, energy and love into this and you can tell. 

Overall rating would be a solid 9.5/10. Docking a half a point for some minor annoyances with combat and some others with tools and items [i](or rather stupid mistakes with tools and items that you quickly learn to avoid doing),[/i] and the fact that I'll have to start a new farm to get the Joja Mart path accomplished. 

Thanks for reading, if you did. Now, I've got some pumpkins to harvest.

A Cozy Escape for Two 

Playing Stardew Valley with my boyfriend has been one of the most unexpectedly wonderful experiences we’ve shared together. What started as a simple farming game turned into hours of laughter, teamwork, and surprisingly heartfelt moments.

From building our dream farm together to running through the mines with him by my side (me usually running from monsters while he bravely fought them off), every moment in the game felt like a little adventure. We picked crops, raised animals, and even argued (lovingly!) over how to organise the chests—somehow, even that was fun.

The best part? Watching our virtual farm grow felt like watching a part of our relationship grow too. We celebrated our first in-game festival together, planted our favourite crops side by side, and even got married in-game (who says digital rings don’t count?).

Stardew Valley has this quiet charm that makes you want to slow down, breathe, and appreciate the little things—and doing that with someone you love makes it even better. It’s more than a game; it’s a cozy little world we built together.

If you’re looking for something sweet to share with your partner, this game is a perfect choice. Just be warned: you might start arguing over whose turn it is to water the crops

The Good:
This is considered a classic for a reason and it is the number one game on Steam (I think) for a reason. For the first part of the game, there is a lot of story and there's always stuff to do and places to go. This is the baseline I use for fishing in every game I play.
The Bad:
I only ever play this game with friends. When I play it alone, I feel like it's slow and monotonous and I just fish all day every day. The mines are very difficult for me to get through. And don't even get me started on the skull caverns. You have to have the big fancy desert sword to even stand a chance, but to get that you need a prismatic shard, but to have a more than 1% chance of getting a prismatic shard, you have to go into the skull caverns and break as many rocks as possible before you get absolutely demolished by monsters.
The Ugly?:
Having played other farming sims, I have both a newfound respect for Stardew Valley's art as well as a feeling of apathy toward it. The game is such a classic that it no longer feels beautiful or stylish, but once you play a different farming sim, you realize how much you miss the simplicity.
I recommend this game to people who have friends to play it with.

beneath your thoughts.
You plant, you mine, you build, you grow.
And the days start slipping faster.

What once was curiosity becomes ritual.
You wake thinking of it.
You sleep dreaming of it.
The seasons change, but only in-game.
Outside, the real world fades to static.

The game doesn’t shout.
It whispers.
It wraps itself around your routine like ivy—
quiet, persistent, tightening.

Until one day, you’re no longer playing.
You’re tending. Obeying.
Bound not by code, but by need.

This is how it begins.
And this is how it becomes the only thing you do.

There’s something truly magical about Stardew Valley—a game that manages to be both simple and endlessly captivating. Now on my third playthrough, and on a different console no less, I can honestly say this charming pixel game has carved out a permanent spot in my heart.

At first glance, it looks like a humble farming simulator. But once you dive in, you realize it’s so much more. It’s about building a life, forming real emotional connections with the characters, finding peace in routine, and embracing the quiet joy of progress—whether it’s upgrading your tools, unlocking community center bundles, or just making your farm a little more "you."

The pixel art? Absolutely gorgeous. There's something timeless about it. In an era of hyper-realistic graphics, Stardew Valley proves that beauty can come from simplicity. Every season feels alive, every character has a soul, and even after hundreds of hours, I still find myself discovering little moments of magic.

What’s amazing is how Stardew doesn’t push you to go fast. It lets you take things at your own pace. You can chase profit, explore mines, focus on relationships, or just fish by the river all day. And somehow, each choice feels equally rewarding.

This game isn’t just about farming—it’s about feeling. And that’s why I keep coming back, even after finishing it multiple times. Different platforms, same love. It just hits different every time.

Whether it’s your first time or your fifth, Stardew Valley always feels like coming home.

Stardew Valley is, in 2025, a deeply intimidating game. It is the sweat, blood and tears of a solo developer, whose dreams were supported by his closest loved ones (Read the chapter on this game's development in Jason Schreier's excellent book "Blood, Sweat And Pixels"). There's so much content, that it is hard to ever truly know what to focus on, and that scared me off the game initially, the first few times I tried it.

After you get through that initial hump (even if just partially) you are greeted by a beautiful, vibrant world and a real feast for a pixel art lover's eyes. Unfortunately, for a player like me, the game soon starts feeling monotonous. NPCs, at first lively, begin seeming like background noise, because the days feel too short to ever talk to them, and they will seldom, if ever, come and strike up conversations first. In order to befriend a fellow villager, you must literally stalk them, to learn their entire weekly schedule, which usually entails wasting entire, precious days on just seeking them out, or perusing the wiki in a frustrated stupor.

There's never enough time to do everything, and, much like 2011's Don't Starve by Klei Entertainment, progress just kind of halts (almost entirely) during Winter. Combat is pretty bad and basic (yes, there's combat), the community center, once I realized its importance, was asking for things exclusive to seasons that had already passed; meaning I would have to wait for the entire in-game year to start over again. The game, the more I played it, just started to feel aimless. The characters failed to make me feel attached to them, and their efforts were only being hampered by the daily race against the clock. I even had to almost entirely skip a cutscene or two, because of being in Multiplayer and not wanting to collapse from exhaustion right after the scene ended (because time still progresses in multiplayer, no matter what you do). The story was basically just a short snippet in the beginning and then tiny story beats spread out across the village, but it was a drip-feed nowhere near constant enough to keep me personally entertained.

TL;DR Stardew Valley is a lovingly crafted game, and love letter to farming games of yore, that simply failed to keep me engaged to the end. The reward is basically just grind for grind's sake, if you're into that. I'm barely into grind as it is, as it is just a shitty archaic way of padding playtime that, in a perfect world, this incestuous industry would've done away with decades ago. So yeah, I just found this highly underwhelming.

Eric did a very good job on this game and its cool to know that throughout the creation process for Stardew Valley, Eric Barone faced a series of challenging situations. Independent development, particularly, brought its own set of difficulties. Barone was mostly alone for the most part of the project, being the one responsible for crucial aspects such as design, programming, art and music. On top of every difficulty surrounding complex development like this, where Eric did every aspect of the game’s creation himself, he was always working around 12 hours a day, every day of the week on his game, and also working half-period at a theater in his town, Seattle. Which meant that all of his money came just from this half-period job. Many times, in the final months nearing the end of the game’s development, Barone claimed he wanted to give up, his confidence having vanished. He had frequent talks with his girlfriend and friends about not keeping the project going, after all, playing the same game every single day for four years got him exhausted and doubting everything due to not knowing if the game was actually good, since he had never made anything about it available to public testing. The Chucklefish distributor hadn't played the game until then. That was when they convinced him to make the game available for Twitch partners to test it out. These people started playing and sending Barone feedback, to fix a few bugs and even suggestions of things to implement, which promptly made Eric get better and perfect Stardew Valley until its launch. On the evening of February 25th, 2016, Barone discovered a fatal bug in the game, a few hours before launch. This bug caused the game to close its executable, a technical issue which would greatly and negatively impact the public’s capacity to play. Such cases in big studios are fixed by huge developer teams, but Eric was alone. He spent the following days releasing update patch after update patch, fixing everything he could. (creds to this arctical "https://umgamer.com/en-us/articles/gamedev-eric-barone-and-the-history-of-stardew-valleys-development". ) And you should get this game NOW

Stardew Valley was pure joy to explore, it incorporates so many game mechanics and ties it all together so well with its cozy pixel graphics. The town's villagers are so sweet mostly and their individual stories as you befriend them over time is one of the most unique mechanics I've seen in a game. 

Stardew is both wholesome and complex, it explores so many topics and the world feels believable. The game primarily revolves around its farming mechanic, where you grow crops within a season to sell and complete tasks for villagers as well as progressing the first main storyline. 

While waiting for your crops to grow you can improve other skills which include foraging, fishing, mining and combat. It does take a while to get used to all the mechanics on offer, but the game rewards you for remembering to complete tasks and going out of your way to help the villagers making it a highly interactive experience.

The amount of content in this game is incredible, so many items to understand as well as areas to discover, it can be a bit overwhelming with how much there is to do late game, but by then it will be a lot easier as much of it becomes automated as you level up. 

I honestly wish I could go back to day one and experience it all over again. One of the few games that has stuck with me throughout the years. I recall finishing Stardew on update 1.4 and then rediscovering it a few years later not knowing update 1.5 was a thing and that was one of the most refreshing feelings I had had with a game. 

Not long after 1.6 came out and the beauty of the games world had me wrapped up once more. Stepping back from it after having done exactly everything it had to offer, I was left with a melancholic feeling as I had become so attached to this wonderful game. I was proud of my farm and satisfied with the experiences I'd had, learning about the villagers and their stories. 

For the price, the game is underselling itself, Stardew is easily the greatest indie game of all time and its popularity is understandable, its seemingly too good to be true. 

ConcernedApe is probably the coolest developer as he produced everything the game offers by himself, the soundtrack is perfect and the moments are not just heard but felt. Very keen for any future updates as well as CA's next game, Haunted Chocalatier whenever that gets released because I know I will be a day one player :P

I am currently using 76 mods, not counting SMAPI itself, to make the game visually paletable, make my favourite spouses interesting, and the town STILL feels dead. The lack of dynamic feeling interactions, of evolving dialogue, growing relations between the residents, muddy and strange plotlines. Everyone in the town is miserable to some degree, or have a few screws loose making them immune to the melancholy blanketing the Valley. The general consensus of a dying backwater speck of dirt town is to talk down to the new farmer in town? 

I literally only enjoy the gameplay mechanics of the game, I don't like most of the villagers, I don't like the original colour palette, I don't like most of the vanilla dialogue. The persistent sense that you're literally the only reason why any of these people will still have somewhere to live in a few years is not nice, in my opinion, when all they do before you hit 3 stars with them is be weird, hostile and downright rude. Makes me want to choose Joja every single time I have to watch one of their vapid ass cutscenes and they anger me a tiny bit more.

I am going for 100%, perfection, all achievements, all this all that community center as a last hurra to this game because it would be nice to at least complete it. But the only character I truly enjoy is Sebastian, and that is almost entirely because he is treated just as shitty by his own household as the farmer is by the entire damn town.

If there was any constructive feedback to give, it would be for the lack of dialogue changes after certain relationship events (looking at you Shane!). There are a lot of farming sim games out there, but Stardew Valley has outpaced Harvest Moon as the example of the genre. Stardew Valley was the catalyst for the indie cozy game trend, and it remains the best of its genre 9 years after, due to its: consistent updates, large community, and frequent developer interaction.

One of the game's biggest strengths however, is how it builds upon the ideas of it's inspiration Harvest Moon and improves them, while developing its own ideas; all of this is executed with many layers of polish, and it all flourishes with detail and mechanical depth. All of this is complimented by the incredibly low system requirements, allowing anyone on any piece of hardware to enjoy Stardew Valley.

The game allows you to play however you want, there's no wrong way to play the game. You can develop your farm, harvesting more crops and creating more produce, or start a family with one of the 12 bachelors and bachelorettes. You could fish by the river and sell tons of fish, or explore caverns filled with monsters and loot. The list is near endless, and I have barely experienced any of it.

It's one of the highest-selling, and highest rated, games on Steam for a good reason. It's absolutely worth every penny, and I'd pay so much more for it. Buy Stardew Valley, now. I am not asking.

I downloaded it thinking it’d be a cute little farming game, and now I’ve got spreadsheets for crop profits, strong opinions on which villagers are shady, and a weird emotional attachment to my chickens. It’s super chill but also weirdly addicting. The music is cozy, the art is adorable, and there’s always something to do ... whether it’s mining, fishing, flirting, or just watering your plants and vibing.

But honestly? What I love most is how low-pressure it is. You can play at your own pace, focus on whatever makes you happy, and it still feels rewarding. Total comfort game.

Unlike what it seems with on this store, I did not found this game "calm and relaxing". The game is very beautiful, and I really liked it, but this is not a game that invite you to "rest and take your time". There is always something to do. Each can last up to 14 minutes with most shopkeepers being opened like 5 minutes per day. You can pause the game but you still need to always keep track of time if you want to talk to someone. Not go see them too early (or you waste time) and not too late (or you would have to wait for the next day, or next year for birthdays). And if you take too long to go to sleep, you will pass out on the spot and wake up home, with a cost both in money and energy. Each passing season lasts 28 days, which means you also have keep track of days if you want to grow specific crops, or you would have to wait for next year. 

With that being said, I still liked this game, even if it wasn't what I expected. The game is very beautiful and the ambiance, if not calm and relaxing, is more energetic and full of life. The musics are great, and you can see your farm grow like your crops with each passing day and seasons. It is very difficult to be bored with this game since there are multiple aspects with this game. If you are tired with farming or raising animals, try fishing or foraging. If you are tired of fishing, try mining and fighting . If you are tired of mining, try decorating your farm or talking to other villagers. 

If I do not find this game "calm", it is still full of life and have many challenges. I consider having "finished" the game, but still enjoy playing it with friends. I recommend, if you like this type of games.

I avoided playing this game for years because I thought it looked like a generic, boring farming sim. Last week, I noticed I had it in my library (not sure when I bought it to be honest), and decided to finally try it out.

I was very, very wrong.

I was immediately hooked by the silly intro scene and once day one started on the farm, the music kicked in. Good god, the music... No other game has had a soundtrack that I immediately started bobbing my head to.
Then I headed into town. There was a whole map to explore. 30 odd NPCs who could all be spoken to daily, with all of them having very well written dialogue and special cutscenes that made my heart melt. 

I didn't even think there was going to be anything besides the farm. There are massive mining, fishing and combat mechanics which are all incredibly addictive (especially the fishing). Additionally this game was all made by one guy, which is insane for the amount of content it offers.

As of writing this review, I am in winter of year 2, about to make my first real attempt at the skull cavern and finally upgrading everything to iridium. I have a good enough farm that earns around 100k every 2 days or so, and I just cannot stop playing. I literally haven't touched another game for almost 2 weeks now.

My only real criticism is needing to have 50+ tabs of the wiki open at all times. Some things aren't explained until you do very specific actions, which without outside help would take several in-game months (maybe even years) to find, even with reading the secret notes and checking the TV every day for tips. Although a lot of other games have this 'problem', so it's not something that really matters.

Anyway, this is my new favourite game of all time. Hopefully this gets someone else who is sceptical to give this gem of a game a go.

[b]Stardew Valley[/b] is my annual pilgrimage to Pelican Town, where I swap real-world chaos for farming and fishing. It’s cozy, addictive, and hilariously chaotic—especially with mods that make it unplayable without them.
[b]The Good[/b]
Endless Replayability: New farm layouts and choices (Community Center or Joja?) keep playthroughs fresh. I’m 200+ hours in and still uncovering secrets.
[b]Quirky Charm:[/b] NPCs like quartz-eating Abigail and shady Mayor Lewis bring laughs.
[b]Addictive Zen:[/b] The soothing soundtrack calms you, but the “one more day” loop traps you. I’ve harvested at 3 AM, regretting my unupgraded watering can.
[b]Variety:[/b] Farming, mining, fishing, and festivals never get old. Skull Cavern’s a rush, and the Stardew Fair is my yearly obsession.
[b]Modding Magic:[/b] A sea of mods transforms the game. I’m hooked on Stardew Valley Expanded, East Scarp, Ridgeside Village, and Sword and Sorcery—they add new areas, NPCs, and quests so rich I can’t play vanilla anymore.
[b]The Funny[/b]
Married Leah for her artist vibe, got salad daily. I’m a farmer, Leah, not a rabbit!
Hoarded sap thinking it was valuable. Spoiler: it’s not. Pierre mocked my sticky inventory.
My chicken “Karen” lays eggs faster than I hold grudges. Sorry, real Karen.
[b]Mods (PC):[/b] Try Stardew Valley Expanded, East Scarp, Ridgeside Village, and Sword and Sorcery for massive content boosts.

[b]Verdict[/b]

Stardew Valley is a funny, heartfelt masterpiece, elevated by mods like Stardew Valley Expanded that make every playthrough epic. It’s perfect for yearly escapes, whether you’re chasing perfection or petting cows.

The game provides a variety of other engaging activities, such as mining for valuable minerals in mysterious caves, fishing for a diverse range of fish in various locations, and building strong social relationships with the residents of Pelican Town, each with their own unique personality.

One of its main attractions is its very relaxing atmosphere. With a charming pixel art visual style and a calming soundtrack, Stardew Valley succeeds in creating an immersive and stress-relieving gameplay experience. The sense of progression from transforming a neglected field into a productive and lively farm provides its own unique satisfaction.

Overall, Stardew Valley is a masterpiece. With its abundant content and affordable price, this game is a highly recommended title for anyone looking for a gameplay experience that is relaxing yet rich in features.

[h1]✅ Recommended | ⭐ 9/10[/h1]

[h2]🌾 Stardew Valley – A Gentle Escape into Simplicity[/h2]

[h3]Objective Review[/h3]

[b]Platform:[/b] PC
[b]Performance:[/b] Excellent. Lightning-fast loading times, virtually no bugs, and it runs on almost any machine, even low potato PCs can handle it . It’s a rare example of technical simplicity done right.

[b]Gameplay:[/b] A very well-rounded and engaging farming sim. While it requires time investment and rewards consistency, it never feels like a grind. It offers a surprisingly open ended experience: you're never forced into one particular path. Whether you prefer farming, mining, fishing, crafting, or socializing, everything has its own rhythm.

[b]Graphics & Art Style:[/b] The pixel art is charming and incredibly well suited to the game’s tone. It doesn’t aim to be realistic, but it nails the cozy, nostalgic aesthetic. The soundtrack and ambient sounds reinforce the laid-back atmosphere perfectly.

[b]Story & Narrative:[/b] The narrative isn’t groundbreaking, but it works. It’s more of a backdrop than a focal point, the real story is the one you build yourself day by day. That said, the world still has personality, and the NPCs are far from generic.

[b]Content & Replayability:[/b] There is a ton to do, especially on your first playthrough. Later runs are still enjoyable (and offer variety depending on your farm layout or playstyle), but nothing quite replicates the magic of discovering it all for the first time. Still, the creative freedom keeps it engaging.

[h3]💛 Personal Experience[/h3]

The first time I played Stardew Valley, I went all in tryhard mode, optimizing every tile, every crop, every second. It was fun, but intense. Later, I returned to it with a different mindset: I focused on aesthetics, livestock, and simply [i]enjoying[/i] the world without pressure. It became the perfect game for long trips, quiet weekends, or winding down after a long day.

It’s not just about growing crops, it’s about slowing down and letting yourself breathe. Like painting or building with Legos, Stardew Valley lets your creativity guide the experience. It relaxes the mind and rewards those who let go of rushing.

Cheesy as it sounds, booting up this game it feels like coming home. I can play back to back for days like an escapism fiend, or come back after months, but that feeling never changes.

You click back in, wake up from your bed and tend to your farm, say hello to a few townsfolk, maybe do a little fishing - and life goes on. And if you miss a certain crop or rarity that season? That's okay. Spring, summer, autumn and winter will come again. Slowly but surely, something beautiful starts to grow from that tiny patch of land in front of your cabin and spreads out.

There's something delightful about the sense of connection it brings as you breath new life into the town. If you're attentive to the townsfolk, the impact of every change you make is rewarding in its own right, and every event feels like a celebration simply because it can be. Don't even get me started on the modding scene - QOL, expansions, outfits, you name it. If you're looking for something it's probably out there.

Stardew Valley is one of those games that you can compare to experiencing your favorite song for the first time. 
In the beginning, you play it over and over again. You can't get enough of it! 
Everyday you start with listening to this song, and end with it too. It becomes a part of your soul. Then one day, you get bored of it. It doesn't hit the same way you once experienced. After a few tries of searching for that hit... you accept it will never be the same. Its like you lost yourself in that moment and you'll never get it back. 
Then, after many months, someone asks you the question that changes everything. 
"If you could listen to one song for the first time, which one would it be?" You think, and suddenly remember your old favorite song. The one you couldn't get enough of. The one that left every other song bellow it because of its mastery... You think this is the song you would love to listen to for the first time, because last you checked it was a mere memory, forgotten to the past. 
Then, you decide to play it again. You go into it knowing it wont be the same, so you just... listen. For what it is instead of what you want it to be... and what you find shocks you. The song is so beautiful in itself. The notes work together in harmony and the beat compliments your heart. It doesn't full your soul... it translates it. Because the fragments that were once lost to history get pieced together in a new light. That's how I feel about Stardew Valley. 
I feel like it translates my soul in a way only my favorite song could understand.

Stardew was one of those games that I never got on the initial hype wave for and especially felt daunting after not playing it for so long. It must not have helped that this game was extremely buzzed as being one of the best farm sim/survival/rpg games of all time. Funnily enough, narrowing down what this game is was a lot more challenging than I thought. Initially I just wanted to play a chill farming game however, I quickly found out that this game had a lot more elements to it than met the eye. Fully thought out stat system that tied in with every aspect of the game (friendship levels, farming, fishing, mining, combat, luck, foraging, etc..) which made the game a lot less surface level than I thought. The guy who created this game literally thought of every quality of life thing you could think of, whenever I thought man this is good but I wish it (BLANK) more often than not, there was a way to get that “blank” or upgrade to it. The game was a lot more satisfying than I thought to play with the multiple ways to earn money making it feel like not just having to sit around and wait for crops to grow, as a matter of fact technically you could  almost completely ignore farming if you wanted. The early game of working toward the big goal of restoring the town centre felt very rewarding to finish, and I was scared that I would feel directionless after doing so but there was still SO MUCH MORE to do around the valley with new content being unlocked each year with things like the movie theatre, ginger island, and all the completionist logs you can do. Not to mention everything involved with Mr. Qi felt like the endgame in its own right. The music and artstyle of this game are great, especially for a single dev at the time this is extremely impressive, even more so in combination with the tens of large systems in the game that all work seamlessly and are intertwined. I loved seeing all the different cutscenes and heart events with the villagers and they were all super interesting characters in their own right no two felt the same. Stardew has instantly become one of my favorite games of all time and I am excited to do a replay and do everything differently on a different farm layout when the itch comes back, great game.

I picked up this game after having owned it for a few years since my internet was down for a week, and my god did I get addicted to it quick. While the early game was a little slow, there was still plenty to do that didn't require energy (basically a resource meter that drains whenever you do something like swing an axe). 

The game might seem really daunting to get into, and that's a fair thing to feel, as there is an absolute mountain of content. As someone who played without any access to the wiki, let me tell you, you really don't need it to fully enjoy the game. Most things can either be figured out yourself with a bit of smart thinking and experimenting, or the answer is out there somewhere in the world, you just need to play enough to find it.

The progression in this game is really satisfying, especially with just how many ways there are to improve your farm, your efficiency, or your character's strength. For example, you start off having to manually water your crops, until you unlock sprinklers, which then opens up a ton of time and energy to be spent on other activities. Then you unlock the greenhouse, which lets you farm whatever you want regardless of the season, meaning you can throw a multi-harvest crop in there and never have to worry about money again.

The art and music of this game is gorgeous; the pixel art is really well done and pleasing to look at, and the music is an absolute treat on the ears, I personally really like the fall theme "Raven's Descent" for the flute.

The characters present all have their own unique events which can be viewed by visiting a given location under the right circumstances, such as raining at night. You can view more of these by increasing your friendship with the villagers, and it helps a lot with making them feel like real people. That being said, that does lead into my biggest complaint about the game, that being the somewhat lacking generic dialogue options.

A lot of generic actions like gifting or casually talking to villagers will lead to the same few dialogues, with some variance depending on how close you are to said villager. This did kind of hurt my immersion, as hearing someone say the exact same thing every time I gift them makes it feel more game-y. For a game that seems to put a lot of emphasis on interacting and forming bonds with the people you meet, I didn't feel super incentivized to talk with most villagers outside of getting friendship points. It's a bit of a shame, as I feel like if everyone had more dialogue it'd really help flesh out the world even more.

A smaller issue I have is that the combat isn't very good, it's pretty much entirely spamming left click. Swapping items can feel kind of clunky at times, since it's pretty easy to accidentally lock yourself into swinging your pick when you meant to swap to your sword and quickly attack, and aiming your attack is a bit of a pain since you need to make your character face the direction you want to swing, but by doing that you move yourself towards the enemy. There is mouse aiming, but you need to have your mouse basically be on top of your character for it to do anything. I understand that it's not meant to be a super combat heavy game, but that doesn't mean that the combat can't be good.

It might seem like most of this review is me talking about negatives, but that's because I'd just be repeating myself saying "the game is really good". I'm also trying to keep things vague as to avoid spoiling anything. Basically, if you want a chill game to relax with that also has a really good sense of progression, consider giving Stardew Valley a try.

This games price is very worth it and I’m pretty sure the game goes on sale too. 100% worth your money if you like the dating simulator/visual novel genre, each bachelorette and bachelors cutscenes and stories are super cute and make your feet kick a bit (Shane’s in particular.) You have an opportunity to grow with each candidate (or even cheat on them, don’t worry there’s cutscenes for that too…)

The game still gets updated (as of writing this review) and you can freely mod it without repercussions! The soundtrack is amazing and just overall this game is great! The game has basically unlimited playtime and you can do so much in the game, you won’t get bored! I would consider this a longer version of animal crossing because this has more content then that. And the fact like I stated before, it still gets updated means you will keep getting more and more content for your game! I’m very glad we haven’t gotten a sequel yet until this game is finally concluded with updates, though, a sequel of the same town wouldn’t be a bad idea. But it comes to show this game isn’t for greed purposes and we can still expand on this game and still be able to grow a fanbase for it. 

What I’m hoping for is more bachelorette/bachelor options, new characters, new cutscenes and more quality of life updates like the recent update where the townees get more outfits for the winter!

Use the wiki if you have to, especially if you're curious about what gifts people like, or what fish are only available during certain conditions. Otherwise... don't sweat it. Don't worry about how much someone else did in Year 1. Don't worry about how nicely organized someone's chests or rooms are, how cool their paths look, or what's the "best" farm layout... just play it however you want. After you've sunk a few dozen hours in, THEN start looking for ways to improve if that's truly your goal. Avoid mods at the beginning too... it's a great game in it's own right and deserves to be played "as is" before you start experimenting.

Reviewing (mostly) every game (or DLC) in my library, part 206:

⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️ (10/10)

I mean, what am I even supposed to say about [i]Stardew Valley?[/i] It's one of those games where you sit down to play for half an hour, and suddenly it's 2 a.m., and you've somehow spent three hours reorganizing your farm instead of doing the thing you originally planned to do. And then you tell yourself you'll just play one more day. We've all been there.

There's just something about this game that makes it so easy to get attached to your little farm and the people in Pelican Town. You start out with a run-down property and a handful of seeds, and before you know it, you're planning your entire life around crop seasons and checking the calendar because someone's birthday is coming up. You get attached to your animals, your favorite villagers, and even the stupid little routines you fall into every day. I

And the fact that one person made this game is still wild to me. ConcernedApe made something that people have put thousands of hours into, and he kept updating it for years without charging extra for all the new content. I genuinely don't know what more you could ask for. This game is an easy 10/10 for me.

[b]Pros:[/b]
[list]
[*] A slow, beautiful life on your terms. Whether you want to farm, fish, mine, romance, decorate, or just walk around petting your animals, [i]Stardew [/i]lets you play at your own pace. There’s no pressure. You can optimize for gold and rare crops, or you can just vibe and grow turnips while chatting with Shane about how bad life used to be. It’s your little world.

[*] One of the best farming loops ever created. There’s something satisfying about planting seeds, watering them, harvesting them, then reinvesting in even more complex crops or artisan goods. 

[*] A cast of characters that feel real. The people of Pelican Town aren’t perfect. Some are prickly, some are shy, some are struggling. And over time, you see them change. You hear their pasts, uncover their trauma, celebrate their birthdays, and maybe even fall in love.

[*] Gorgeous pixel art and serene music. The visuals are simple, but warm and expressive. Every season has its own palette and charm. And the soundtrack? It’s iconic. Peaceful, nostalgic, and instantly grounding. Every track feels like a warm mug of something sweet.

[*] The best version of “daily tasks” you’ll ever find. Watering plants, checking the coop, upgrading tools, and remembering villagers’ schedules sounds like work, but it feels like love. The rhythm of a [i]Stardew [/i]day is cozy, not stressful. You do what you can. You go to bed when you're ready. 

[*] Freedom to play however you want. There’s no "wrong" way to play. Want to marry Emily and become a wine magnate? Go for it. Want to live alone, max out the Community Center, and raise cows? You’re valid. Want to spend five in-game years just fishing and watching the leaves fall? That’s living, baby.

[*] Mines, combat, and mysteries. Beyond the surface-level farming sim is a full-on dungeon crawler with weapons, gear upgrades, and secrets to uncover. 

[*] Incredible post-launch support. ConcernedApe has continued to update the game for free for years. New festivals, dialogue, late-game systems, and even co-op? 
[/list]

[b]Cons:[/b]
[list]
[*] Lol. Imagine thinking [i]Stardew Valley[/i] has cons. (Okay, fine: some people don’t like real-time energy systems or pixel graphics, and that’s valid, but it’s not the game's fault you don’t like comfort.)
[/list]

A Heartwarming Escape into a Peaceful Pixel Paradise

Stardew Valley is nothing short of a masterpiece in the world of indie gaming. Created by a single developer, ConcernedApe, this charming farming simulator offers far more than just planting crops and raising animals—it delivers a deeply rewarding, peaceful, and emotionally rich experience that players can sink into for hours on end.

From the moment you arrive in Pelican Town, you're welcomed by a vibrant world full of character, mystery, and possibility. The pixel art is gorgeous and nostalgic, paired beautifully with a calming soundtrack that evolves with the seasons. Whether you're tilling the soil, mining deep within the caverns, fishing by the river, or forming bonds with quirky townsfolk, there’s always something meaningful to do.

What truly sets Stardew Valley apart is its depth. Beneath its cozy surface lies a thoughtful game full of choices, consequences, and hidden stories. Each character has a distinct personality and background, with relationships that evolve in heartfelt ways. You can even get married, start a family, and help restore the town to its former glory—all at your own pace.

Stardew Valley is a perfect blend of relaxation and engaging gameplay. It respects your time, rewards your curiosity, and encourages creativity. Whether you’re a casual player looking to unwind or a completionist aiming to perfect your farm, the game offers something special for everyone.

I Came Here to Relax, Now I’m a Full-Time Farmer

I bought Stardew Valley to “chill.” Next thing I know, I’m waking up at 6 AM every in-game day to water 200 blueberries, sprint to the mines, fight shadow monsters, flirt with every villager, fish like my life depends on it, and pass out in a field because I forgot to check the time.

This game turned me into a sleep-deprived gremlin with a crippling addiction to virtual agriculture.

The villagers all have personalities, and yes, I judged them all. Some give you cookies. Some give you trauma. Some give you mayonnaise machines. It’s beautiful.

The soundtrack is so peaceful that you don’t realize hours have passed and your real-life responsibilities are on fire.

Stardew Valley isn’t just a farming game.
It’s a life simulator, a dungeon crawler, a fishing rage-game, a dating sim, and a sweat-inducing min-maxing spreadsheet disguised as pixel art.

10/10. I started a farm to relax. Now I’m basically running a small agricultural empire and trying to marry the entire town.

As a huge fan of pixel art games, Stardew Valley immediately captured my heart. This isn't just another farming sim; it's a vibrant, living world that truly lets you explore and play at your own pace. What I love most is the incredible freedom it offers. You're not just limited to farming; you can go fishing, delve into the mines to battle monsters and find treasures, or even focus on building relationships with the charming townsfolk. Every day feels like an adventure, and there's always something new to discover. The sense of progression is incredibly satisfying, whether you're upgrading your farm, completing bundles for the Community Center, or just decorating your little virtual home. The pixel art style is absolutely gorgeous and perfectly complements the game's relaxed vibe. Plus, the soundtrack is incredibly calming and really adds to the immersive experience.

If you're looking for a game where you can truly escape, express your creativity, and lose yourself for hours on end, then Stardew Valley is an absolute must-have. It's a masterpiece that offers endless enjoyment!

As someone who grew up surrounded by all three species, it would mean a lot to me to see this fixed. Worst case scenario I suppose I can learn to mod and create a mod that includes all three cactus species to a more accurate degree. ive had stardew valley for years and i'm not a review writer by any means but this game deserves it, especially after 2,000+ hours into it lol.

this game is worth every penny and more. $15 for a game with this much love and care into it is the steal of a lifetime. to preface, i was never a farming sim girly. i grew up on FPS games. i'd heard of stardew valley but the graphics turned me off in judging-a-book-by-its-cover fashion. but i had friends who played, and they invited me to join them, so i gave it a chance that i never would have otherwise. and thank god i did.

this game is therapeutic in ways that are hard to describe. i've grappled with a lot of trauma in my life that i'd buried so deep over the years i didn't even recognize anymore. i wasn't until i'd found solace in an escape that i could recognize the impact something simple and calming like this game could have. when people call this game relaxing, it's the truth.

many will argue that the time limit on each day is stressful, and tbh, it can be! i coach new players and one of my biggest pieces of advice is to play at your own pace. there are NO missables in this game, with the exception of a single cutscene in year 1 that impacts absolutely nothing and is just for storytelling purposes. anything else can be "redone" with no consequence. the time limit each day is not a punishment or a race, it's just a way to direct the pace of a game with seasons and adds a little extra challenge when it comes to time management. as you progress, you'll naturally fall into line with a routine that makes sense for you. and even if you never come up with a routine, the game goes on. you still make money, you still make friends, you still get things done.

the story is open enough that players can insert themselves into the game while still following a theme of finding happiness and purpose in the world. and i think that's why it resonates so well with so many people - in addition to the replayability, it can apply to any of us who have ever wished for a greater sense of belonging, and i think that includes almost all of us in some way or another.

besides the story, there is SO MUCH to do besides farming. fishing, collecting, designing, adventuring, animal husbandry, etc. there is a lot of depth to the NPCs as well - they all have a backstory, insecurities, dreams, and more. there is more than one way to complete the main storyline, and the game is incredibly playable outside that storyline as well. there is no "end" to stardew valley.

i would encourage new players to find a friend to play with. the game is SUPER fun single player but it does help to play with someone who has played before, since you are kind of thrown into the fray with minimal instruction. the discord and subreddit are great ways to connect with other players! but even playing with another newbie has its benefits, if you feel the game is lacking connection.

lastly i want to emphasize how amazing the developer is. for those who don't know, stardew valley was created by a single person, and he's been super receptive to feedback, suggestions, questions, etc from the community. i think he has a small team now to help him out but it's quite obvious that this game was - and continues to be - a labor of love from the developer. you can feel the emotion in the music, and the seasons, and the story. stardew valley and the person behind it deserve the support. i have hundreds of hours in other games, all AAA, and this is the only game i could say that about. hopefully that speaks for itself.

Stardew Valley is the best game I've played in a very long time. I haven't dabbled in any mods yet, but the vanilla OG game gives so much to explore and do and easily has 100+ hours of extremely engaging content. 

[b]FULL DISCLOSURE:[/b] I did not expect to love this game. I thought it was going to be a mediocre farming sim with light RPG elements with maybe 7 hours worth of content I'd somewhat enjoy. Quite honestly, I think that's why many people are hesitant on playing this game. However, not only are the farming and RPG elements very engaging, but other elements such as mining, fishing, and completing quests are just as well thought out. I've had multiple days where I completely lose track of time from getting so immersed in Stardew. The game is also just made really well, which is so rare from most games these days. The art, sound design, style, and lore are all very top notch.  

Stardew is not without it's flaws. The first 2-3 hours of playtime DRAGS because of your lack of energy. The first spring and summer was very unproductive for me because of how limiting your starting energy is. However, the slow start almost works in Stardew's favor. When I finally began to get upgrades, the game became a lot more fun, largely because I could do so much more in one day. My other major gripe with Stardew is how shallow marriage is in its current state. I feel like after 10, and especially after 14 hearts, I feel like I cycle between the same 10 dialogues on a daily basis. I will say that this is a really minor gripe, but I would love to see a bit more expansion of marriage in the base game. 

Regardless, Stardew is one of the best games I've ever played. Easily some of the best $15 I ever spent. ConcernedApe, THANK YOU for making this masterpiece!

[h2]Stardew Valley: A Gentle Harvest of Heart and Time[/h2]

In a world that often spins too fast, Stardew Valley invites you to slow down to feel the sun on your face, the soil beneath your hands, and the rhythm of a simpler life.

Its pixel art doesn’t shout, it sings, softly. Each dawn and dusk is painted with charm, cozy as a wool sweater on a cool spring morning. It’s not about realism it’s about warmth. The graphics feel like flipping through an old storybook, where every frame is drawn with care and memory.

The music is no mere background hum. It’s a seasonal symphony gentle, melancholic, joyful, and serene. Every track cradles the moment, from the buzz of summer fields to the quiet hush of a snowy night. It doesn’t demand attention, it holds it, like an old friend humming while you work.

And the people? They’re not perfect but that’s what makes them feel real. The NPCs in Pelican Town have their own stories, struggles, and rhythms. Over time, they open up, revealing layers that go beyond first impressions. Conversations are well-written, often quietly profound, and sometimes even a little odd, but always human.

Co-op adds a fresh wind through the valley. Building a life with friends, watering crops side by side, exploring the mines, or proudly comparing fish sizes like rival fishermen at a county fair, brings a new kind of joy. “You caught a 10-inch sardine?” your friend boasts. “Well,” you reply with a smirk, “mine was twelve.” It’s silly. It’s wonderful.

Yet, Stardew isn’t without its rough edges. The early days can feel overwhelming for new players, with little guidance in the sprawling to-do list of farm life. The pacing is gentle, sometimes to a fault, and the grind for perfection might not suit every soul. But those willing to plant roots will find something deeper than pixels, a quiet, enduring kind of magic.

This isn’t just a farming game. It’s a meditation on growth of land, of friendships, of self.

And like the best things in life, it doesn’t rush you. It simply asks you to stay awhile.

At first glance, Stardew Valley seems like just a simple little farm game — but under the surface, it’s so much more. The graphics are modest and the gameplay is straightforward, yet there’s something truly addictive and relaxing about it. It doesn’t punish you for making mistakes, but instead gives you the space to learn, improve, and come back stronger next season. That kind of gentle game design is rare these days.

I wouldn’t necessarily recommend it for PC, but great on the Steam Deck. It’s the perfect way to unwind. You can pick it up for a quick session and suddenly realize you’ve been immersed for hours. There’s a real comfort to it — a peaceful rhythm that lets you just chill out and enjoy your time.

This game reminds me of the early days of gaming — the good days — but it also shows how far those ideas have come. It proves you don’t need flashy graphics or endless tutorials to make something truly great. If you grew up with games in the Gen X era like I did, or just enjoy simple, well-crafted experiences, I highly recommend Stardew Valley. It’s one of those rare games that feels like home.

I'd like to start out by saying that Stardew Valley is, all in all, a good game. It's really the only farming game I've played, so I don't have a good point of reference for what some of the other ones are like - say, Animal Crossing, or Harvest moon. That being said, it feels like a good farming game to me. It's very strongly cycle-based, where you'll be waiting on crops to finish growing in order to get money to progress, or waiting for seasons to change so that you can catch new fish, et. cetera. It excels at that.

The early game is especially great, since you're tight on money and have to manage your limited energy, funds, and time. When you start out, there is tons of stuff to do, and you just won't be able to do it all. But there's not a ton of pressure to finish things quickly - the game's tone is relaxed, and the soundtrack does a great job at setting the mood. If you want to go quickly, and rush content like the community center and beyond, then you can do that as well, and that can be fun - to the game's credit, it give you a lot of freedom to play as you'd like (within the constraints of seasonal cycles and the like, of course). Getting things done and building out your farm and your character is very, very fun.

Stardew is also unique (maybe not among modern farming games, I dunno) in that there's plenty of not-quite-farming stuff to do. Combat, although rudimentary, allows for a pretty enjoyable experience in the mines, where you fight monsters and gather resources. That and fishing allow for an entire other mechanically-engaging non-farming side of the game you can play if you just...don't want to farm at the moment.

The story is, admittedly, loose, and the character writing is generally good. It's never been the focus for me, really. See, I've played most of my hours on Stardew offline out of shame so that the hours wouldn't be tracked, but I've done plenty of playthroughs with the different marriage candidates way back when (before Ginger Island was a thing), so the characters and the setting are very familiar to me. But it's not bad. There's a bit of an edge to Pelican Town beneath its calm exterior and vibrant colors, and even if at some points I feel like Concernedape could improve how the setting is written and add more depth to the characters, the writing works well enough.

Overall, a fun game. It's engaging, even if it gets to feel shallow after spending enough time with it.

But that's the problem. For me, anyway. It starts fun, it's engaging - it's REALLY engaging. It grabs you, and then it keeps you coming back. You go to bed in-game fully intending on it to be where you stop for the session, but then one thing leads to another and - oops, look at that, it's nighttime! You keep going because you think of what you might be able to get up to in Spring, or Summer, and what you might be able to do with the money you'll get - what about going deeper in the skull cavern, just one more time, for that two-thousandth piece of iridium ore, or what if I added more sheds so I could have more kegs to brew up more wine so that-

You get the point.

Stardew is a fun game. It's an engaging game. It's an addictive game. And when you're in deep, and you recognize every line of dialogue from every NPC, and you've got your morning routine of animal husbandry and crop tending and the like memorized - the point where you keep playing despite not actually having fun - that's the point that Stardew can take you to. The point where you're working instead of playing. And then you wonder if it was all worth your time.

I got back into Stardew after swearing off playing it for years because an update was released that added an "end goal" you can achieve (that didn't always exist). Getting it is very, VERY grindy, but doable. I've gotten that goal. I will not be playing Stardew Valley ever again.

TL;DR - It's a good game. It's addictive. Know what you're getting into.

I play this game for all sorts of reasons: stress relief, social gaming, nostalgia factor, new experiences, and more. 
Need a challenge? You can definitely make this game challenging for yourself.
Need something simple and easy? Everything can be a breeze, if that's how you like it.
Prefer the original game? No problem, plenty of others do too - and single player is available, if you don't like playing in a group.
Enjoy playing games with mods? Say less - there's so many, and it's easier than ever to manage your game mods these days. Plus, there's whole communities built around modding this specific game!
Finished the game, but want a fresh run-through? You go, dude!
Enjoy mining in deep, dark caves for rare gemstones and minerals? There's not one, not two, but three different places in this game I can think of off the top of my head for mining. They come complete with all sorts of monsters that, honestly, aren't difficult to fend off once you get the hang of the combat system.
Enjoy setting up a museum? There's plenty of artifacts to find, and a place for every single one to be displayed! (And you get rewards for helping complete the museum, too!)
Do you like fishing and sitting in the sun? There's tons of fish to catch, and you can improve your odds with special fishing tackle!

From crops and flowers to skeletons and rock-crabs, there's always something to do in Stardew Valley.

However you prefer to play, this game is good for just about everybody. There's a little bit of everything!

The art style? Simple but charming.
The music? A perfect mix of peaceful and nostalgic.
The gameplay? As relaxing or as intense as you want it to be.

And don’t even get me started on the community each character has their own story, their own quirks, and it honestly makes you feel like you're part of something bigger.

For anyone who’s feeling burned out, overwhelmed, or just needs a break from the noise of real life Stardew Valley is like a warm cup of tea for your soul.

I’ve played a lot of games over the years but Stardew Valley really stands out as something special. It has this unique and relaxing gameplay style that honestly helped me clear my mind and escape from stress after long days.
When I first started playing I was pretty lost. I didn’t really know what I was supposed to do or where to begin. But the more I played the more things started to make sense. I slowly got into the rhythm of the game and began to enjoy it a lot. 
I have been spending hours on my little farm just planting crops, fishing, and exploring the mines even making friend with the NPs in game. It was peaceful and it gave me a surprising sense of calm.
One of the coolest things about the game is how much it teaches you without ever feeling like a lesson. I found myself learning about different kinds of fish, what crops grow in each season, and how to plan out my farm depending on the time of year. It made me feel more connected to nature in a simple but meaningful way.
I played mostly with a controller and I have to say it made the whole experience even more comfortable. There’s just something satisfying about sitting back with a controller in hand and watching your farm slowly come to life day by day.
What really surprised me was how real the NPCs felt. They weren’t just there to fill space. Each character had a personality, a routine, and their own little story. It really felt like I was getting to know them like neighbors or friends. The developer clearly put a lot of heart into making every part of the world feel alive and personal.
I also got the chance to play in co-op mode with a friend and that turned out to be one of the best parts of my time with the game. Sharing the same farm, splitting up tasks, exploring caves together or even just fishing quietly side by side was such a fun and memorable experience. We laughed a lot, messed up a few times, and had some great moments that I’ll always remember.
If you haven’t played it yet I really recommend giving it a try. Whether you play solo or with a friend you’ll probably end up loving it just like I did.

Few games manage to capture the hearts of players across all ages, cultures, and skill levels quite like Stardew Valley. What began as a solo project by developer Eric Barone has blossomed into a timeless, genre-defining experience. It’s not just a farming simulator—Stardew Valley is a gentle escape, a meaningful life sim, and a masterclass in player-driven storytelling.

🎮 Gameplay that Grows with You
At its core, Stardew Valley is about revitalizing a rundown farm. But the beauty lies in how freely you're allowed to grow—not just crops, but your own experience. Whether you want to build an agricultural empire, explore mysterious caves, court a partner, fish the day away, or simply decorate your home, there’s no wrong way to play.

The game doesn’t rush you. There’s no looming pressure, no fail state. Instead, it invites you to take things at your own pace. In a world filled with overstimulation and urgency, this design choice feels revolutionary.

🌍 A World That Feels Alive
Pelican Town is more than a setting—it’s a community. The characters have depth, struggles, hopes, and relationships that evolve with or without your involvement. From Linus’s solitary life to Shane’s personal struggles with depression, Stardew Valley handles social storytelling with remarkable empathy.

Seasons change, festivals bring the town together, and even the soundtrack evolves throughout the year. These small details build a sense of time and place that’s emotionally immersive in ways most games can only dream of.

🎨 Artistry in Simplicity
The pixel art style is cozy and charming without sacrificing expression. The animations are fluid, the colors vibrant, and the UI intuitive. This aesthetic choice not only makes the game accessible on nearly every platform—including mobile and the Steam Deck—but also gives it a timeless visual appeal.

And the music? A soothing, seasonal masterpiece. Each track feels carefully composed to evoke mood and memory. It’s the kind of soundtrack you’ll hum to yourself on rainy days in real life.

🤝 A Game That Gives Back
Unlike many modern titles, Stardew Valley has zero microtransactions, no exploitative DLCs, and continues to receive free updates. These updates add new mechanics, characters, and quality-of-life improvements—all as gifts from a developer who clearly loves the game as much as the fans do.

There’s also an enormous modding community, giving players the tools to personalize their experience even further.

🧠 Emotional Resonance & Escapism
Perhaps what makes Stardew Valley truly great is the emotional connection it fosters. It's a place where players find calm during anxiety, structure during chaos, and joy in the simple. It’s not just a game—it’s therapy, a creative outlet, a place where life feels just a little bit lighter.

⭐ Final Verdict
Stardew Valley isn’t just a game—it’s a phenomenon. With its thoughtful design, emotional depth, and infinite replayability, it quietly redefines what gaming can be. In a world of flashy graphics and endless monetization, Stardew Valley reminds us that sometimes, all you need is a pixelated chicken, a well-watered parsnip, and a dream.

Rating: 10/10

I play everything from FPS to ancient point and click puzzlers. I bought this game because I wanted something chill and cute to try, and it was on sale. I knew it had hype for an indie game, but I didn't know much about it. 

Over a hundred hours later, I have literal google docs filled with my goals for various seasons, and I've built an empire off by selling mayonnaise, cheese, and cranberry wine (don't ask why I have so many cranberries. It just happened.) I've stayed up all night in real life preparing for the annual fall fair.

This game will consume your life. In the best way.

Obviously, it's not for everyone, but there are so many different ways to play it and things to focus on that it appeals to quite a wide range of players -- even those who don't typically enjoy cozy sims. My brother is a a hardcore Fortnite player and a god at platformers, so this game is completely outside his usual picks... and I've gotten even him hooked on it. 

Also, it's basically made entirely by one person, which is insane. It gets frequent updates, it has an insane amount of content, it's not buggy, and the soundtrack itself is worth listening to. I use it as study music.

Please, if you are considering getting Stardew Valley at all -- or even if you weren't considering it -- just do it. Chances are you'll be hooked soon!

Playing as a farmer in Pelican Town is really nice and slowly but steadyly not only building your knowledge about what it is you can produce, but also building out the relationships with your fellow villagers is fantastic. I also like a lot of the story elements when living through the game and the "heart events" (cutscenes when you reach specific friendship levels with the NPCs). The musics great too, although it sometimes randomly cuts out and it feels very eerie just hearing nothing.

The only downsides I have is that the game is packed with too much activity and that it can get over as work than as gameplay. Especially when you start running between your farm, the mines and the ocean. I mean, it is also encouraged to pick one specialization, but this is immediately thrown out of the window as you have to pay enormous amounts of money to just buy the stuff you need. I also think it is way too overloaded with mystical elements, monsters and creatures, while it presents itself as a "return to monke" game.

Overall, I can still recommend it!

I'm not a fan of only being able to save when I sleep, as if I play a day it often feels like a massive chore to finish the day before stopping.  And also, there's just a lot of tedium walking around.  Days feel both too short and too long somehow.  (It's supposed to be a chill cozy game but the short time on days makes it feel faster paced)  But those are all rather inconsistent feelings.  There were a few times I found myself having some fun with the game and jamming out a bit to the music (especially in summer) but those feelings don't last long or hold over long period of time for me, and before I know it I'm either waiting for day to end or just running to bed early so I can close the game.

Yes, you should get this game! I purchased it because there was an orange tabby in the game (silly reason, right!), however, it has turned into one of my all-time favorite games. You can use this game for whatever you want - farming sim or a way to spend time either by yourself or in a group to to work toward a common goal - perfection. There are some times I wish I had an undo button, but most of my game play was fun, interactive, and allowed me to feel like I was part of something unique and special.

Stardew Valley isn’t just a game I played — it’s a place I lived in for a while. A place I came back to when life felt overwhelming, when I needed a break, or when I just wanted to remember that slow, quiet progress still counts. On the surface, it’s a farming sim. But underneath, it’s about connection — to land, to people, to yourself. There’s a stillness to it, a sense of rhythm, like exhaling after holding your breath too long.

It’s hard to describe how powerful that first spring feels. Clearing out your tiny patch of land, planting seeds, waiting. And then — one morning — something grows. Not much, just a few sprouts. But it’s enough. Enough to make you want to keep going. The relationships, the small town rituals, the changing seasons — it all unfolds at its own pace, and Stardew never rushes you. It trusts you to find your own way, and that’s rare. There's a kindness in its design that makes it feel more like coming home than completing objectives.

I think the reason Stardew Valley means so much to me is that it showed me progress doesn’t have to be loud or flashy. You can build something beautiful out of small routines, slow days, and a lot of patience. It reminded me to appreciate little victories — a good harvest, a rainy day, a new heart in someone’s dialogue. I didn’t just escape into Stardew — I learned from it. And for a game made by one person with a dream, that’s one hell of a legacy.

Stardew Valley is a farming sim game.

After 275 hours in game, and ending at Day 15 of Spring, Year 6. The summit was reached and the last achievement had been earned. I have to admit, despite how difficult it was to get to this point I still had a great time!
Before I continue, I wanted to mention too that for my first play-though, I did play it without mods because i wanted to get the full vanilla experience. 

To kind of keep things from being cluttered. I did my best to separate things into sections to help with the reading and writing of this review. Thank you for your time!

[b]Farming[/b]: The bread and butter of the whole game of course! Plant crops, raise farm animals, make a tree farm, have fish ponds, or turn your entire farm into a keg factory. The farm is your canvas! Anyways, there is a a lot to talk about with the farming aspect of this game so I'll do my best not to ramble. To begin, there are a ton of crops to plant, grow, and sell with each having their own times and seasons to be planted and harvested. Don't like crops? Well once you get enough money and resources for a barn you can try your hand at raising farm animals. Won't be much to do at first since you will have to wait till they grow to maturity, but once the wait is over you can get a decent amount of eggs, milk, and other stuff over time. Caught a fish you really like, but don't wanna sell them? Use them in a fish pond and they will give you resources to help make you some money over time. The creativity on the farm is all up to you, design it how you like and enjoy the process. One more thing to mention too, at the start of the game there is also a choice of the farm you'd like to work with, and it comes with a small selection of farms to choose from; examples are: Beach farm or Forest farm.

[b]Fishing[/b]: I won't lie, I spent so much time just fishing, this was one of my favorite parts of the whole game. You have such wide variety of fish to catch from in this game, some being very unique to this game, while some others are based on real life fish (like the Tuna).  The fishing mini-game is pretty straightforward and is fairly easy once you get the hang of it, although it can be a bit tricky at times depending on the fish, however it's not terrible since there are baits and tackles that can assist when it comes to catching the more difficult ones. Another thing to bring up on fishing, each fish has its own requirements when it comes to catching them and those can vary depending on what you're after; examples to this are: Locations, seasons, weather conditions (such as; only spawning on rainy days), Specific times, Certain fishing rod, and the level of your fishing mastery if you are aiming for the Legendary Fish. 

[b]Mining[/b]: to be honest, I didn't spend too much time in this area after I maxed out the stat. At the beginning, it really takes the energy (literally) out of you since you just have a pickaxe and nothing else. As you level up your mining mastery, do you then get introduced to better equipment; such as bombs. However, after that it really just becomes a speed run through the mines to collect the necessary ore and get out. With all that being said though, even though I didn't do too much with the mining, I did like all the special gems and minerals the game had you hunting down for the museum collection.

[b]Combat[/b]: It plays well with the mining side of things. While you traverse the mines in search for minerals and stones (Rock and Stone!) you will have a lot of monsters trying to prevent you from leaving unscathed. The monsters; from Slimes and bugs to Mummies, ghosts, skeletons, there is a wide variety to fight through. You will never get can get enough on the combat. I will admit however, it does start off slow. You will be putting in a lot of effort to take down monsters with the first sword you come across, and only after a bit of grinding, luck, finding equipment, or buying better equipment from the Guild hall will the journey of combat be easier. With that being said, lets talk about the weapons briefly. There are swords, daggers, and hammers. Each come in varying levels, special abilities (like Vampirism), and attributes that can either hinder or help you in the mines or caverns. During my run, I mostly found a lot of the gear in combat or mining around so it won't be to difficult to find this stuff. In addition to all of this, there will come a point in the game where you will be introduced to a forge that can give you quite the upgrade on your gear and it saves the pain of having to get newer gear if you really like a specific weapon like I did.

[b]Foraging[/b]: There's not much to say about this one honestly. Lots of berries, veggies, mushrooms, and occasional flowers that can be found all over the valley that can help you get a little more coin in your pocket at the end of the day. Granted some of those foragables can be used in certain cooking recipes, or given to people as gifts, and can even be eaten to give you a quick energy pick me up if you forget to come prepared like I always did. There is also a few crafting recipes that come along as you level up the stat so that is a plus.

As the days go by on the farm, there will be a few special events to look out for that will take place throughout the seasons. These Seasonal events bring a different pace to the game, being more of side mission or a time of relaxation. Play some minigames (depending on the event), or take the chance to talk to all the towns folk you been avoiding this whole time, even partake in the shop that have a chance to sell some useful items. It really does bring some charm to this game. 

Now let's talk about the towns people. There's a lot of people to talk to in Pelican Town. Each with personalities and characteristics that make them so unique. Talk to them, give them gifts, and form friendships with them. After some time while forming those friendships, unique dialogue and cutscenes will occur depending how far along you are with the person (Not everyone has this though). The game does also let you marry someone from a small cast of characters who are considered bachelors or bachelorettes, so you could also take the relationship further and then eventually raise your own family if you wanted to.

The story in this game was really good. I really enjoyed it. Nothing crazy or intense, just a simple and effective story. Granted getting to that ending was a challenge in itself, but still worth seeing it to the end.

Finally, the last thing i wanted to bring up; True Perfection. I won't lie... it's rough. Without a good strategy in mind to tackle this challenge, it really becomes a grind to try and reach that 100%. What starts off as a fun, enjoyable, and relaxing time, can slowly become a feeling of madness and then eventual insanity just to reach that full Perfection. Luckily, the game does give you some helpful features to make the progression to perfection a little more bearable: by giving a progression tracker and an additional method (I won't spoil) to help speed things up a tiny bit.

Highly recommend to anyone—but especially if you’ve got a partner who enjoys games. It’s wholesome, rewarding, and endlessly charming.

You´re not forced to quickly make progress tho, since it´s up to you if you want to continue with the story asap or if you just want to relax and go mining/fishing/farming,etc. Later on though, there´s a variety of things you can do. A lot of easter eggs and other stuff can also be found during exploration. 
Only being able to grow the crops in certain seasons and the difference in time it takes for them to grow is both exciting (looking forward to being able to grow certain crops again) and challenging (since you need to watch out for how much time of the season you have left to grow the crops, otherwise they will wilt).
The design of the game is very cute and the sounds and music also add on to the game´s atmosphere. The characters and the story are also very well written. The option of being able to grow close with the village ppl and also marry them is also smth you can grind on, since it takes some time to actually increase the amount of hearts you have with them. 
There´ are also conditions for some items as to how to obtain them, for example the only way to get the "prismatic jelly" is when a specific quest is active).
Since there´s a lot of content, it´s smth you can spend a lot of time on and won´t need to worry abt the game being over/finished too soon. 
Overall, it´s a super relaxing and addicting farm-game and I would def recommend this!!! 😼
